F92.1.p: A person visits the lower world by going down a hole made when clumps of grass are pulled up from the ground.

F92.2.p: A person is swallowed up by the earth and carried off to the lower world.

F92.2.1.p: A girl who is picking flowers is swallowed up by the earth and taken to the lower world.

F92.3.p: A person visits the lower world through rocks that open when a charm is spoken.

F92.4.r: Patch PMLA XXXIII 614 n. 48.—Irish myth: Cross; Babylonian: Gilgamesch-Epos IX; Chinese: Graham.
F92.4.p: The entrance to the lower world is through a mountain.

F92.5.p: The entrance to the lower world is a hole that someone makes in the ground.

F92.6.p: The entrance to the lower world is a cave.

F92.7.p: A hole in the ground leads down to an underworld kingdom ruled by snakes.

F93.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
F93.p: The entrance to the lower world is through water.

F93.0.1.p: A boat carries a person across the water to the lower world.

F93.0.1.1.r: Feilberg Sjæletro 65ff.; Frobenius Erlebte Erdteile VI 278f.—Icelandic: Boberg; Greek: Fox 142.
F93.0.1.1.p: A ferryman takes people by boat to the lower world.

F93.0.2.p: The entrance to the lower world is under water.

F93.0.2.1.p: The entrance to the lower world is a well.

F93.1.r: Wimberly 108ff.; Kruyt Het Animisme 357ff., Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 1157, IV 196; Frobenius Erdteile III 69, 73, 76.—Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 103, MacCulloch Eddic 320, Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 16; Greek: Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Acheron” I 9; Egyptian: Müller 176; Aztec: Krickeberg Märchen der Azteken 146, 215.
F93.1.p: The entrance to the lower world is a river.

F93.1.1.p: A net is stretched across a river to keep a living man from returning to the earth from the land of the dead.

F93.2.p: The entrance to the lower world is a lake.

F94.p: A stairway leads down to the lower world.

F95.p: A path leads to the lower world.

F95.0.1.p: A path leads to the world of the dead.

F95.1.p: A path runs from a grave down to the lower world.

F95.2.p: A wide, easy road is the way down to hell. The path to the underworld is described as broad and simple to follow.

F95.3.p: The path down to hell is dangerous and hard to travel. Reaching the underworld means crossing a perilous route.

F95.4.p: The way to the underworld is marked by knots tied in grass by spirits. Travelers find their route by following these knotted tufts.

F95.5.p: A tree serves as the road down to the underworld. A traveler descends into the lower world by way of the tree.

F96.p: A rope is used to descend into the lower world. The traveler goes down to the underworld by climbing or lowering along a rope.

F98.p: A traveler goes down into the lower world riding an animal. The descent to the underworld is made on the back of a creature.

F98.1.p: A traveler goes down to the underworld riding on a tiger.

F100.p: A general heading for various motifs about visits to the lower world (the underworld or hell) that do not fit the more specific groups. It covers miscellaneous episodes of such visits.

F101.p: A general heading for ways a person gets back up from the lower world after visiting it. It covers the various means of returning to the living world.

F101.1.p: The visitor climbs back up out of the lower world by a steep slope. The return is made by going up a steep incline.

F101.2.p: The visitor is flung back up to the living world by a bent tree. The tree is bent down and released so that it hurls the person upward.

F101.3.r: *Type 301; *BP II 300; Penzer VI 122 n. 2. See references under B322.1, nearly all of which refer to escape from lower world. Indonesia: De Vries Volksverhalen I 161ff. No. 35.
F101.3.p: The visitor flies back up from the lower world riding an eagle. The eagle carries the person out of the underworld.

F101.3.1.p: The visitor returns from the lower world riding a vulture. This is a variant of the eagle escape, with a vulture as the carrier.

F101.4.p: The visitor escapes from the lower world by means of magic. A magical act or charm allows the person to get out.

F101.5.p: The visitor escapes from the lower world on a tree that grows miraculously. The tree rises quickly, carrying the person up to the living world.

F101.6.p: The visitor rides an animal up out of the lower world. An animal carries the person back to the living world.

F101.6.1.p: The visitor escapes from the lower world on a bird. A bird carries the person up out of the underworld.

F101.6.2.p: The visitor escapes from the lower world on a horse made of lightning. The magical horse carries the person up out of the underworld.

F101.7.p: The visitor escapes from the lower world by climbing a spider's thread. The spider's silk is the means of getting back up to the living world.

F101.8.p: A man who returns from hell brings heat back with him. The returning visitor carries warmth from the underworld into the living world.

F102.p: A person arrives in the lower world by accident rather than on purpose. The visit to the underworld happens unintentionally.

F102.1.r: *Type 301; *Krappe Balor 100 nn. 22, 23; *De Vries Nederlandsche Tijdschrift voor Volkskunde (1924) 97—123.—Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 163, Dixon 213 n. 12; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 99.
F102.1.p: A hero shoots an animal or monster, follows it, and accidentally ends up in the underworld.

F102.2.p: A hero follows the sound of a drum and arrives by accident in a town of ghosts.

F102.3.p: A rescued princess drops her necklace while escaping; the hero goes back for it and is trapped in the underworld.

F102.4.p: A boy chases a nut that rolls away and follows it down into the underworld.

F105.r: (Cf. F93.1.1.) Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 596—97, 602, MacCulloch Eddic 321, Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 16.
F105.p: The dead resist and oppose a living person's attempt to bring someone back from the land of the dead.

F106.p: Young people are made to grind grain in a mill operated by the inhabitants of the underworld.

F107.p: Young people are taught smithing by Vulcan, the blacksmith of Hell.

F108.p: Describes what the inhabitants of the underworld are like.

F108.1.p: The people of the lower world are as tall as a broom is long, i.e. very small.

F108.2.p: The people of the lower world come out in the evenings to drink and dance.

F109.p: Additional miscellaneous details about a visit to the lower world.

F109.1.p: The visitor enters the lower world head first.

F109.2.p: A fish shows Jonah a view of hell.

F110.r: *Graf Miti, leggendi e superstizioni de medio evo I 1ff.; Gaster Oldest Stories 51, 168.—Irish myth: *Cross.
F110.p: Journeys to otherworlds that lie on earth rather than under it or in the sky.

F110.1.r: **Jacobs Book of Wonder Voyages; *Chauvin VII 77ff.; Ward II 516ff.; Krappe Philological Quarterly XXIII (1944) 97—107.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Japanese: Anesaki 363; Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 183; Africa (Benga): Nassau 208 No. 33.
F110.1.p: Voyages made to wondrous otherworld places, full of marvels.

F111.r: Land of happiness. (Cf. F132.1.) **Nutt in Meyer Voyage of Bran I 105ff.; Patch *Other World 381 s.v. “paradise”; *Graf La leggenda del paradiso terrestre (Torino, 1878); *BP IV 269 n. 1; Gaster Oldest Stories 48; Norlind Skattsägner 88ff.; Hartland Science 194, 199, 202; *Loomis White Magic 116.—Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 145 (Parthenope of Blois); *Celtic: K. Zimmer Brendans Meerfahrt (Zeitschrift für deutsche Altertum XXXIII [1889] 129—220, 257—338); Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; Hindu: Tawney I 525; Chinese: Giles 8ff., 397ff.
F111.p: A journey to a paradise on earth, a place of perfect happiness hidden from ordinary people.

F111.0.2.p: A swineherd searching for a lost sow finds an earthly paradise by chance.

F111.1.p: A journey to an island where people laugh constantly, a land of endless mirth.

F111.2.p: A voyage to a promised land, a place of hoped-for happiness across the sea.

F111.2.1.p: A mythical island called Tir Tairngire, the Land of Promise, cannot be reached by a boat made of soft animal skins.

F111.3.p: A voyage to a land whose inhabitants eat lotus, a fruit that makes people forget home and want to stay.

F111.4.p: Paradise of the Blessed, a happy otherworld located underground.

F111.5.p: A land where all creatures, including animals, get along peacefully with one another.

F111.6.r: S. A. Indian (Guaraní): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 94.
F111.6.p: A voyage to a land where there is no evil or wrongdoing.

F112.r: *Patch PMLA XXXIII 624 n. 81, Other World *381 s.v. “maidenland”; Hartland Science 202.—Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Fox 109, 111; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 390f.; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth XXXVI; Marquesas: Handy 56, Beckwith Myth 472, 502; West Indies: Flowers 432.
F112.p: A journey to an island or country inhabited only by women, such as an island of maidens or a land of Amazons.

F112.0.1.p: Fairyland, identified with Ireland, is settled only by women.

F112.0.1.1.p: A journey to an island where only one beautiful woman lives.

F112.0.2.p: In the otherworld, men and women live separately from each other.

F112.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Oceanic: Dixon 66, 140, 141 n. 22; N. A. Indian (Assiniboin): Lowie PaAM IV 106 No. 6, (Cree): Skinner PaAM IX 87.
F112.1.p: A man visiting the Island of Fair Women is overpowered by the women's love and cannot leave easily.

F112.2.p: A city inhabited entirely by women.

F113.p: A journey to a land inhabited only by men.

F114.p: A journey that goes inside the earth, down into a world beneath the ground.

F115.r: Zemmrich Internationales Archiv für Ethnologie IV 231. Cf. Maeterlinck’s “L’Oiseau Bleue”.
F115.p: A journey to the Land of the Unborn, a realm where souls not yet born dwell.

F116.p: A journey to the Land of the Immortals, where beings who never die live.

F116.1.p: A voyage to the Land of Youth, a place where people stay young and do not age.

F117.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 334 n. 206, (Cherokee): Alexander N. Am. 69; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 202, 359.
F117.p: A journey to the Land of the Thunders, the realm of thunder.

F118.p: A journey to the Mother of Time, a figure who personifies time itself.

F121.p: A journey to the world of spirits, the realm where spirits and the dead dwell.

F122.r: Irish myth: Cross (F129.10); Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 17; India: Thompson-Balys.
F122.p: A journey to a land where giants live.

F123.r: Irish myth: Cross; Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 17.
F123.p: A hero travels to a land inhabited by very small people, the pygmies.

F124.p: A hero travels to a land inhabited by demons.

F125.r: Jewish: *Neuman; American Indian: Thompson Tales 349 n. 256; Africa: Werner African 204.
F125.p: A traveler journeys to an otherworld where people are healed or made whole, so anyone who arrives is cured.

F126.p: A journey to a land with no sky that takes a whole lifetime to reach.

F127.r: Usually underground. India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Eskimo (Mackenzie area): Jenness 154; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 348 nn. 252, 253.
F127.p: A journey to a realm ruled by animals rather than people.

F127.1.p: A journey to a kingdom of serpents.

F127.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 390.
F127.1.1.p: A hero finds a palace under the water at the bottom of a lake, where the king of the serpents lives.

F127.2.p: A journey to a land ruled by elephants.

F127.3.p: A journey to a land inhabited by crocodiles.

F129.p: A collection of other miscellaneous strange lands that travelers visit.

F129.1.p: A journey to a land whose inhabitants are men with only heads and no bodies.

F129.2.p: A voyage to the land of the Mossynoikoi, a people from classical geography and legend.

F129.3.r: People who dwell amid clouds of gloom and never see sun. Greek: Fox 145.
F129.3.p: A voyage to the land of the Cimmerians, a people said to live in perpetual darkness.

F129.4.p: A journey to an island in the otherworld.

F129.4.1.p: A voyage to an island where everyone weeps.

F129.4.2.p: A voyage to an island where no one can lie; people there cannot tell falsehoods.

F129.4.3.p: A voyage to an island where visitors are transformed into beautiful people.

F129.4.4.p: A voyage to an island of the dead, where anyone who falls asleep dies.

F129.4.5.p: A voyage to an island shrouded in permanent darkness.

F129.4.6.p: A voyage to an island where there is no sound at all.

F129.5.p: A journey to a land from which no one ever returns. The traveler goes there knowing they will not come back.

F129.5.1.p: A hero rides a mare toward the land of no return. The mare has just given birth, and her worry for her foal makes her carry him back home.

F129.6.p: A land in which everyone is wise, from the king on his throne down to the beggar in the market.

F129.7.p: A journey to a land where all the people go naked.

F130.p: Where the otherworld is located, meaning the place a tale says the otherworld lies.

F130.1.p: A real land, India (or Greece in some versions), is said to be the otherworld.

F130.2.p: Spain is said to be the otherworld.

F130.3.p: Ancient Ireland is said to be the location of the otherworld.

F131.r: *Patch PMLA XXXIII 612f., Other World *381 s.v. “Mountain”; Wimberly 130.—Irish myth: *Cross; German: Grimm No. 127; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3594.
F131.p: The otherworld is inside a hollow mountain.

F131.1.r: **Barto Tannhäuser and the Mountain of Venus; *Patch PMLA XXXIII 612f.; *Meyer Zs. f. Vksk. XXI 1ff.; Bockel Alemannia XIII (1885) 142; *Norlind Skattsägner 88ff.—Icelandic: Boberg.
F131.1.p: A hollow mountain otherworld where men live in ease and pleasure with beautiful women, given over to lust and enjoyment.

F131.1.1.p: A mountain otherworld whose inhabitants are fair-haired women.

F132.r: *Patch PMLA XXXIII 606ff., Other World *381 s.v. “mountain, on the”; Wimberly 132.
F132.p: The otherworld is on a high mountain top.

F132.0.1.p: The otherworld can be seen from a high mountain, though it is not reached by climbing there.

F132.1.p: An earthly paradise is located on a mountain.

F132.1.1.p: The earthly paradise floats in the air above a mountain.

F132.2.p: The dwelling of Fortune, the goddess of luck, is on a high mountain.

F133.r: Patch PMLA XXXIII 627 n. 92, Other World *380 s.v. “Land-beneath-the-waves”; Wimberly 134; Ward II 525; Chauvin V 151 No. 73; Penzer VI 280; Smith Dragon 109.—Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Campbell Tales III 420; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 112f.; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 636; Breton: *Le Braz Légende de la Mort II 37ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Slavic: Máchal 270; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 69; Maori: Clark III; N. A. Indian (Klikitat): Jacobs U Wash II 7; Africa: Werner African 188, 206, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 39 No. 4, (Basuto): Jacottet 122 No. 17, 204 No. 30, 224 No. 33.
F133.p: The otherworld lies under the sea.

F133.1.r: *Chauvin VII 54 No. 241 B n. 1.—Irish myth: *Cross; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 636.
F133.1.p: The undersea world is a mirror of the land: everything on earth has a counterpart in the sea.

F133.2.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 81.
F133.2.p: An underwater house that stands empty with no one living in it.

F133.3.p: An underwater monastery, a religious house beneath the sea.

F133.4.p: The otherworld of the dead or the supernatural is reached by going beneath a pond, and its entrance is into the water's depths.

F133.5.p: The otherworld is located at the bottom of a well, so travelers descend into the well to enter it.

F134.r: *Patch PMLA XXXIII 628f. nn. 93—96, Other World 379 s.v. “island”.—Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 55, Beal XXI 321; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 72, 79; Samoa, Fiji: ibid. 76.
F134.p: The otherworld is located on an island.

F134.0.1.p: The otherworld consists of a succession of islands, one after another.

F134.1.p: The Hebrides or the Isle of Man (called Falga) is regarded as the otherworld.

F134.2.p: The otherworld island vanishes, leaving the voyagers stranded in their boat on the open sea.

F134.3.p: The otherworld island is split into four separate parts.

F134.4.p: Divine swans live on an island that cannot be reached, lying in the middle of seven seas.

F135.p: The otherworld is a banqueting hall, a feasting house where the supernatural dwell.

F136.p: Tales state the direction in which the otherworld lies from the traveler's world.

F136.1.p: The otherworld lies to the east.

F136.2.p: The otherworld lies to the west.

F136.3.p: The otherworld lies to the northwest.

F137.p: Tales state how far away the otherworld is from the traveler's world.

F140.p: Tales describe the limits or boundaries that separate the otherworld from the ordinary world.

F140.1.p: A guardian stands at the boundary of the spirit land and watches over the crossing.

F141.p: A body of water forms the barrier that must be crossed to reach the otherworld.

F141.0.1.p: A traveler mistakes an otherworld beyond water for one located under water.

F141.0.2.p: A traveler mistakes an otherworld beyond water for one located under a hill.

F141.1.p: A river forms the barrier that must be crossed to reach the otherworld.

F141.1.1.r: (Cf. F767.1.) *Patch PMLA XXXIII 630, 638ff.; Alphabet No. 603.—Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 78, III 165; N. A. Indian: Thompson Tales 140; Africa (Yoruba): Ellis 245 No. 1.
F141.1.1.p: A dangerous river forms the boundary that separates the ordinary world from the otherworld.

F141.1.2.p: A river that living humans cannot cross stands between them and the otherworld.

F141.1.3.p: The river dividing the realms of giants and gods is so warm or fast-flowing that it never freezes over.

F141.2.p: A mist or fog serves as a barrier that keeps people from reaching the otherworld.

F141.2.1.p: A storm, snow, or hail serves as a barrier that keeps people from reaching the otherworld.

F141.3.p: Waves rise up to form a high wall encircling an island that is the otherworld.

F141.4.p: A waterfall serves as a barrier that blocks the way to the otherworld.

F142.r: (Cf. A671.2.2.3.) Patch PMLA XXXIII 638f.; Krappe Archiv für das Studium der neueren Sprachen (1937) 172ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
F142.p: A river of fire forms the boundary that keeps people out of the otherworld.

F143.r: *Siuts 30ff.; MLN XXXIV 321; Irish: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Africa (Yoruba): Ellis 245 No. 1.
F143.p: A forest grows along the edges of the otherworld and forms its border.

F144.p: An open plain or field lies at the edge of the otherworld and forms its border.

F144.1.p: On the way to the otherworld, travelers must pass through a forked valley full of toads and must face lions.

F145.r: *Siuts 42ff.; Patch Other World 381 s.v. “mountain”; Gaster Thespis 184f.; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
F145.p: A mountain lies at the edge of the otherworld and forms its border.

F145.1.r: *Siuts 43; Patch PMLA XXXIII 610 n. 30, Other World 381 s.v. “mountain.”
F145.1.p: A glass mountain stands at the border of the otherworld; it is extremely slippery, so climbing it is nearly impossible.

F147.p: Houses stand at the border of the otherworld.

F147.1.p: Empty houses with no inhabitants stand at the border of the otherworld.

F147.2.p: A hermit's hut stands at the border of the otherworld.

F147.3.p: A witch's house stands at the border of the otherworld.

F147.4.p: An inn stands at the border of the otherworld where travelers can stop.

F148.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 209a s.v. “Baum bewacht”; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
F148.p: A wall surrounds the otherworld and keeps outsiders from entering.

F148.1.p: A fiery rampart encircles an island that is the otherworld, and it turns round and round.

F148.2.p: The otherworld, a realm of marvels beyond ordinary life, is enclosed by a wall made of silver.

F148.3.p: The otherworld is surrounded by a fence or palisade made of gold and silver.

F148.4.p: The otherworld is surrounded by a palisade made of bronze.

F148.5.p: The otherworld is enclosed by seven walls, with locked iron doors and iron bars.

F149.p: Miscellaneous motifs about the boundaries that separate the otherworld from the ordinary world.

F149.1.r: (Cf. F150.3.2.) Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 95, III 165, Rink 461.
F149.1.p: The otherworld is cut off from the ordinary world by a barrier of stone.

F150.p: Miscellaneous ways of getting into the otherworld, the realm of marvels beyond ordinary life.

F150.1.r: Siuts 29; English: Gawain and the Green Knight; Chinese: Graham.
F150.1.p: The way into the otherworld is difficult to locate or find.

F150.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Babylonian: Spence 171; Jewish: *Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 47, 74, 80, Rasmussen I 81.
F150.2.p: The entrance to the otherworld is guarded by monsters or animals that stop intruders.

F150.2.1.p: The entrance to the otherworld is guarded by a giant or a champion.

F150.2.2.p: The entrance to the otherworld is guarded by spirits.

F150.2.3.p: The entrance to the otherworld is guarded by the north wind and the south wind.

F150.3.p: The adventurer must meet a challenge at the entrance of the otherworld, either by issuing one or by answering one.

F150.3.1.p: A shield hangs on a pole before the otherworld palace; when the adventurer sees it, he must fight its owner.

F150.3.2.p: A standing stone surrounded by a withe (a flexible twig binding) serves as a challenge at the entrance of the otherworld.

F151.p: Miscellaneous motifs about the road that leads to the otherworld.

F151.0.1.p: A kind host along the road to the otherworld feeds, entertains, guides, or advises the adventurer.

F151.1.r: Patch Other World 382 s.v. “path”; Irish myth: *Cross; N. A. Indian: Alexander N. Am. 147, 164, 273 n. 8, (California): Gayton and Newman 101; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 78, (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 586.
F151.1.p: The path to the otherworld is dangerous and full of hazards.

F151.1.1.p: The route to the otherworld passes through a perilous valley.

F151.1.2.p: The route to the otherworld passes through a perilous glen (narrow valley).

F151.1.3.p: The route to the otherworld passes through a dangerous forest that the traveler must survive.

F151.1.4.p: The route to the otherworld requires crossing a dangerous ford, a shallow place where a river can be waded.

F151.1.5.p: Somewhere in the underworld there is a boundary that the hero cannot pass without being tattooed.

F151.1.6.p: The path to the otherworld runs over sharp, jagged rocks that cut or hurt the traveler.

F151.2.p: The way to the otherworld goes through a mountain pass.

F152.r: *Type 471; Encyc. Rel. Ethics II 852ff.; Patch PMLA XXXIII 630ff., Other World 374 s.v. “bridge”; Ward II 399, 441; Róheim Animism 39ff.; Fb “bro” IV 62b; Darmesteter Sacred Books of the East IV 212f.; Alphabet No. 603.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 130, 305; Siberian: Holmberg Siberian 488ff.; Melanesia: Codrington 257; Eskimo (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 153; N. A. Indian: Brinton Myths of the New World (New York, 1868) 248, (Menomini): Skinner PaAM XIII 86.
F152.p: A bridge gives access to the otherworld, and the hero must cross it to get there.

F152.0.1.p: The bridge to the otherworld is guarded by animals that the traveler must get past.

F152.1.p: This heading covers the materials from which a bridge to the otherworld is made.

F152.1.1.r: Fb “regnbue” III 32a; RTP VI 361, X 596; Mélusine II 16; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 329; Celebes: Dixon 156; Hawaii, Indonesia: ibid. 67, Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 38, 321; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 333 n. 204a.
F152.1.1.p: The bridge to the otherworld is a rainbow.

F152.1.2.p: The bridge to the otherworld is made of sunbeams.

F152.1.3.r: Patch PMLA XXXIII 639 n. 130, Other World 374 s.v. “bridge.”
F152.1.3.p: The bridge to the otherworld is made of gold.

F152.1.4.r: Patch PMLA XXXIII 636 n. 118, Other World 125f.; Irish myth: *Cross.
F152.1.4.p: The bridge to the otherworld is made of glass.

F152.1.5.p: The bridge to the otherworld is made of rope.

F152.1.6.r: Hibbard Romanic Review IX (1913) 166; Patch PMLA XXXIII 635ff., Other World 374 s.v. “bridge”; Irish myth: *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 197.
F152.1.6.p: The bridge to the otherworld is a sword laid across a gap, so crossing it is dangerous.

F152.1.6.1.r: BP III 43; Von Hegelein Zs. f. Vksk. XI 150 n. 2.
F152.1.6.1.p: The sword bridge to the otherworld is covered with knives, so crossing it cuts the traveler.

F152.1.7.p: On the way to the world of the dead there is a bridge made of thread, which is fragile to cross.

F152.1.8.p: The northern lights (aurora) serve as a bridge to the otherworld.

F152.2.p: A drawbridge to the otherworld slams shut behind the hero as he leaves, nearly injuring him, because he has failed to do the one thing required of him.

F153.r: *Brown Iwain 76; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 148; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G 3/1301).
F153.p: The otherworld is reached by diving into water, such as a well or a lake.

F235.p: Fairies can be seen or not seen by humans, and their visibility varies in the various stories told about them.

F235.1.r: Tobler 94f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “invisibilité”; India: Thompson-Balys.
F235.1.p: Fairies are normally invisible to human eyes and cannot be seen by ordinary people.

F235.2.p: Fairies can be seen only at certain times of day or night and are hidden at other times.

F235.2.1.p: Fairies can be seen only at night and are invisible during the day.

F235.2.2.p: Fairies can be seen only at noon, when the sun is at its highest.

F235.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; English: Sir Launfal (Ritson ed.) line 501.
F235.3.p: Fairies can be seen by only one particular person, while others cannot see them.

F235.4.p: A magic object is used to make fairies visible to a person who could not otherwise see them.

F235.4.1.r: (Cf. E361.3.) *Fb “salve” III 150b; *Hartland Science 59—67; English: Child I 339, II 505b, III 505b, V290a; England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, U.S.: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 449.

F235.4.6.p: Carrying a four-leaf clover makes fairies visible to the carrier.

F235.5.2.p: Fairies become visible when a person steps into a fairy ring, a circle of mushrooms or grass where fairies dance.

F235.6.p: Wearing a magic ring makes fairies visible.

F235.7.p: Fairies appear to humans only as dark shadows rather than as clear figures.

F271.0.2.p: Fairies who have no axes do their woodwork using their teeth instead.

F271.1.p: Fairies milk cows, doing the dairy chore for humans or for themselves.

F271.2.p: Fairies work as builders, constructing buildings, roads or other structures.

F271.9.p: Fairies wash clothes, and people only ever hear them when they are doing this laundry.

F301.1.p: A mortal calls a fairy lover to come to them, usually by some action.

F301.2.1.p: An elf-knight blows a horn that fills the listener with longing for him.

F301.3.p: A girl goes to fairyland and marries a fairy there.

F301.6.p: A fairy lover carries off the fairy wife of a mortal man.

F330.p: Fairies who repay kindness shown to them by people with help or favors.

F331.p: A mortal earns the gratitude of fairies by joining in their games or sports.

F331.1.r: *Type 503; BP III 324ff.; England, Scotland, Wales: *Baughman (F379.5.); Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bossu”; Japanese: Mitford 191, Ikeda.
F331.1.p: A mortal earns fairy gratitude by joining in their dance.

F331.2.p: A mortal earns fairy gratitude by letting the fairies cut his hair and shave him.

F331.3.p: A mortal earns fairy gratitude by joining in the fairies' song and finishing it by adding the names of the days of the week.

F331.4.p: A mortal earns fairy gratitude by playing music for the fairies' dance.

F332.r: England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales: *Baughman; Scotch: Campbell Tales II 51, Macdougall and Calder 215, 217.
F332.p: A fairy shows gratitude to a person who has given it hospitality.

F332.0.1.p: A fairy shows gratitude to a human for supplying its daily food.

F333.r: (Cf. F372.1.) Hartland Science 55f.; Scotland, Ireland, Wales: *Baughman.
F333.p: A fairy shows gratitude to a human midwife who helped at its birth.

F334.p: A fairy shows gratitude to a human who healed it.

F335.p: A grateful fairy repays a mortal who has lent it something.

F335.1.p: A fairy is grateful for a loan of meal, and afterward the mortal's vessel always stays full.

F336.p: Fairies remain loyal to a mortal who owns the hill or knoll where they live.

F337.p: A fairy shows gratitude to a mortal who saved its life.

F337.1.p: A fairy is grateful to a mortal who saved the life of the fairy's child.

F338.p: Fairies are grateful to a man who repairs their tools or household utensils.

F339.p: Other tales of fairies who reward mortals out of gratitude for various kindnesses.

F339.1.p: A fairy who is carried on a man's back repays him by warning that his cow is choking.

F339.2.p: Fairies tend a tulip bed out of gratitude to an owner who did not pick any of its blossoms.

F339.3.p: A fairy is grateful to a mortal family for returning a lost fairy child.

F339.3.1.p: Fairies do all the housework and farm work for a family that returned their lost child.

F339.3.2.p: Fairies make all the ewes of a man who returned their child bear twin lambs.

F340.r: Type 503; BP III 324; Hdwb. d. Märch. s.v. “Elbengeschenke”, “Geschenke des kleinen Volkes”; Irish myth: *Cross; French: Saintyves Perrault 72ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction; India: Thompson-Balys.

F340.1.p: Fairies who are leaving after a birth give gifts to the newborn princess.

F341.r: Hartland Science 55; Scotch: Campbell Tales II 51; English: Wells 32 (Layamon’s Brut); Wales: Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
F341.p: Fairies grant a mortal the fulfillment of wishes.

F341.1.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “dons”. Rotunda: Italian Novella.
F341.1.p: Fairies give a mortal three gifts.

F341.2.p: A captured fairy buys her freedom by granting a wish.

F341.2.1.p: A water fairy who has been captured promises to make an ugly man handsome in exchange for being set free.

F342.r: Hartland Science 39, 53, 56; Irish myth: Cross; English: Wells (Sir Launfal); Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bourse”; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3594.

F342.1.r: *Type 503; BP I 366, III 324ff.; Hartland Science 57; Fb “kul” II 326b, “guld” I 512, “hövlspån” I 762, “jord” II 45b.—England: Baughman; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 308 No. 2; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 47 No. 388; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 434, Index No. *771, 3648; India: *Thompson-Balys.
F342.1.p: Fairies give coals, wood, or earth that turn into gold.

F342.2.r: German, Swedish, Finnish-Swedish, Estonian, Livonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Ukrainian, Kashubish, and Wendish: Balys Tautosakos Darbai VI 163—195.
F342.2.p: A man borrows money from a fairy, dwarf, or devil. When he returns it, he finds the lender has been killed by thunder, so he simply keeps the money.

F343.p: A general heading for other kinds of gifts that fairies give to humans.

F343.0.1.p: A fairy lets a mortal pick one magic object from several offered.

F343.1.p: Fairies give a woman silver spoons.

F343.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 285ff.
F343.2.p: Fairies give a hunter a dog.

F343.2.1.p: Dogs given to people as gifts from fairies.

F343.3.r: English: Wells 32 (Layamon’s Brut); Scotch: Campbell Tales III 122.
F343.3.p: A fairy smith gives a knight a magic sword.

F343.4.p: Fairies give a greedy man a gift that makes him generous.

F343.5.r: Irish myth: Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 10.

F343.5.1.p: A fairy gives a magic cloak, sometimes with a shirt.

F343.6.p: A bonga, a supernatural being, lends dishes to humans.

F343.7.p: A fairy wife provides food and supplies for her human husband's household.

F343.8.p: A fairy leaves goats as payment for a girl he has carried off.

F343.9.p: A fairy gives a man horses, cattle, and other livestock.

F343.10.p: A fairy gives a warrior equipment for his soldiers.

F343.10.1.p: A fairy gives a person a magic sword.

F343.10.2.p: A fairy gives a person a magic spear.

F343.10.3.p: A fairy gives a person a shield that cannot be harmed.

F343.11.p: A fairy offers a man the power to change his form and appearance in return for help in battle.

F343.12.p: A fairy who is thanked for a kindness gives the mortal a ring as a reward.

F343.13.p: A fairy gives a human couple a child.

F343.14.p: Otherworld beings give a mortal a golden cup, bowl, or urn as a gift.

F343.15.p: Fairies give a mortal a magic apple as a gift.

F343.16.p: Fairies give a mortal a huge ox rib as a gift.

F343.16.1.p: Fairies give a mortal a huge hog rib as a gift, a variant of the ox rib gift.

F343.17.p: Fairies feed haymakers a dinner each year until one man keeps a fairy knife. After that they give no more food, even when the man returns the knife.

F343.18.p: Fairies find and return a hatchet head that was lost in a river.

F343.19.p: Fairies give mortals a special bread called fairy bread.

F343.19.1.p: Fairy bread must be eaten on the day it is given, or it turns into toadstools.

F343.20.p: Fairies give a mortal a sack of coals as a gift.

F344.p: Fairies heal human beings who are sick or injured.

F344.1.r: *Type 503; BP III 324ff.; RTP I 129, 186, III 582, V 690, VIII 549, IX 285, X 124, XX 389, XXII 79, XXVII 490; Clouston Tales I 352; FL XIX 324ff.—Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 205ff.; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bossu”; cf. Japanese: Mitford 191ff., Ikeda.
F344.1.p: Fairies remove a hunchback's hump, or put one on, as a form of healing or punishment.

F344.2.p: A fairy physician can cure anyone whose spine has not been cut through.

F344.3.p: Fairies give a man a white powder that cures sick people, and they refill his supply whenever he runs out.

F345.p: Fairies teach human beings skills or knowledge.

F345.1.p: Fairies teach a human how to walk under water.

F345.2.p: A supernatural person, such as a poet, reveals that a spouse has been unfaithful.

F346.r: England, Scotland, Wales: *Baughman; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 187; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3695; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 4; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 181 No. 36.
F346.p: A fairy helps a human being with hard work or a task.

F346.0.1.p: A fairy works as a servant to a human being.

F346.1.p: A fairy secretly makes shoes for a shoemaker, doing his work for him while he sleeps or is away.

F346.2.p: Fairies secretly build a house for a mortal, doing the construction work for him.

F347.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 199, 223; Icelandic: *Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 14f.
F347.p: A fairy gives a mortal advice or guidance on how to act or what to do.

F347.1.p: A fairy named Bonga makes a mortal the village headman, and people then come to him for advice.

F348.p: Taboos, or forbidden actions, attached to gifts a mortal receives from fairies.

F348.0.1.r: German: Grimm No. 182; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. *771.
F348.0.1.p: A fairy gift vanishes or turns worthless if the mortal breaks the taboo attached to it.

F348.1.p: A mortal must not take a fairy's gift down to earth, or into the human world.

F348.2.r: Hartland Science 156f.; Gröning Am Urquell IV 101f., 208f.; Sprenger ibid. V 34, VI 41, *191 n. 1; Grimm Deutsche Sagen No. 547.
F348.2.p: A cup given by a fairy must never be broken; breaking it brings bad luck.

F348.3.p: A fairy gift must never leave the mortal's family, or bad luck will follow.

F348.4.p: A mortal must not accept gifts of gold or silver from fairies.

F348.5.p: A mortal must not recognize or identify the fairy who gives him a gift.

F348.5.1.p: A mortal must not reveal the secret of a gift received from fairies.

F348.5.1.1.p: A mortal must not tell the secret of a gift of meat that never runs out.

F348.5.2.p: A mortal must not thank the fairy for the gifts received.

F348.6.p: Fairy gifts must never be measured or counted.

F348.7.p: If a mortal tells others about fairy gifts, the gifts stop coming.

F348.7.1.p: Misusing or abusing fairy gifts causes them to be lost.

F348.8.p: The mortal for whom a fairy works must not watch the fairy at work.

F348.9.p: A barrel of ale that never runs dry stops giving ale when a maid looks into its bunghole.

F348.9.1.p: Fairy gifts turn to paper when they are shown to others.

F349.p: Miscellaneous gifts that fairies give to mortals.

F349.1.p: A fairy helps a human to fly or travel through the air.

F349.2.p: A fairy helps a human win a battle.

F349.3.p: Fairies drive out or banish a destructive army.

F349.4.p: A fairy promises a mortal abundant crops and similar prosperity.

F350.p: A mortal steals something from fairies.

F351.p: A mortal steals money from fairies.

F351.1.p: A mortal steals fairy money by joining the fairies unseen in their game of throwing money about.

F351.2.p: A mortal steals fairy money by frightening the fairies away from it.

F352.r: Fb “guldhorn” I 513; Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 206ff., (1928) 144ff.; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 590, *Boberg; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 65 No. 559.
F352.p: A mortal steals a cup or drinking horn from fairies.

F352.1.r: Hartland Science 141—159 passim; Boberg Festskrift til Hammerich, 1952, 53—61.—England: *Baughman.
F352.1.p: A mortal steals a fairy cup when the fairies offer the mortal a drink.

F352.2.p: A mortal steals a vessel belonging to a water deity.

F353.r: (Cf. F343.17.) Hartland Science 244; England: *Baughman; India: Thompson-Balys.
F353.p: A mortal borrows a kettle from fairies and never gives it back.

F354.p: A mortal snatches an ornament from a fairy.

F355.p: A king's crown is stolen from fairyland.

F356.p: Fairy cattle, a bull or a cow, are stolen.

F357.p: An attempt to steal a fairy's necklace fails.

F358.p: A mortal borrows money from fairies and fails to return it on time.

F359.1.p: A mortal steals eggs from fairies.

F359.2.p: Fairies have a golden bird, and a mortal steals it from them.

F360.r: Saintyves Perrault 83ff.; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 62, Beal XXI 324; Icelandic: Boberg, Papua: Ker 73.
F360.p: Fairies who are malicious or harmful to humans, the kind often called pixies.

F360.0.1.p: Hostile or malicious beings who live in the otherworld, the land of the fairies.

F360.1.p: Fairies chase or carry off children who have not been baptized.

F361.p: Fairies take revenge on humans who have wronged them.

F361.1.p: A fairy takes revenge on someone who has slighted or insulted her.

F361.1.1.p: A fairy takes revenge on someone for not inviting her to a feast.

F361.1.2.p: A fairy takes revenge on someone for not offering her food or drink.

F361.1.2.1.p: A fairy takes revenge because a mortal failed to bring food and drink to the wedding of her fairy son.

F361.2.r: Hartland Science 141, 143; Jacobs’s list s.v. “Red Cap”; Scotch: Campbell Tales II 52.
F361.2.p: A fairy takes revenge on someone who has stolen from her or from fairies.

F361.2.1.p: A fairy gets back a stolen cup by disguising herself as a beggar.

F361.2.2.p: Fairies make a man lose his wits after he steals a flower while visiting them.

F361.2.3.p: Fairies bind a man fast to the ground after he tries to capture a fairy prince and princess.

F361.2.4.p: A man steals a fairy knife, and the fairy gifts to him stop.

F361.3.r: Hartland Science 66ff.; Jacob’s list s.v. “Fairy salve”.—Irish: Cross, E. Andrews Ulster Folklore (New York, 1919) 66f.; Welsh: Rhys Celtic Folklore I 63, 98f., 198, 213, 220—228, 241f., 292; English: FLJ II 154; Icelandic: Rittershaus 303; Färoe: Jiriczek Zs. f. Vksk. II 13 No. 14; Danish: Thiele DF II 202f.; German: Meyer Germanen 182; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3276f.; Legends Nos. 429, 431, 433, 438ff., 442, 444, 447; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 47 No. 388; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 308 No. 2; India: Thompson-Balys.
F361.3.p: Fairies take revenge on someone who spies on them, by tearing out the spy's eye after the spy uses a magic salve on one eye to see them.

F361.3.1.r: (Cf. F271.2.1, F271.5.) Irish myth: *Cross; England: Baughman.
F361.3.1.p: Fairies leave their work unfinished when someone watches over them.

F361.3.2.p: Fairies chase a person who watches them dance.

F361.4.r: *Fb “stald” III 534ab; Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 191; Scotland, Ireland, U.S.: Baughman.
F361.4.p: Fairies take revenge on people who trespass on land they consider their own.

F361.5.p: Fairies punish a girl who pours hot water into their spring.

F361.6.p: Fairies kill a suitor, or his relatives, who wants to marry a fairy maiden.

F361.7.p: Fairies get revenge on people who have captured their king and hold him prisoner.

F361.8.p: A fairy takes revenge on a person who has killed his relatives.

F361.9.p: Fairies take revenge on someone who has shamed or disrespected them.

F361.10.p: Fairies take revenge on someone who has mocked or teased them.

F361.11.p: Fairies threaten a person who watches over sheep.

F361.12.p: Fairies take revenge on humans who destroy their homes.

F361.13.p: Fairies take revenge on someone who has cheated them.

F361.14.p: A fairy punishes a servant girl who does not leave food out for him as expected.

F361.15.p: Fairies punish people who refuse to eat fairy food that has been given to them.

F361.16.p: Fairies punish a person who deserves punishment for how he has treated other people.

F361.17.p: Fairies inflict various other punishments on people, not covered by the more specific headings.

F361.17.1.p: A miller who throws a clod of turf into his kiln, where fairies are cooking oatmeal, is lamed, and the scalding oatmeal burns the fairies.

F361.17.2.p: A smith who returns to his smithy after dark to fetch medicine disturbs fairies there, and they take revenge on him.

F361.17.3.p: A plowboy who breaks the fairies' wooden oven while plowing is pinched by them.

F361.17.4.p: A fairy breaks the leg of a servant girl who tells lies about him.

F361.17.5.p: Fairies bathe children in a churn when the housewife forgets to leave clear water out for them.

F361.17.6.p: A fairy kills a dog that will not let him sleep in a haystack.

F361.17.7.p: A fairy kills a man who refuses his hospitality, specifically a man who refuses to visit the fairy after being invited.

F361.17.8.p: A man dares fairies to chase him, and they do; he barely reaches home ahead of them, and they drive an iron javelin through his iron-covered door.

F361.17.9.p: A fairy mistress strikes her disobedient human lover on the face and predicts his death.

F362.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 33, 147, cf. 218; Irish myth: *Cross; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 225; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.

F362.1.p: Fairies cause blindness in mortals, striking them with loss of sight.

F362.2.r: *Fb “ellepige” I 242a, “ellefolk” I 241b, “sær” III 723b; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
F362.2.p: Fairies drive mortals insane, causing madness.

F362.3.p: Fairies make mortals weak, draining their strength.

F362.4.p: A fairy injures a mortal, maiming or mutilating them.

F363.1.p: At a druid's command, fairies cause a king's death by lodging a fish-bone in his throat.

F363.2.p: A brownie or redcap kills travelers and collects their blood in his cap.

F363.3.p: Merely seeing fairies is fatal to a mortal.

F363.4.p: A fairy's glance reduces a mortal to ashes.

F363.5.p: A fairy calls her intended victim only once or twice, and the person dies when the call is answered.

F363.6.p: Fairies tickle mortals so severely that they die of it.

F364.p: Fairies and mortals wage war against each other.

F364.1.p: Fairy warriors kill mortals by sitting on them.

F364.2.p: Fairies fight mortals by wrestling with them.

F365.r: *Fb “ellefolk” I 241b, “stjæle” III 576a; Irish myth: *Cross; England, Scotland, Ireland: *Baughman.
F365.p: Fairies steal things or people from mortals.

F365.3.p: Fairies take over a peasant's house and live in it.

F365.4.p: A fairy (called bonga) steals part of a person's crop.

F365.5.p: A mortal plays draughts (checkers) with a fairy woman, and the fairies steal pieces from the board.

F365.6.p: Fairies steal a person's cattle, here in the form of a pig.

F365.7.p: Fairies steal food that is being cooked.

F366.p: Malevolent fairies harm or mistreat a person's livestock.

F366.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 166, 484 n. 23; Fb “ko” II 240b; England: Baughman.
F366.1.p: Fairies milk a mortal's cows until they run dry.

F366.1.2.p: Fairies let calves suckle the cows, so the children of the household get no milk.

F366.2.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 219f., 526ff. nn. 65—77; Fb “marelok” II 553; England, U.S.: *Baughman; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 127 No. 60; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 44 No. 60.
F366.2.p: Fairies ride a mortal's horses at night, leaving them exhausted.

F366.2.1.p: Fairies braid the manes and tails of horses.

F366.2.2.p: A fairy rides behind a man on his horse.

F366.3.p: Fairies take the form of wild animals that devastate and kill a flock.

F366.4.p: Fairies control whether a household prospers or fails.

F366.5.p: A fairy hangs on to a carriage on the road.

F367.p: A mortal who has returned from the fairy world pours out a drink the fairies had offered, and it burns up whatever it touches.

F368.p: Humans are hunted as game by fairies in a fairy chase.

F369.p: A miscellaneous group of fairies who are harmful or destructive to people.

F369.1.p: Fairies set fire to houses and other buildings.

F369.2.p: Fairies pollute or defile water sources. Irish myth.

F369.3.p: A fairy kills a person's hound or horses. Thompson's headline names the victims as hounds and horses.

F369.4.p: A malicious fairy plays a trick on a human being.

F369.4.1.p: A fairy stirs up people so that they go to war with one another.

F369.5.p: Fairies damage or destroy a farmer's crops.

F369.5.1.p: Fairies cut the kernels of corn off the stalks, stealing or ruining the harvest.

F369.6.p: A fairy stops butter from forming when a person churns cream.

F369.7.r: (Cf. E272.10, F401.3, F491.1.) Canada, England, Ireland, U.S., Wales: *Baughman.
F369.7.p: Fairies mislead travelers so that they lose their way.

F369.8.p: Elephants grow thin from listening too long to fairy music, and become too weak to graze.

F370.r: BP II 329.—Irish myth: *Cross; Danish: Feilberg DF V 55ff.; Norwegian: Solheim Register 18f.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
F370.p: A human being visits the land of the fairies and returns or stays there.

F371.p: A human child is raised among the fairies in fairyland.

F372.r: Irish myth: *Cross; English: *Child I 358 No. 40; England, Scotland: Baughman; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “nourrice”.
F372.p: Fairies take a human nurse to care for a fairy baby.

F372.1.r: (Cf. F333.) *Hartland Science 37—92; *Fb “jordemoder”; *BP I 367; Wentz Fairy Faith in Celtic Countries (London, 1911) 49f., 54, 131, 140, 175, 182; Tobler 76.—English: Child I 358ff. No. 40, II 505f., III 505f., IV 459a, V 215b, 290b; Scottish: J. G. Campbell Superstitions 147; England, Scotland, Ireland, U.S.: Baughman; Icelandic: Göngu Hrólfs saga 275ff.; Lappish: Qvigstad FFC LX 44 No. 41; Danish: Feilberg DF V 69ff., Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 330ff., (1928) 210ff.; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “sage-femme”, “fées”; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
F372.1.p: Fairies take a human midwife to help a fairy woman give birth.

F372.2.p: Fairies look for a human to act as godparent to their child.

F372.2.1.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 43 No. 56; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 126 No. 56.
F372.2.1.p: An old man becomes godfather to the underground folk, the fairies who live beneath the earth.

F373.p: A human being gives up the ordinary world and goes to live in fairyland for good.

F374.p: A human being who is in fairyland longs to go back home to visit.

F375.p: Human beings are held as prisoners in fairyland.

F376.r: *Hdwb. d. Märch. I 396 s.v. “Dienst bei elbischen Wesen”; Irish myth: *Cross; Danish: Feilberg DF V 84ff.; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 440.
F376.p: A human being works as a servant in fairyland.

F376.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 439, Balys Historical.
F376.1.p: A tailor works sewing in fairyland.

F377.r: *Hartland Science 161—195; Jacobs’s list s.v. “Time flies”; *Child I 321 n.; *Burnham PMLA XXIII 394 n. 2; Fb “glemme” IV 181a.—Irish myth: *Cross; England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales: Baughman; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 585; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 265, Ikeda; Koryak: Jochelson JE VI 280; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 157, (Cumberland Sound): Boas BAM XV 185, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 177.
F377.p: A human being experiences a supernatural lapse of time in fairyland, so that years seem to pass as days.

F377.1.p: A mortal spends what seems a short time in fairyland, but on returning finds that a great deal of time has passed in the human world.

F377.2.p: A year spent in the otherworld feels like only a few hours to the person who was there.

F378.p: Rules a mortal must obey when travelling to fairyland; breaking them has consequences.

F378.0.1.p: A human is thrown out of fairyland for breaking one of the fairies' taboos.

F378.1.r: Hartland Science 164f.; Irish myth: *Cross; England: Baughman.
F378.1.p: The taboo that a mortal must not touch the ground when coming back from fairyland.

F378.2.p: The taboo that a mortal in fairyland must not bathe in or touch the water of a lake there.

F378.3.p: A mortal visiting fairyland must keep his mind fixed on the fairies and not wander off in thought elsewhere.

F378.4.p: The taboo that a mortal in fairyland must not drink from a certain well; the one who does ends up alone on a hillside.

F378.5.p: The taboo that a mortal in fairyland must not pick flowers from a bed the fairies tend.

F378.6.p: The taboo that a mortal, while bathing a fairy child, must not put fairy bath water, soap, or ointment on his own body.

F379.p: Miscellaneous episodes of mortals visiting fairyland that do not fit the more specific headings.

F379.1.p: A mortal comes back from fairyland to the human world.

F379.1.1.p: A mortal who visits fairyland never gets back to the human world.

F379.2.p: Objects that a mortal carries home from fairyland.

F379.2.1.p: A medical book is brought back from the otherworld by a mortal.

F379.2.2.p: A mortal who returns from fairyland brings back tokens as proof of the visit.

F379.3.p: A man lives among the fairies for seven years.

F379.4.p: A saint is invited by the fairy king to visit fairyland; he sprinkles holy water on the fairy king and is left alone on a hill.

F380.p: Ways of defeating fairies or getting free of their influence or company.

F381.p: Methods by which people get rid of fairies, such as driving them off or banishing them.

F381.1.p: A fairy vanishes and leaves the person's company as soon as the person speaks the fairy's name aloud.

F381.2.p: A fairy stops following or leaves a person when the person scatters peas on the path behind them, since the fairy cannot resist stopping to pick them up.

F381.2.1.p: A person escapes pursuing fairies by strewing bananas on the path, which delays them.

F381.3.r: BP I 364; England, Scotland, U.S.: Baughman.
F381.3.p: A fairy leaves a person's house once the person gives the fairy clothes.

F381.4.p: A person gets away from a fairy by learning the fairy's secrets and then using that knowledge against it.

F381.5.p: A fairy is lured away from a house by a treasure, which the fairy then claims for itself and goes off with.

F381.6.p: A fairy vanishes when a druid speaks a spell that drowns out her voice.

F381.7.p: Fairies leave a place when people relieve their bodily needs where the fairies live.

F381.8.p: Fairies who are spinning are lured away from a house when a fire alarm is raised.

F381.9.p: Fairies will not come near a place when dogs are present.

F381.10.p: Fairies leave when a person watches them at their work.

F381.11.p: A fairy leaves when it is given tasks that cannot possibly be done.

F381.12.p: Fairies leave when they are ordered to fight each other.

F381.13.p: A fairy leaves when someone thanks it for its work.

F382.r: Hartland Science 107, 127, 130, 138f., 166; Fb “Kristen” II 300, “døbe” I 227, “messevin” II 582, “trold” III 852a; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; England: Baughman; Scotch: Campbell Tales II 74; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 50 No. 416.
F382.p: Fairies disappear when a Christian name, prayer, or ceremony is used against them.

F382.1.r: England, Scotland, Ireland, Wales, U.S.: Baughman; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.
F382.1.p: Fairies are afraid of the cross and will not come near it.

F382.2.p: Holy water breaks a spell cast by fairies.

F382.3.p: Saying God's name cancels the power of fairies.

F382.4.p: Opening the Holy Bible in the presence of fairies cancels their spells.

F382.5.p: Singing the song of St. Nicholas makes a fairy go away.

F382.6.p: When someone says grace at a fairy banquet, the fairies and the feast vanish.

F383.p: A fairy is made helpless or stripped of its power, so that a human can overcome or get rid of it.

F383.1.p: A fairy cannot cross a crossroads, so it is kept from going further or doing harm there.

F383.2.p: A fairy cannot cross a running stream, so flowing water stops it.

F383.3.p: A fairy cannot cross freshly plowed ground, so the furrowed field stops it.

F383.4.r: Type 503; Hartland Science 145; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 229.
F383.4.p: A fairy must leave or lose its power when the rooster crows at dawn.

F383.4.1.p: A fairy prince turns into a mortal man when daylight surprises him.

F383.4.2.p: Fairies must leave when the morning star rises.

F383.5.p: Fairy warriors who have been transformed into other shapes lose their enchantment when they are attacked and return to their true form.

F384.p: Certain objects have magic power against fairies and can harm or control them.

F384.1.p: Salt has power over fairies and can be used against them.

F384.1.1.p: Salt turns a fairy into a mortal human.

F384.1.2.r: Hartland Science 128; Lithuanian: Balys Legends Nos. 523f.
F384.1.2.p: Salt sprinkled on food belonging to fairies makes it harmless to eat.

F384.2.p: Steel has power against fairies and can be used to drive them off or defeat them.

F384.3.r: Hartland Science 163f.; Penzer II 166; Irish myth: Cross, Baughman; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 59 No. 504; Japanese: Ikeda.
F384.3.p: Iron has power against fairies and can be used to drive them off or defeat them.

F384.4.p: Wearing flowers behind one's ears protects a person from fairies.

F385.p: Ways of preventing or undoing a fairy's spell.

F385.1.p: A fairy's spell is reversed by turning one's coat inside out.

F386.p: A fairy is punished for wrongdoing.

F386.1.p: A fairy is shut up inside a tree as punishment.

F386.1.1.p: A fairy harper is trapped inside a yew tree as a punishment, so that he can no longer trouble people.

F386.2.p: A fairy is punished for marrying a human being.

F386.3.p: A troublesome bonga (a kind of fairy or spirit) is pinned to the ground with pegs and buried under a stone to stop it bothering people.

F386.4.p: A fairy is changed into another form as a punishment.

F386.5.p: A fairy is locked away as a punishment.

F387.p: A fairy is caught by a human being.

F388.p: The fairies leave the place where humans live and go away.

F388.1.p: The fairies leave by going up to heaven.

F388.2.p: The fairies leave for a floating island.

F389.p: Fairies are got rid of by some means other than those already listed.

F389.1.p: Fairies are driven away by fire.

F389.2.p: A saint prevents fairies from carrying off a fairy woman who has become Christian.

F389.3.p: A human being wounds a fairy.

F389.4.p: A human being kills a fairy.

F389.5.p: A fairy is defeated by the magic of a druid (a Celtic priest-magician).

F390.p: A collection of miscellaneous motifs about how fairies interact with human beings.

F391.p: Fairies borrow things from human beings.

F391.1.p: Fairies borrow animals from human beings.

F391.1.1.p: An ox lent to fairies must not be worked after sunset, the fairies' rule for the loan.

F391.2.p: Fairies borrow food from human beings.

F391.3.p: Fairies borrow tools from mortals in order to make a coffin. The motif shows fairies needing human implements for a task.

F392.p: A fairy changes its shape so it can fly, lets itself be swallowed by a woman, and is reborn from her as a fairy.

F393.p: A fairy comes to visit people in the human world.

F393.0.1.p: A fairy who is unhappy in fairyland leaves to live among humans.

F393.1.p: A fairy minstrel lives among humans in order to learn about their heroic deeds.

F393.2.p: A fairy appears to a particular person every Hallowe'en night.

F393.3.p: A poor fairy goes among humans to seek its fortune.

F393.4.p: A woman from the otherworld appears to a human while he or she is asleep.

F394.1.p: A human gives advice to a fairy.

F394.1.1.p: A druid gives instructions to fairies.

F394.2.p: Humans help fairies fight in a war.

F395.p: A fairy has the power to keep a human from coming near.

F396.p: Humans put themselves under the protection of fairies.

F397.p: A fairy woman shows her figure to warriors. She is said to be the most beautiful of women.

F398.p: Someone burns hair in order to call fairies.

F399.p: Miscellaneous other motifs about fairies that do not fit the more specific headings.

F399.1.p: Fairies carry a dead warrior away to fairyland.

F399.2.p: Fairies protect themselves by using smoke.

F399.3.p: Fairies hate members of the clergy.

F399.4.p: Fairies who play tricks on people or cause trouble for them, without being wholly harmful.

F399.4.1.p: Fairies amuse themselves by teasing or tormenting a human being.

F400.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics s.v. “Demons and Spirits”; Roscher s.v. “Daimon” I 938; Pauly-Wissowa s.v. “Daimon” IV 2010; Wehrhan Die Sage 59f.; *Runeberg Witches, Demons and Fertility Magic (Helsinki, 1947); *Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Dämonen”.—Irish myth: *Cross; Dutch: *Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 52ff.; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 37ff. Nos. 1—39; Slovenian: *L. Kretzenbacher Germanische Mythen in der epischen Volksdichtung der Slowenen (Graz, 1941); Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 316, IV passim, Neuman; Chinese: Werner 402; Africa (Yoruba): Ellis 244.
F400.p: General category of spirits and demons, supernatural beings that are not fairies or gods and that appear in folk belief.

F400.1.p: Named supernatural beings in Irish tradition who are linked with confusion, quarrels, or fighting among people.

F401.p: Spirits or ghosts who show themselves to people in various forms.

F401.1.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 309 No. 19. See Irving’s Rip Van Winkle.
F401.1.p: A spirit appears wearing clothing from an earlier time.

F401.2.p: A spirit appears glowing or shining with light.

F401.3.p: A spirit takes the form of an animal.

F401.3.0.1.p: A demon has the feet of an animal.

F401.3.1.p: A spirit takes the form of a horse.

F401.3.2.p: A demon appears in the form of an ox.

F401.3.3.p: A spirit appears as a black dog.

F401.3.3.1.p: A monster that leaves enormous dog-like footprints, named Waumpaus.

F401.3.4.p: A spirit takes the form of a fly and goes into a bottle.

F401.3.4.1.p: A demon appears in the form of a wasp.

F401.3.4.2.p: A spirit appears in the form of an ant.

F401.3.5.p: Spirits have feet like a goose or chicken.

F401.3.6.p: A demon takes the form of a hare.

F401.3.7.p: A spirit appears in the form of a bird.

F401.3.7.1.p: A demon appears in the form of a crow.

F401.3.7.2.p: Evil spirits appear as black birds.

F401.3.8.p: A spirit takes the form of a snake.

F401.4.r: *Grunwald Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXX—XXXI 317 (cf. F511.0.1., F531.2.1); Irish myth: *Cross.
F401.4.p: Spirits that have no head, or that carry their head under one arm.

F401.4.1.p: A spirit that has only half a head.

F401.5.p: Spirits that look horrible or frightful in appearance.

F401.5.1.p: A spirit that appears as a horrible, frightful head.

F401.6.p: A spirit that appears in human shape.

F401.9.p: A spirit whose feet are turned backward.

F402.r: Demons. See whole chapter “G” for witches and ogres.—Greek: Grote I 66.
F402.p: Evil spirits in general, and the harm they do.

F402.1.p: The harmful actions carried out by evil spirits.

F402.1.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 215, 523 nn. 19, 20.—Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 313 No. 83; India: Thompson-Balys.
F402.1.1.p: An evil spirit misleads a person and leads them off the right path.

F402.1.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 99, Beal XXI 331; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 298 No. 12.
F402.1.2.p: An evil spirit blocks a person's way on the road.

F402.1.3.p: Evil spirits tangle up a peasant's cows.

F402.1.4.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 223f., 530 nn. 98—101.—Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Mono-Alu: Wheeler 4, 6f., 18f., 32, 39, 41f., 46, 49, 51f., 60f., 61, 188.
F402.1.4.p: Demons take on human form in order to trick people.

F402.1.4.1.p: A demon pretends to be God in order to fool believers.

F402.1.5.p: A demon brings on an illness.

F402.1.5.1.p: Demons try to steal a king's soul away.

F402.1.6.p: An evil spirit makes a person weak.

F402.1.7.p: A demon of gluttony gets into a man and eats his food from inside his throat, so he cannot keep anything down.

F402.1.8.p: Evil spirits carry a dead body and throw it into a river.

F402.1.9.p: An evil spirit gives someone a false message that misleads them.

F402.1.10.p: An evil spirit chases or follows a person.

F402.1.11.p: An evil spirit causes a person's death.

F402.1.11.1.p: A spirit or devil sent by druids brings about the death of a Christian king.

F402.1.11.2.p: An evil spirit kills a person and then eats them.

F402.1.11.3.p: An evil spirit spears sleeping people with a harpoon, killing them.

F402.1.11.4.p: An evil spirit kills a person with a kiss.

F402.1.12.p: An evil spirit fights against a person.

F402.1.13.p: Women from the otherworld hold a ship back so it cannot move on.

F402.1.14.p: A spirit is involved with horses.

F402.1.15.p: Demons compete to court a girl and want to marry her.

F402.1.15.1.p: A demon seduces a princess while she bathes at the seashore.

F402.2.p: Demons are organized under a ruling government with leaders.

F402.2.1.r: Jewish: *Ginzberg Jewish Encyclopaedia s.v. “Asmodeus”, bin Gorion Born Judas I 230, *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
F402.2.1.p: Asmodeus is the king of the demons.

F402.2.2.r: Jewish: Neuman, bin Gorion Born Judas II 177, 351.
F402.2.2.p: A demon has a queen who rules over the demons.

F402.2.3.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 234ff., 243ff., 249, 376f.
F402.2.3.p: A child of the demon king marries a human.

F402.3.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 229.
F402.3.p: Demons live in a city of their own.

F402.4.p: Demons eat greedily and in great quantity.

F402.5.p: Demons are brought into being by some magical process or act of creation.

F402.5.1.p: A demon is made from apples that have been enchanted with magic.

F402.6.p: Demons have particular places where they live or stay.

F402.6.1.p: A demon makes its home inside a tree.

F402.6.1.1.p: A demon lives at the base of a tree, among its roots.

F402.6.2.p: Demons live in a mound of waste or refuse.

F402.6.4.p: Demons live in a white cliff that has a hole in it.

F402.6.4.1.p: Spirits make their homes in caves.

F402.7.p: Demons come in families, with relatives living together.

F403.p: Good spirits who are kind to humans and do them favors.

F403.1.p: A spirit gives money to a human.

F403.2.r: Familiar spirits. **Feilberg Nissens Historie; *Polívka Zs. f. Vksk. XXV 226 n. 8, XXVIII 41 n. 2; Dickson 121 n. 64, 213 n. 143; Kittredge Witchcraft 613 s.v. “familiars”.—Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 97, 267, (Labrador): Hawkes GSCan XIV 91; West Indies: Flowers 433.
F403.2.p: A spirit gives help to a human being.

F403.2.1.p: A person gets a familiar spirit, a helper spirit that serves them.

F403.2.1.1.p: A familiar spirit is obtained by carrying an egg under the left armpit.

F403.2.2.p: The form a familiar spirit takes when it helps a person.

F403.2.2.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 613 s.v. “familiars”; Tobler 37; Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 61.
F403.2.2.1.p: A familiar spirit appears in the shape of an animal.

F403.2.2.2.p: Angels serve as familiar spirits, working as servants in the houses of saints and helping them in other ways.

F403.2.2.3.p: A familiar spirit is the same as a person's soul.

F403.2.2.4.p: A spirit kept in a bottle or bag acts as a helper to its owner.

F403.2.2.5.p: A demon serves a person as a familiar spirit, a helper that takes an animal-like or other form to assist its master.

F403.2.2.6.p: A helpful spirit appears in the form of a small black man.

F403.2.3.p: A general heading for the things that helpful familiar spirits do for a mortal person.

F403.2.3.1.p: A familiar spirit takes the form of a hornet and stands guard over a treasure.

F403.2.3.2.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 310 No. 22; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 225, Rink 120.
F403.2.3.2.p: A familiar spirit warns a person of danger.

F403.2.3.3.p: Familiar spirits teach a boy how to sing.

F403.2.3.4.p: A familiar spirit carries news very quickly, far faster than any ordinary messenger.

F403.2.3.5.p: A familiar spirit discovers and reveals that a man's wife has been unfaithful to him.

F403.2.3.6.p: A familiar spirit gives advice to its human master.

F403.2.3.7.p: A person commands a great army made up of spirits and ghosts.

F404.p: Ways in which a person can call up or summon spirits.

F404.1.p: A summoned spirit must answer immediately as soon as it is addressed.

F404.2.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 301 No. 22, 304 No. 24, 313 No. 98, 319 No. 31; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 78.
F404.2.p: A person calls up spirits by conjuring them, using magic words or rites.

F405.p: Ways in which spirits can be fought off or defeated.

F405.1.p: A priest drives a spirit away or bans it using a sword.

F405.2.p: Spirits are driven off by being stabbed with knives and shot with pistols.

F405.3.p: Spirits are tricked by drum-beats and by being blindfolded or hoodwinked.

F405.4.r: English: Child I 20—22, 485a, II 496b, 509a, III 496a, IV 440a.
F405.4.p: A spirit or demon is defeated by being scolded and by having the last word in an argument.

F405.5.p: A cat, a dog, and a mouse together protect a person against an evil spirit. The man takes these animals with him as protection.

F405.5.1.p: Dogs guard a house and keep spirits from entering.

F405.6.p: Scattering grain on the ground drives away spirits, who stop to count or gather every grain.

F405.7.r: *Taylor Washington University Studies X (Humanistic Series) 23—60; **Boberg Sagnet om den Store Pans Død (København, 1934).—Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 45 No. 374; Scandinavian: Hartmann Die Trollvorstellungen (Stuttgart, 1936) 73; Dutch: Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 58 No. 101.
F405.7.p: A spirit leaves when it is told that one of its own kind has died.

F405.7.1.p: A spirit is driven off by the message that the field-mouse is dead, sent to the mill-mouse.

F405.8.r: Denied readmittance. *Taylor Washington University Studies X (Humanistic Series) 77—79 n. 181.
F405.8.p: Spirits leave when they are told that their home is on fire.

F405.9.p: A spirit inhabiting a body is overcome when a stake is driven through that body.

F405.10.p: Demons run away from a stone once a saint has stepped on it.

F405.11.p: A house spirit departs when it is given a gift of clothing.

F405.13.p: A man traps a spirit by hiding its stick and its copper leg-wrappers; if the spirit tricks its way back to them, it vanishes.

F405.14.p: An evil spirit is laid to rest after an exorciser torments it.

F406.p: Spirits are appeased with offerings, courtesies or gifts so that they do not harm people.

F406.1.p: People leave doors open at night so that night creatures can come and go freely.

F406.2.p: Food is set out at night for spirits.

F406.3.p: Spirits let people who have faces pass through the ground they guard.

F406.4.p: A demon of gluttony is coaxed out of a man's throat by offering it bits of food.

F407.p: Spirits depart from the human world, sometimes in notable ways.

F407.1.p: A spirit disappears in a puff of smoke.

F407.1.1.p: Spirits rise to heaven by building a fire.

F407.2.p: A spirit fades away into the air and is gone.

F408.p: Where a spirit lives or makes its home.

F408.1.p: A demon speaks from inside or takes up residence in a lance or sword.

F408.2.p: A spirit, sometimes a fairy, lives inside a person's heart.

F411.p: Describes the various ways spirits and demons move from place to place.

F411.0.1.p: A spirit moves extraordinarily fast, faster than any ordinary creature.

F411.1.r: *Taylor FFC LXX 24 n. 1; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 190—197.
F411.1.p: A demon travels riding inside a whirlwind.

F411.2.p: A spirit floats through the air without support.

F411.3.p: A demonic ship sails directly against the wind.

F412.p: Covers the ways spirits may or may not be seen by people.

F412.1.p: An unseen spirit is heard speaking but cannot be seen.

F412.1.1.p: A spirit can be seen by only one particular person, while others cannot see it.

F412.2.r: Irish: Beal XXI 336; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 297 No. 1, 298 No. 7.
F412.2.p: A spirit becomes visible when a person stands on its foot.

F413.p: Tells how spirits came to exist.

F414.p: A spirit carries people through the air or from place to place.

F414.1.p: A spirit carries a lover to his sweetheart's rooms inside a fortress.

F414.2.p: A spirit carries a miserly man to a tree that holds treasure.

F415.p: A demon lives inside an artificial head that answers people's questions like an oracle.

F416.r: Meet on Christmas (Easter) night. Cease to meet after mortal spies upon them. Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 46 No. 379.
F416.p: Spirits set a mill on fire.

F416.1.p: Spirits prevent a mill from grinding or operating.

F417.p: Spirits are owed and claim a portion of everything produced at certain set times.

F417.1.p: Spirits borrow goods from people at weddings and later return them.

F418.p: Spirits or demons hover in the air, shrieking over a battle.

F418.1.p: Spirits answer a warrior's war cry by shouting back.

F419.p: Miscellaneous motifs about spirits and demons that do not fit a more specific group.

F419.3.r: S.A. Indian (Caviña, Tumupasa): Métraux RBAE CXLIII (3) 448.
F419.3.p: Each kind of animal has its own spirit that acts as its guardian and protector.

F420.p: Water-spirits: supernatural beings that live in water, appearing in various human and animal forms.

F420.1.1.p: A water-spirit that appears as a man.

F420.1.1.1.r: German: Ebermann Elbsagen 93 (No. 55); French: Sébillot France II 409; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 57 No. 487.
F420.1.1.1.p: A water-spirit that appears as a handsome man.

F420.1.1.2.p: A water-spirit that appears as a black man.

F420.1.1.3.p: A water-spirit that appears as a small gray man with green eyes and gray hair.

F420.1.1.4.p: A water-spirit that appears as a man dressed in white, accompanied by about twelve attendants.

F420.1.2.r: (Cf. F423.1.) *Type 316; *BP III 322; *Fb “nøkke” II 725ab.—England, Ireland, Wales: Baughman, Ireland: Beal VII 11; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 261; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 55 Nos. 468—469; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 44 No. 58; Germanic: Meyer Germanen 199ff., 202ff., De la Saussaye 323; Slavic: Máchal 254f., 271f.; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 126 No. 58; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 42 No. 30; Armenian: Ananikian 84; Japanese: Ikeda.
F420.1.2.p: A water-spirit that appears as a woman, such as a water-nymph or water-nix.

F420.1.3.p: Water-spirits that take the form of animals.

F420.1.3.1.p: A water-spirit that takes the form of a toad.

F420.1.3.2.r: Tobler 97; Icelandic: Boberg, German: Henne-Am Rhyn 113 (No. 216), Ebermann Elbsagen 74 (No. 39); French: Sébillot France II 196.
F420.1.3.2.p: A water-spirit that takes the form of a fish.

F420.1.3.2.1.p: A water-spirit takes the form of a fish that has only one eye.

F420.1.3.3.r: England, Scotland, Ireland: Baughman; Icelandic: Boberg; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn (1893) 163ff., (1928) 112ff.; Norwegian: Solheim Register 17; Swedish: Hartmann 27; German: Künzig Badische 31 (No. 87), Karstens Sagen 79.
F420.1.3.3.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a horse.

F420.1.3.4.r: England: Baughman; German: Weichert II 176 (No. 166), Pfeil 292; Icelandic: Boberg.
F420.1.3.4.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a bull.

F420.1.3.5.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a stork.

F420.1.3.6.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a cat.

F420.1.3.7.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a goat.

F420.1.3.8.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a mouse.

F420.1.3.9.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a snake.

F420.1.3.10.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of a frog.

F420.1.3.11.p: A water-spirit appears as a creature resembling an ape or monkey.

F420.1.3.12.p: A water-spirit appears in the form of an otter.

F420.1.4.p: Water-spirits are described as having unusual or deformed bodily forms rather than ordinary ones.

F420.1.4.1.p: A water-spirit has a human upper body and a fish or snake lower body.

F420.1.4.2.p: A water-spirit's body is covered in fish scales.

F420.1.4.3.r: (Cf. F451.) Austrian: Calliano I 141; German: Henninger 74; French: Sébillot France II 202, 347, 417.
F420.1.4.3.p: Water-spirits are described as small, dwarf-like beings.

F420.1.4.4.r: (Cf. F451.2.1.4.) German: Plöckinger 87, Ebermann Donausagen 139 (No. 85); French: Sébillot France II 202.
F420.1.4.4.p: A water-spirit has a hunched back.

F420.1.4.5.r: Tobler 98; German: Henne-Am Rhyn 113, Pröhle Deutsche Sagen 153 (No. 119); French: Sébillot France II 403.
F420.1.4.5.p: A water-spirit has a human body but webbed feet and hands.

F420.1.4.6.p: A water-spirit has horse's feet instead of human feet.

F420.1.4.7.r: England, Wales: Baughman; German: Bindewald 95, Siess 1.
F420.1.4.7.p: A water-spirit has green hair and a green beard.

F420.1.4.8.r: England: Baughman; German: Schöppner I 219—223, Schultze-Gallara 23; French: Sébillot France II 343 (green eyes).

F420.1.4.9.p: Water-spirits appear as giants. The water-spirit takes the form of a huge being.

F420.1.4.10.p: A water-spirit is described as having unusually long hair.

F420.1.5.p: Water-spirits cannot be seen by ordinary people; they are invisible.

F455.p: Trolls are supernatural underground beings, sometimes thought of as mountain spirits, and in many tales they are the same as ogres.

F455.2.p: Trolls have a particular appearance as described in the tales.

F455.2.1.p: Trolls are about the size of a ten- or twelve-year-old child.

F455.2.2.p: Trolls are usually ugly, hideous, and big and strong.

F455.2.3.p: Trolls are black or dark in color.

F455.2.4.p: Trolls wear clothing made of animal skins.

F455.2.5.p: A troll takes on human form.

F455.2.5.1.p: A troll in human form is the size of an ordinary human.

F455.2.9.p: A troll appears as a whirlwind.

F455.2.10.p: Trolls are very old, often centuries old.
