F455.4.2.p: Trolls have food of their own.

F455.4.2.1.p: Eating troll food gives a person supernatural strength.

F455.4.2.2.p: Trolls seem to eat from golden dishes, but what they actually eat is frogs and snakes.

F455.4.2.3.p: Trolls must live on food that people have failed to bless, so they depend on what humans leave unblessed.

F455.5.p: Trolls can or cannot be seen by people, depending on circumstances.

F455.5.1.p: Trolls are unseen but can be heard.

F455.5.2.p: An invisible troll attends a wedding and eats the food there without being seen.

F455.5.3.p: Trolls have a cap that makes the wearer invisible.

F455.5.4.p: Certain people are able to see trolls that ordinary people cannot.

F455.5.4.1.p: Certain people, such as some animals or special persons, are able to see trolls, which ordinary people cannot.

F455.5.4.2.p: Trolls can be seen by children who have not yet been confirmed (received into the church), though adults cannot see them.

F455.5.4.3.p: A person can see a troll by looking through another person's arm or a similar gap, even though the troll is otherwise hidden.

F455.6.p: A general heading for stories in which trolls and human beings deal with one another in various ways.

F455.6.1.p: Trolls form friendships with human beings.

F455.6.2.p: Trolls and humans lend things to one another and later return or repay them.

F455.6.2.1.p: A troll repays a loan with a valuable item or an object that has magic powers.

F455.6.3.p: Trolls steal things from human beings.

F455.6.3.1.p: Trolls steal fish from people at Christmas time.

F455.6.4.p: A human steals something from a troll.

F455.6.4.1.p: A person steals a costly cup belonging to a troll.

F455.6.4.2.p: A person gets a troll's treasure by throwing steel at it, since steel breaks the troll's power over it.

F455.6.5.p: Trolls come to visit human beings.

F455.6.5.1.p: Trolls visit people on Christmas Eve.

F455.6.6.p: Trolls seize and carry away human beings.

F455.6.6.1.p: A woman who has been carried off by trolls is rescued from their dance.

F455.6.7.p: Trolls substitute themselves for human children, leaving a troll in the place of a stolen baby.

F455.6.8.p: Trolls assist human beings with their work or in other ways.

F455.6.8.1.p: Trolls help people bring in the grain harvest.

F455.6.9.p: Trolls and human beings are always enemies of one another.

F455.6.10.p: Trolls can take over and control human beings, making them act under the troll's power.

F455.7.p: A general heading for stories in which trolls are opposed or overcome by Christian faith and practices.

F455.7.1.p: When confronted with Christianity, trolls run away.

F455.7.2.p: A troll becomes powerless and unable to act when it sees the sign of the cross.

F455.7.3.p: Trolls are unable to speak holy names, and doing so is harmful or forbidden to them.

F455.8.p: A general heading for stories in which a troll is killed.

F455.8.1.p: A troll is turned to stone when the sun rises on it.

F455.8.2.p: A troll is destroyed by a bolt of lightning.

F455.9.p: A general heading for stories in which people drive off or forbid trolls from an area.

F455.9.1.p: Certain people have the power to forbid trolls from entering or staying in a place.

F455.10.p: A general heading for ways of telling whether a child or person is a troll.

F455.10.1.p: A child is tested to see if it is a troll: a snake is hidden in the dough the child is kneading, and if the child calls the snake "brother", it is a troll.

F455.11.p: A general heading for stories about the children that trolls have.

F456.p: A general heading for spirits that live in mines and work underground.

F456.1.p: Knockers are mine spirits said to tap or knock in the mines, known by names such as Tommy Knockers or spriggins.

F456.1.1.p: A general heading for accounts of where knockers or spriggins came from.

F456.1.1.1.p: Knockers are believed to be the ghosts of Jews who crucified Christ, condemned to work in Cornish tin mines as punishment.

F456.1.1.2.p: Knockers are believed to be the ghosts of giants who once lived in the area.

F456.1.1.3.p: Knockers are believed to be the spirits of miners who have died.

F456.1.2.p: A general heading for what knockers or spriggins do, such as the tapping and other behavior attributed to them in mines.

F456.1.2.1.p: Knockers, the spirits said to dwell in mines, do harm to miners in various ways.

F456.1.2.1.1.p: If a miner whistles in the mine, the knockers bring bad luck.

F456.1.2.1.2.p: Knockers hide the miners' tools so the men cannot find them.

F456.1.2.1.3.p: Knockers tamper with the dynamite fuses in the mine, making them dangerous.

F456.1.2.1.4.p: Knockers kick the rungs out of ladders, so trapped miners cannot climb out to escape.

F456.1.2.1.5.p: Knockers make lame any miner who bothers them too much.

F456.1.2.2.p: Knockers sometimes act to help miners.

F456.1.2.2.1.p: By knocking in certain places, knockers guide men to the richest veins of ore in the mine.

F456.1.2.2.2.p: Knockers do a miner's work at night while he is away.

F456.1.2.2.3.p: Knockers test the mine's passages and roof supports by tapping them with hammers.

F456.1.2.2.4.p: Before an accident, a knocker appears to miners, and seeing one warns them to leave the mine.

F456.1.2.3.p: Other things that knockers do, not clearly helpful or harmful.

F456.1.2.3.1.p: Knockers hold a midnight mass deep in the mine on Christmas Eve.

F456.1.2.3.2.p: Knockers, said to be the ghosts of Jews, are forced to sing Christmas carols in the mines at Christmastime.

F456.1.2.3.3.p: Knockers do not work on Saturdays or other Jewish holidays.

F456.2.p: A mine spirit called Bluecap is said to help miners in the mine.

F456.2.1.p: Bluecap pushes the coal tubs (carts) for the miners.

F456.3.p: A mine spirit called Cutty Soams is said to haunt the mine.

F456.3.1.p: The spirit Cutty cuts the ropes by which miners pull the coal tubs.

F456.4.p: Miscellaneous motifs about mine spirits that do not fit the other groups.

F456.4.1.p: Fairy-like underground spirits are said to run a coal mine.

F460.r: (Huldra.) See also F200—F399 (Fairies and Elves), F420 (Water-spirits), and F451 (Dwarfs) for many common motifs. Meyer Altgermanische 101; *Fb “vætte” III 1122b, “dværg” I 220b, “höj” I 740a, and especially “bjærgmand” I 41b, 42a; Hdwb. d. Abergl. I 1071 s.v. “Berggeister”; *Wehrhan 80; Scandinavian: **Hartmann 35ff., 57, 64 (“huldra”); *Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 60ff. Nos. 513—564; Slovenian: *L. Kratzenbacher Germanische Mythen in der epischen Volksdichtung der Slowenen (Graz, 1941) 28—35; India: Thompson-Balys.
F460.p: A general heading for folk beliefs about mountain spirits, supernatural beings who live in or near mountains.

F460.0.1.p: Mountain spirits are believed to be the souls of the dead.

F460.1.p: A heading for the ways mountain spirits, called mountain men, are seen to appear and look.

F460.1.1.p: A mountain man appears in the form of an animal.

F460.1.1.1.p: A mountain man appears in the shape of a hog or pig.

F460.1.2.r: (Cf. F232.2, F441.2.1.2, F531.1.5.1, G123.) Fb “patte” II 791b; Scandinavian: Hartmann 38.
F460.1.2.p: A mountain wife has breasts so long that she flings them over her shoulder.

F460.1.3.p: A mountain man carries a pair of shears at his side like a sword.

F460.1.4.p: A heading for the clothing mountain men are described as wearing.

F460.1.4.1.p: Mountain men are described as wearing white caps.

F460.1.4.2.p: Mountain men are described as wearing red caps.

F460.1.4.3.p: A huldra woman wears a particular cap that marks her out.

F460.1.5.p: Huldra women are said to have cows' tails.

F460.1.6.p: Huldra men are said to have long teeth and a long nose.

F460.1.7.p: Huldra beings are able to make themselves invisible.

F460.2.p: A heading for the typical habits, fears and abilities of mountain men.

F460.2.1.p: Mountain folk are afraid of thunder.

F460.2.2.p: Mountain folk travel through the air riding on horses.

F460.2.3.p: Mountain men cannot come into a house until the light has been put out.

F460.2.4.p: A mountain man leaves a stack of butter in front of a door.

F460.2.5.p: Huldra, supernatural mountain women of Scandinavian folklore, have a lake of their own. Their lake is part of their mountain-dwelling life.

F460.2.6.r: Have own churches, king, soldiers, etc. Hartmann 37.
F460.2.6.p: Huldra and similar mountain-spirits live in houses and in a way of life much like ordinary people.

F460.2.11.p: Huldra look after herds of animals grazing in the mountains.

F460.2.12.p: A mountain-man can only be killed for good after dying six separate times.

F460.2.14.p: Mountain-spirits eat their food raw, not cooked.

F460.2.15.p: Mountain-spirits can change from male to female or back whenever they choose.

F460.3.p: Mountain-folk have their own forms of entertainment and enjoyment.

F460.3.2.r: Hartland Science 166ff., 178; cf. Irving’s Rip Van Winkle.

F460.4.p: Describes how mountain-men relate to human beings, including marriages, love affairs, and help given to people.

F460.4.1.r: Fb “döjs” I 229b; Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1928) 282—283.
F460.4.1.p: A mountain-girl marries a mortal man. Their child is supernaturally strong.

F460.4.1.1.p: Mountain-men court or love girls who tend herds.

F460.4.1.2.p: A mountain woman has sexual relations with a man.

F460.4.1.2.1.p: A child is born from a man's dreamed sexual relations with a mountain woman.

F460.4.2.p: Mountain-men help human beings, often in practical ways.

F460.4.2.2.p: Mountain-spirits leave money on a hill as a reward to repay a man who helped them. The payment is a thank-you for past kindness.

F460.4.2.3.p: A mountain-spirit teaches a hero how to fight with a sword. The spirit gives him skill as a helper.

F460.4.2.4.p: Mountain-spirits give a book to children. It is a friendly gift from the spirits to human youngsters.

F460.4.2.5.p: Huldra, female mountain-spirits, trade cattle with men. The spirits and humans exchange livestock by bargain.

F460.4.3.p: Mountain-men leave a broken tool for a man to repair. The man is expected to mend it, and the spirits reward or depend on him.

F460.4.4.p: Mountain-men are hostile to humans and do harm to them. This heading groups the tales where they act maliciously.

F460.4.4.1.r: *Fb “karet” II 91; Icelandic: *Boberg; Norwegian: Solheim Register 19, *Hartmann 109, 112; Chinese: Werner 345; Japanese: Ikeda; Mono-Alu: Wheeler 39; New Hebrides: Codrington 409.
F460.4.4.1.p: Mountain-men carry off people. They kidnap humans and take them away to their world.

F460.4.4.1.1.p: A woman who has been seized by mountain-men is rescued. Someone frees her from the spirits who took her.

F460.4.4.2.p: Mountain-men put a chain on a peasant and hold him captive. The farmer is bound against his will.

F460.4.4.3.p: Mountain-men hurl a person up and over a church roof. It is a violent prank or attack by the spirits.

F460.4.4.4.p: Mountain-men make sausage out of Christians. They are cannibalistic and kill humans to prepare the meat.

F460.4.4.5.p: Mountain-folk steal from a peasant. The spirits take the farmer's goods.

F460.4.4.6.p: Mountain-men drive away a man's herds of livestock. The spirits take his animals.

F460.4.4.7.p: A mountain-spirit causes a ship to sink. The spirit wrecks a vessel at sea.

F460.4.5.p: Mountain-men borrow things from a peasant. The spirits ask a human for loans of items.

F460.4.6.r: Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 301 No. 18; Icelandic: Boberg.
F460.4.6.p: If a person fails to bless the mountains, the mountain-men gain power over him. Neglecting a blessing gives the spirits control.

F460.4.7.p: A mountain-man serves as a godfather to a human child. The spirit takes on the role of sponsor at a baptism.

F460.4.8.p: A person pays a visit to the mountain-men in their home. A human travels into the spirits' realm.

F465.r: *Wehrhan 68; **Jungbauer Die Rübezahlsage (Reichenberg, 1923); Koch **Rübezahl (Breslau, n.d.); Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXXV—XXXVI 68; *Loewe Zs. f. Vksk. XVIII 1, 151, XXI 31, 126.
F465.p: Rübezahl is a mountain and storm spirit found in folk tales. He is a named figure of the mountains who controls weather.

F470.r: Poltergeister; goblins; hobgoblins. *Kittredge Witchcraft 214, 521f. nn. 7, 9ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish-Swedish: *Wessman 30ff.; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 305 No. 4.
F470.p: Night-spirits are supernatural beings who appear and act at night. This heading covers spirits associated with the dark.

F470.0.1.p: Friar Rush, a mischievous spirit, plays pranks and causes trouble among people.

F470.1.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 217, 524f. nn. 37—44; England, Scotland, Wales, U.S.: *Baughman.
F470.1.p: Night spirits pull the blankets off a sleeping person.

F471.p: Dream demons are demons that come to people while they sleep and trouble their dreams and bodies.

F471.1.r: **E. Jones Der Alptraum (Leipzig-Wien, 1912); *Tegethoff Amor und Psyche 87ff.; Hdwb. d. Abergl. 1 282 s.v. “Alp”; Laistner Rätsel I 41ff., II 1ff.; Wehrhan 62; Hdwb. d. March. s.v. “Alp”; *Meyer Germanen 129ff.; Jellinek Zs. f. Vksk. XIV 322; *Fb “mare” II 551f.; *Kittredge Witchcraft 218, 525f. nn. 54—62.—Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 288ff., De la Saussaye 293f., *Boberg; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 241ff., (1928) 154ff.; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 88 Nos. 748—770; Dutch: Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 63 No. 171; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 44 No. 60; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 127 No. 60; Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Penzer III 131 n. 3.
F471.1.p: The alp, or nightmare, is a demon that sits on a sleeping person's chest and presses them, causing the frightening dream of that name.

F471.1.1.p: Alps, or nightmares, behave in certain ways: they ride horses and dance.

F471.1.1.1.r: *Fb “mare” II 551b, 552a; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 44 No. 60; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 127 No. 60; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 3683f.
F471.1.1.1.p: An alp rides a horse at night, leaving it sweaty and exhausted.

F471.1.2.p: Ways of protecting oneself from the alp or nightmare demon.

F471.1.2.1.p: The nightmare is driven out through a ritual or charm.

F471.1.2.2.p: An alp is killed or destroyed.

F471.1.3.p: Children who died unbaptized return as nightmares. When caught they beg to be baptized; usually they are illegitimate children who were murdered.

F471.1.4.p: The ghost of a hunter appears as a nightmare that presses on sleepers.

F471.1.5.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3687; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 67 No. 183.
F471.1.5.p: Certain people turn into nightmares at night and press others or things, especially on Thursdays. They are those born on a Thursday and christened on a Sunday.

F471.2.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 116, 444ff. nn. 103—155 passim; *Loomis White Magic 77; Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: ibid.; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 44 No. 59; Germanic: De la Saussaye 293f.; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 126 No. 59; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3682; S. A. Indian (Araucanian): Alexander Lat. Am. 328; Africa (Fang): Einstein 175.
F471.2.p: An incubus is a male demon that comes to women in their sleep and has sexual intercourse with them.

F471.2.0.1.p: A demon who becomes a lover to a person, usually a woman, in their sleep.

F471.2.1.r: *Loomis White Magic 77; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. *369, *423f., 3681; Armenian: Ananikian 87; West Indies: Flowers 433.
F471.2.1.p: A succubus is a female demon that comes to men in their sleep and has sexual intercourse with them.

F472.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 220f., 528f. nn. 78—79; Dutch: Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 68 No. 291; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3425, Legends Nos. 827—832.
F472.p: A huckauf is a goblin that jumps onto a person's back.

F473.p: A poltergeist is an invisible spirit, sometimes thought to be a ghost or witch, that causes all kinds of mischief in or around a house.

F473.2.p: A poltergeist, a mischievous unseen spirit, makes ordinary objects act against their normal nature, such as moving or behaving in impossible ways.

F473.2.1.r: (Cf. D1601.28.) U.S.: Baughman, (North Carolina): Brown Collection I 640.
F473.2.1.p: An invisible spirit makes a chair rock back and forth on its own.

F473.2.2.p: A spirit hides household items in odd places where they are hard to find.

F473.2.3.p: A spirit extinguishes lamps or candles, leaving the room dark.

F473.2.4.p: A house catches fire and burns with no ordinary cause that anyone can find.

F473.3.p: A poltergeist harasses, abuses, or otherwise mistreats people.

F473.4.1.p: A spirit rides horses or mules at night and leaves them exhausted and worn out.

F473.5.p: A poltergeist makes strange noises, such as knocking, banging, or other sounds with no visible source.

F473.6.p: A collection of other miscellaneous mischievous acts done by a poltergeist that do not fit the other categories.

F473.6.1.p: A spirit tears newly hung wallpaper or paper off the walls of rooms in a house.

F473.6.2.p: A spirit slashes or cuts up people's clothing.

F473.6.3.p: A spirit takes food from the table or from a cupboard.

F473.6.4.p: A spirit eats food that has been left out.

F473.6.5.p: A spirit sends back bullets or shots that were fired at it.

F473.6.6.p: A spirit causes the wheels to fall off a wagon.

F473.6.7.p: A spirit pushes a wagon off the road into a ditch.

F473.6.8.p: A spirit plays a man's fiddle at night, even though no one is playing it.

F473.6.9.p: A spirit disturbs the coffins inside a burial vault, moving or disordering them.

F475.p: Night-spirits who are helpful or kind to people rather than harmful.

F475.1.r: (Named from Bertha, the mother of Charlemagne.) Also called Frau Holle. *Meyer Germanen 23ff.; *Wehrhan 85f.; Slovenian: *L. Kretzenbacher Germanische Mythen in der epischen Volksdichtung der Slowenen (Graz, 1941) 84—94.
F475.1.p: Dame Berchta is a figure believed to travel across the countryside at night with a troop of followers. She is counted among the friendly night-spirits.

F480.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 215f., 523f.; Meyer Germanen 213ff.; Meyer Altgermanische 109.—Icelandic: Boberg; Finnish: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 159ff.; *Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 30ff. Nos. 263—374 passim, 42 Nos. 337, 339; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 324 No. 153; Slovenian: *L. Kretzenbacher Germanische Mythen in der epischen Volksdichtung der Slowenen (Graz, 1941) 49—79; Eskimo: Boas BAM XV 331, RBAE VI 636.
F480.p: House-spirits are supernatural beings that live in and look after a home. This heading groups the tales and beliefs about them.

F480.1.p: A house-spirit appears in the shape of a sow (female pig).

F480.2.p: A house-spirit takes the form of a serpent (snake).

F480.3.r: Finnish: Holmberg Finno-Ugric 172; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 3468, 3472.
F480.3.p: A household spirit steals things and brings them to its master.

F480.3.1.p: A household spirit (cobold) that steals is forced to give up its loot, by means of a trick or method involving the house.

F480.4.p: A house-spirit appears in the form of a baby.

F480.5.p: A house-spirit has no bones or hair, so it is boneless and hairless.

F481.r: A house-spirit. **Feilberg Der Kobold in nordischer Überlieferung (Zs. f. Vksk. VIII 1, 130, 264); *Kittredge Witchcraft 215f., 523f. nn. 23, 25.—Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 41ff., (1928) 29ff.; Estonian: L. v. Schroeder Germanische Elben und Götter beim Estenvolke (Wien 1906), Loorits Grundzüge I 266—281, 295—304.
F481.p: A cobold is a household spirit that lives in a house or farm and does work for its owners. This heading groups tales about cobolds.

F481.0.1.p: This heading covers the various ways a person comes to get a cobold for their household.

F481.0.1.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3461; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 213 I*.
F481.0.1.1.p: A cobold is hatched from the egg of a seven-year-old cock, or from a boar's testicle.

F481.0.1.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3462f.; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI 62 No. 159.
F481.0.1.2.p: A cobold is bought, usually from someone who sells it, and taken home.

F481.0.1.2.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3463; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 125 No. 55.
F481.0.1.2.1.p: A man who bought a cobold throws it away, believing he was cheated, but later finds a heap of corn or money at the same spot.

F481.0.1.3.p: A cobold is attracted by leaving food, such as scrambled eggs, in a particular place.

F481.0.1.4.r: Found to be a cobold. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3464.
F481.0.1.4.p: A cobold is accidentally acquired when someone finds a rope or a chicken and takes it home.

F481.1.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 43 Nos. 53, 54; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3477; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 124f. Nos. 53, 54.
F481.1.p: A cobold takes revenge when someone gives it an uncivil answer or treats it badly.

F481.2.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 43 No. 54; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 125 No. 55; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3471.
F481.2.p: Cobolds provide goods or supplies to their masters.

F481.2.1.p: A household spirit (cobold) supplies an endless amount of grain to a man who grinds with a handmill; the man kills the spirit out of disgust.

F481.2.2.p: A house-spirit provides an endless supply of food for its household.

F481.3.r: (Cf. F482.3.1.) *Taylor MPh XV 736 n. 2; *BP II 422 n. 1; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3467.
F481.3.p: It is impossible to get rid of a cobold once it has come to live in the house.

F481.4.r: (Cf. F321.1.1.1, F451.5.17.1.) *BP 368; Keightley 126, 418, 436, 473; Germania V 376; Kristensen Danske Sagn I (1892) 314—24 Nos. 1049—1075; Jahn 72 No. 87; Euphorion III 784; Zs. f. Vksk. XVI 414; Zs. f. deutsche Mythol. I (1853) 290.
F481.4.p: A cobold is driven away by brewing beer in an eggshell.

F482.p: A brownie, the small household spirit (called nisse in Scandinavian lore) that lives in and helps look after a house or farm.

F482.1.p: A description of what a brownie looks like.

F482.1.1.p: A brownie is described as having red hair.

F482.2.p: A description of what a brownie wears.

F482.3.1.p: Brownies live inside a house and move along when the people living there move.

F482.3.1.1.r: He piles all furniture on wagon and starts for new home, meets acquaintance who remarks: “I see you’re flitting.” Brownie sticks his head out of the churn on top of the load, answers: “Yes, we’re flitting.” Farmer goes back to former home. England, Ireland, Wales: *Baughman.
F482.3.1.1.p: A farmer is so troubled by a brownie's pranks that he decides to move house to escape it.

F482.3.2.p: Brownies live in a small hill or knoll rather than in a house.

F482.3.3.p: Nisser are bound to one particular farm and belong to it.

F482.4.1.p: A brownie owns horses of many different colors.

F482.5.1.r: (Cf. F471.1.1.2. and cross-references there given.) *Fb “danse” IV 93a.

F482.5.3.p: Brownies play mischievous tricks and tease the people they live with.

F482.5.4.p: A brownie or other household spirit does helpful deeds for the household.

F482.5.4.1.p: A brownie rides out to fetch a midwife when one is needed.

F482.5.4.2.p: A brownie gets back stolen goods for the owner and gives the thief a twitching eyelid as punishment.

F482.5.5.p: Brownies (helpful household spirits) sometimes cause mischief or harm to the people they live with.

F482.6.p: Explains how household spirits (brownies) came to exist.

F482.7.p: Household spirits quarrel and fight with one another.

F482.8.p: A household spirit (brownie) courts or wants to marry a human.

F485.r: (Klabautermann, Kabonterken.) Similar to house-spirit. Meyer Altgermanische 110; Zs. f. Vksk. II 409, 416, IV 299f., VIII 14 n. 4, 277, XXI 178, XXIX 68; Anglia Beiblatt VI 144, XVII 73; Frischbier Am Urquell I 134; Mitteilungen d. Schles. Ges. f. Vksk. Heft XII 76; Basset Legends and Superstitions of the Sea (New York, 1885).—Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 32 No. 273, 35 Nos. 295—296, 37, 41; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn II (1893) 44ff., (1928) 32ff.
F485.p: A spirit that lives in and protects a ship.

F488.p: A household spirit that is foolish or dim-witted rather than clever.

F488.1.p: A foolish household spirit tries to herd sheep but has great trouble gathering the lambs (or rabbits) into the pen.

F488.2.p: A farmer holds a mowing contest with a household spirit; he hides harrow teeth in the grass, and the spirit mows right through them, thinking they are dock weeds.

F490.p: A general heading for other spirits and demons not covered by the more specific categories.

F491.r: Kittredge Witchcraft 215, 523 n. 22; *Fb “lygtemand” II 473; Icelandic: Boberg; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 51 No. 438; Dutch: Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 63f.; India: Thompson-Balys; U.S. (Georgia): Harris Nights No. 28; Africa (Fang): Einstein 96.
F491.p: A mysterious light seen over marshy ground, known as the Will-o'-the-Wisp or Jack o' Lantern.

F491.1.p: The Will-o'-the-Wisp leads travelers off their path and into danger.

F491.2.p: The Will-o'-the-Wisp guides lost people safely back to their homes.

F491.3.p: The Will-o'-the-Wisp is driven away or banished by some ritual or act.

F491.3.1.p: A person who has been led astray by a Will-o'-the-Wisp breaks its power by turning a garment inside out.

F491.3.2.p: A person loses the Will-o'-the-Wisp's power over him by sticking his knife into the ground.

F491.3.3.p: Steel protects a person from the Will-o'-the-Wisp.

F491.4.p: The Will-o'-the-Wisp hops or jumps about over the ground.

F491.5.p: The Will-o'-the-Wisp takes revenge on someone.

F492.r: Fb “hvid” I 700b; von Negelein Zs. f. Vks. XIII 257ff., 368ff.; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “mort”. Cf. the “four horsemen” in Revelation.
F492.p: Death appears as a rider on horseback.

F493.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Dutch: Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 67f. Nos. 251—283; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Yukon): Alexander N. A. Myth. 78.
F493.p: A spirit or personification of plague who spreads disease.

F493.0.1.p: A plague or pestilence takes the form of an animal. The disease is imagined as a creature that travels and attacks people.

F493.0.1.1.p: Plague appears as a monster. The disease is pictured as a frightening creature that brings sickness.

F493.0.1.2.p: A spirit of sickness enters a princess's body and she falls ill. The illness is caused by the spirit possessing her.

F493.0.2.r: Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 28f. Nos. 246—252; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3494.
F493.0.2.p: A plague or pestilence takes the form of a human being. The disease is imagined as a person who spreads sickness.

F493.0.3.p: A plague or pestilence takes the form of some object. The disease is imagined as an inanimate thing that spreads sickness.

F493.0.3.1.p: A plague or pestilence takes the form of a severed or floating head. The disease is imagined as a head that spreads sickness.

F493.0.4.p: A plague or pestilence becomes visible to people. The disease is seen as a clear figure rather than felt only as sickness.

F493.1.p: Various kinds of disease are each personified as a separate spirit. Different illnesses are imagined as different demons or spirits.

F493.1.1.r: N. A. Indian (Cherokee): Terrell JAFL V 125.
F493.1.1.p: Consumption, the wasting disease, is personified as a demon. The disease is imagined as a demon that causes wasting.

F493.1.2.p: Colic, a severe stomach pain, is personified as a demon. The pain is imagined as a demon causing the stomach ache.

F493.2.p: Various stories describe what happens to people who encounter a pestilence spirit. These tales show the effects of meeting the disease spirit.

F493.2.1.p: A person who speaks with a pestilence spirit dies. Hearing or talking with the disease spirit is fatal.

F493.2.2.p: Two pestilence spirits talk to each other. Their conversation is overheard or described in the tale.

F493.3.p: Ways of guarding against a pestilence spirit. These motifs describe how people protect themselves from the disease demon.

F493.3.1.p: When the pestilence spirit is destroyed, the plague stops. Killing or defeating the spirit ends the epidemic.

F493.3.2.p: A pestilence spirit is held in place by magic. The spirit is bound or trapped so it cannot spread the disease.

F493.3.3.p: Magical means are used to protect people from a pestilence spirit. Charms or spells keep the disease spirit away.

F493.4.p: Demons spread plague through intense heat and rage. The disease is carried by a fierce, burning fury.

F493.5.p: The sky appears to be on fire as a sign that a great plague is coming. A fiery-looking sky warns of a terrible epidemic.

F494.p: Spirits that dwell in and belong to the land. These are local nature spirits tied to a particular place.

F494.1.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 228, Herrmann Saxo II 22ff., *Boberg; Danish: Ellekilde Ellekongen i Stevns, Danske Studier 1929, 10ff.
F494.1.p: A spirit that protects a piece of land and the things on or under it.

F494.1.1.p: A spirit living in a swamp watches over buried treasure and keeps it from being taken.

F494.2.p: A spirit that guards or lives at the boundaries between lands or properties.

F494.3.p: A spirit of the earth, the ground itself personified as a being.

F495.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 II 205; India: Thompson-Balys.
F495.p: A spirit that dwells in or belongs to stones and rocks.

F496.p: A demon whose nature is excessive eating and greed for food.

F496.1.p: A holy man is possessed by a demon of gluttony that makes him crave food.

F497.r: Dutch: *Sinninghe FFC CXXXII 64ff Nos. 191—220; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 111, III 64, 88, 176—178.
F497.p: Spirits made of or associated with fire.

F497.1.r: *O. Loortis Das misshandelte und sich rächend Feuer (Tartu, 1935).
F497.1.p: Two fire-spirits talk together, asking whether a house will be burned down.

F499.p: A miscellaneous group of spirits not classed under the other headings.

F499.1.r: German: Grimm No. 166; India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Warrau): Kirchoff BBAE CXLIII (3) 880.
F499.1.p: A spirit that lives in the sky.

F499.1.1.p: A sky spirit that is a spirit of light.

F499.2.p: Beautiful nymph-like women of Paradise, called houris.

F499.3.p: Jinns, supernatural beings that can be helpful or harmful to humans.

F499.3.1.p: Jinns have no bones in their arms, and each hand has only four fingers and no thumb.

F499.3.2.p: Jinns have a right to take a share of the fruits and produce of the earth.

F499.3.3.p: Jinns haunt graveyards, ruined houses, or a place where sacrifices were made.

F500.r: Extraordinary size, form, appearance, or habits. **DeCock Volkssage 99ff.; Chinese: Werner 386.
F500.p: A general heading for people who are remarkable or extraordinary in some way.

F501.p: A person who is nothing but a head, with no body.

F510.r: *Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 175; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 464, 469.
F510.p: A general heading for monstrous or deformed people.

F510.1.p: A general category for monstrous races: peoples or kinds of beings whose bodies are grotesquely unlike ordinary humans.

F511.p: A general category for people whose heads are unusual in shape, number, or form.

F511.0.1.r: (Cf. F401.4, F531.1.2.1.) *Chauvin VII 77 No. 121; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
F511.0.1.p: A person who has no head at all.

F511.0.1.1.r: *Chauvin VII 87 No. 373 bis n. 2; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg. Chinese: Werner 387.
F511.0.1.1.p: A headless person whose eye and mouth are located on the chest.

F511.0.1.2.p: Headless persons are unable to smell or hear.

F511.0.2.p: A person who has more than one head.

F511.0.2.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman N. A. Indian (Quinault): Farrand JE II 124 No. 14.

F511.0.3.r: Koryak and American Indian: *Jochelson JE VI 375.
F511.0.3.p: Persons whose heads are made of stone and serve as hammers.

F511.0.3.1.p: A person whose head is made of iron.

F511.0.4.r: Loomis White Magic 54, 93, 125; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda (F1041.14); Africa (Kaffir): Theal 51.
F511.0.4.p: A man who carries his own head under his arm.

F511.0.4.1.p: A man cuts off his own head and throws it against an enemy.

F511.0.5.p: A man who has only half a head.

F511.0.6.p: A beheaded man's head is reattached crookedly.

F511.0.7.p: A man has a venomous worm living in his head.

F511.0.8.p: The discovery of an enormous skull belonging to an ancient king.

F511.0.9.p: A person who has an animal's head on a human body.

F511.0.9.1.p: A being whose body is human but whose head is that of a horse.

F511.0.9.2.p: A being whose body is human but whose head is that of a calf.

F511.0.9.3.p: A being whose body is human but whose head is that of a serpent or snake.

F511.1.p: A person whose face is strange or unnatural in some way.

F511.1.0.1.p: A person who has no facial features, the face being smooth and flat.

F511.1.1.r: Janus. Roman: Fox 297; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 49 No. 327F*; N. A. Indian (Teton): Dorsey AA o.s. II 151ff., (Ponka): Dorsey Contr. to N. Am. Ethnology VI 207; Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 85.
F511.1.1.p: A person who has two faces, one on the front and one on the back of the head.

F511.1.2.p: A person who has three faces on one head.

F511.1.3.p: A person whose face is that of an animal.

F511.1.3.1.p: A person whose face is that of an ape or monkey.

F511.1.4.p: A person whose face is green in color.

F511.2.p: A person whose ears are strange or unusual in form or number.

F511.2.1.p: A person who has ears growing on the chest or breast.

F511.2.2.r: Midas. Köhler-Bolte I 383 n. 1, 511, 587; RTP I 327, VII 356; *Zs. d. deutschen morgenländ. Gesel. XL 549; Crooke FL XXII 183; *BP IV 147 n. 7 (Celtic); *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 397; Huet 45; Penzer III 188 n., VII n. 1, VI 26 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross, *Porter Proc. Royal Irish Academy (1932) 142.
F511.2.2.p: A person who has the ears of a donkey or horse.

F511.2.2.1.p: A person who has the ears of a cat, in addition to being a person with donkey or horse ears.

F511.2.3.p: A person who has many ears on the head or body.

F511.2.4.p: A person who has no ears at all.

F511.3.p: A person who has horns growing from the head.

F511.3.1.p: A person whose horns are made of silver.

F512.p: A person whose eyes are strange or unusual in number or form.

F512.1.r: *Type 511; Herbert III 238; Oesterley No. 175; Laistner Rätsel II 48ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 206 No. 154.
F512.1.p: A person who has only one eye.

F512.1.1.r: (Cf. F441.4.1, F531.1.1.1.) *Krappe Balor 5 n. 19, 9 nn. 33—35; Fb “menneske” II 577b, “öje” III 1165b; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 4 n. 1; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 389.
F512.1.1.p: A person has only one eye, set in the middle of the forehead.

F512.1.2.r: Pass it around. (Cf. F513.1.1.) *Fb “öje” III 1166a; Greek: Fox 33, *Frazer Apollodorus I 155 n. 4.
F512.1.2.p: Three women share a single eye between them, passing it back and forth.

F512.1.3.p: A person has only one eye, located at the back of the head.

F512.1.4.p: A doorkeeper has one ordinary human eye and one eye like a cat's.

F512.2.1.p: A person or animal has four or six eyes.

F512.2.1.1.r: *Type 511; Cosquin Contes Indiens 520; Jacob’s list s.v. “Three-eyed stepsister”; India: Thompson-Balys.

F512.2.1.2.r: Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 233; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/15).

F512.2.2.r: Krappe Balor 19 n. 69; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 130 n. 3, Fox 29, 193.
F512.2.2.p: Argos is a being whose eyes cover his whole body.

F512.3.r: (Cf. F511.0.1.1.) *De Cock Volkssage 102ff.; *Chauvin VI 66 No. 233; Persian: Carnoy 298.
F512.3.p: A person has eyes in the stomach.

F512.4.r: Krappe Balor 19 n. 69; S. A. Indian (Fuegian): Alexander Lat. Am. 340, (Yuracare): ibid. 314.
F512.4.p: A person has eyes in the back of the head.

F512.5.p: A person has no eyes at all.

F513.p: A person has an unusual mouth.

F513.0.1.p: A person has a mouth in the stomach.

F513.0.2.p: A person has mouths all over the body.

F513.0.3.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 78.
F513.0.3.p: Some people have no mouth at all.

F513.0.4.p: A person has a mouth in the breast.

F513.1.1.r: Pass it around. (Cf. F512.1.2.) *Fb “øje” III 1166a; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 155 n. 4, Fox 33.
F513.1.1.p: Three women share a single tooth between them.

F513.1.2.p: A person who has an unusually large number of teeth.

F513.1.2.1.p: A person who has three rows of teeth.

F513.1.3.p: A person whose tooth is poisonous. The poison dissolves flesh.

F513.1.4.p: A person who has no teeth at all.

F513.2.p: A person who has no tongue.

F513.3.p: People who take their lower jaws off and leave them at home when they go to market, so that they will not quarrel.

F514.p: A person who has an unusual nose.

F514.1.r: Herbert III 238; Oesterley No. 175; Tobler 63; Jewish: Neuman.
F514.1.p: A person who has no nose.

F514.2.r: DeCock Volkssage 105; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 599, Boberg.
F514.2.p: Men who have birds' beaks in place of noses or mouths.

F514.3.p: A person who has a cat's snout instead of a human nose.

F514.4.p: A person who has one or more hooks or crooks at the end of the nose.

F514.5.p: A person who grows a second nose.

F515.p: A person who has unusual hands.

F515.0.1.p: A person who has no hands.

F515.0.2.1.p: Giants who each have a hundred hands.

F515.1.p: A person whose fingers are unusual in some way.

F515.1.1.p: A person whose fingers are joined together and not separated from one another.

F515.2.p: A person who has unusually long or large fingernails.

F515.2.1.p: A fingernail large enough to hide a basin's worth of food.

F515.2.2.r: Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 170.
F515.2.2.p: A person whose fingernails are extraordinarily long.

F515.3.p: Men who have tails growing on their hands.

F515.4.p: A boy whose hands are shaped like seal flippers.

F515.5.p: A whole tribe or people who are all left-handed.

F516.p: A person whose arms are unusual in some marvelous way.

F516.1.p: People who have no arms at all.

F516.1.1.p: Armless people who have legs growing out of their shoulders, using their toes in place of fingers.

F516.2.1.p: Earthborn men who each have six arms.

F516.2.3.p: A man who has a thousand arms.

F516.3.p: People whose arms are unusually long.

F516.4.p: A man whose arms can stretch far beyond normal length.

F517.p: A person whose legs are unusual in some marvelous way.

F517.0.1.p: A person who has only one leg.

F517.0.2.p: People whose legs are unusually long.

F517.0.2.1.p: A man with legs so long that, standing in the ocean, he can steady a boat.

F517.1.p: A person whose feet are unusual in some marvelous way.

F517.1.1.p: A person who has no feet.

F517.1.1.1.p: A person who has only one foot.

F517.1.2.p: A person who has many feet instead of the usual two.

F517.1.2.1.p: A man who has four feet instead of two.

F517.1.3.p: Men whose feet are shaped like sponges, so they can soak up or hold water.

F517.1.4.p: A person who has claws instead of ordinary nails on the feet.

F517.1.5.p: A person whose knees bend the wrong way, so the legs point backward at the knee.

F517.1.5.1.p: Men whose feet turn backward so they will not stub their toes when walking.

F517.1.6.p: A person whose feet are hooves like a horse's.

F517.1.7.p: A person whose feet are shaped like an elephant's feet.

F517.1.8.p: A man whose soles, the undersides of his feet, are covered with hair.

F518.p: A person who has a tail.

F521.p: A person whose body is covered in an unusual outer layer, such as hair, feathers or metal.

F521.1.r: *Williams 17ff.; Gaster Oldest Stories 43; Irish myth: *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 189; India: Thompson-Balys; Persian: Carnoy 298.
F521.1.p: A man whose body is covered with hair like an animal's.

F521.1.1.r: Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 189 No. 130; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen I 213.
F521.1.1.p: A woman whose body is covered with animal-like hair.

F521.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Chinese: Werner 390; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G 3/1353, z-G 13/380); Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 109.
F521.2.p: People who are covered in feathers.

F521.3.p: People who are made of metal or have metal bodies.

F521.3.1.r: (Talos). Has single vein from neck to ankle and bronze nail at end of vein. This is the only vulnerable spot. Frazer Apollodorus I 118 n. 1.
F521.3.1.p: A man whose body is made of bronze.

F521.3.2.p: A man whose body is made of iron.

F521.3.3.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 214, 468, 742, 761, 1293; India: Thompson-Balys.
F521.3.3.p: A person whose body is made of gold.

F521.3.3.1.p: A girl whose dirt, the grime rubbed off her body, is gold.

F521.3.3.2.p: A person whose anus is made of gold, so that their excrement is gold.

F521.3.4.p: A person whose whole body is made of silver.

F521.3.4.1.p: A silver king who rides a silver horse, accompanied by silver attendants: a silver cock, bird, and dog.

F522.r: Greek: Grote I 216; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 390; Persian: Carnoy 298.

F522.1.p: A person who has wings on the feet or on the head.

F523.r: Siamese twins. Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 248 n. 2.
F523.p: Two people whose bodies are joined together into one.

F524.p: A person born or existing with several bodies, a marvelous monstrous being.

F524.1.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 211 n. 2, Fox 86 (Geryoneus).
F524.1.p: A person with three bodies: three men's bodies grown together into one at the waist, but separate from the flanks and thighs down.

F525.p: A person who has only half a body, as if the body had been split in two.

F525.1.r: Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen II 13, III 75, Rink 237, (Smith Sound): Kroeber JAFL XII 171.
F525.1.p: A man who has only one side of his body.

F525.1.1.r: Fb “jærn” IV 249b; Hawaii: Dixon 89 (stone); Africa (Kaffir): Theal 129 (iron).
F525.1.1.p: A man whose one side of the body is made of stone or iron.

F525.2.r: Chauvin VII 40 No. 153 n. 1; Tonga: Gifford 32.
F525.2.p: A man who splits into two separate parts.

F525.3.p: A people or tribe whose members each have only one eye, one foot, and one hand.

F525.3.1.p: A person with only one foot, one hand, and one eye.

F525.4.p: The Antichrist, pictured as a person with a flat body.

F525.5.p: A giant who has limbs and organs only on his left side.

F525.6.r: Eskimo (Mackenzie Area): Jenness 49 (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 179, 181.
F525.6.p: A person who has no back.

F526.p: A person whose body is a combination of several different creatures.

F526.1.p: Typhon, a monster human down to the thighs, with a coil of vipers below and dragon heads growing from his hands, bigger than mountains.

F526.2.p: Scylla, a monster with a woman's breast and face, whose flanks bear six heads and twelve dog feet.

F526.3.p: The Gorgon, a monster with a head turned about, dragon scales, boar tusks, brazen hands, and golden wings.

F526.4.p: A hermit who has become beast-like: walks on all fours, is covered with hair, and has beast's horns.

F526.5.p: A monstrous person whose body is made up of unusual combinations of parts, such as two faces, three legs, or seven arms.

F526.6.p: Cecrops, a figure whose body is part man and part serpent.

F527.p: A person whose skin or coloring is unusual for a human, marking them as a marvel or monster.

F527.1.p: A person whose whole body is red.

F527.1.1.p: A knight whose body or armor is entirely red.

F527.2.p: A knight whose body or armor is entirely green.

F527.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 547.
F527.3.p: A man whose body is blue.

F527.4.p: A brown man whose back is white.

F527.5.p: A man who is black in color.

F527.6.p: A very strong man who is half red and half blue.

F529.p: Miscellaneous monstrous people not covered by the other categories of this group.

F529.1.p: People whose bodies have holes pierced right through them; one may be carried on a pole run through the hole, or hung up on a peg.

F529.2.1.p: People without anuses make an opening for themselves by sitting on pegs.

F529.3.p: A man from whose joints grass or plants grow.

F529.4.p: A person who has a small animal living inside his body.

F529.5.p: A person whose body is see-through.

F529.6.p: A person with an extremely large belly.

F529.7.1.p: A person who has no joints, so cannot bend their body normally.

F529.8.p: A small, monkey-like people who are counted among the monstrous beings of folk tales.

F531.5.6.p: Giants give gifts to men, often lavish or valuable ones.

F531.5.6.3.p: A giant's gifts stop working once the recipient reveals where they came from.

F531.5.11.2.p: A giant and a human man race on foot against each other as a contest.

F531.5.14.p: A man kills a giant's baby.

F531.5.15.p: Giants lead men into sin and wrongdoing.

F531.6.1.2.p: A giant is a man who has been transformed into a giant.

F531.6.2.0.1.p: Giants live in a land called Risaland or Jotunheimar, with no more specific location given.
