F577.3.p: A king and a fool who look exactly alike.

F577.4.p: Two lovers who look exactly alike.

F577.5.p: Everyone in a certain place looks exactly alike.

F582.r: *Penzer X 265 s.v. “Poison Damsel”; **Penzer Poison Damsels 3ff.; Herbert III 211; *Oesterley No. 11; **Hertz Abhandlungen 156ff.; Krappe Mitt. d. schles. Gesell. f. Volkskunde XXVIII (1927) 131ff.; *bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 360f.
F582.p: A woman who has been fed on poison, so that any husband she takes is killed by her. The poison may pass by her gaze or breath, or through sex.

F582.1.p: A woman with a serpent living inside her, which comes out and kills her bridegrooms.

F582.2.p: A man who spews venom from his mouth.

F582.3.p: A man whose body is poisonous, so that contact or touch with him is deadly.

F583.r: Koryak, Mongol Turk, Russian: Jochelson JE VI 363.
F583.p: A hero who has lain motionless since birth and only later begins to move or act.

F584.p: A person who is unusually light, so weightless they barely press down on things.

F584.1.p: A princess who weighs no more than five flowers.

F585.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 61 No. 445B.
F585.p: Ghostly apparitions or spirits that appear as phantoms.

F585.0.1.p: A fairy or god who appears in the form of a phantom.

F585.1.p: Phantom women lure men to their deaths through irresistible enticements.

F585.2.p: A phantom army is conjured by magic from puffballs and withered leaves.

F585.3.p: Phantom women drain a person's strength, leaving them weak.

F585.4.p: Treasure is taken from the hand of a phantom.

F591.r: Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 347, 1288.
F591.p: A person who never laughs, an extraordinary figure marked by constant solemnity.

F591.1.p: A prince who is never seen to laugh.

F591.2.r: *BP IV 189 n. 2; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction.
F591.2.p: A sad-faced princess who is unable to laugh.

F592.p: A man's fierce glance kills people or makes them faint.

F593.p: A person whose body temperature is extraordinarily high.

F593.1.p: A person's body heat is so great that snow melts for a wide area around them.

F594.p: A man whose entrails show through his body when he laughs.

F595.p: A man's body gives off a sweet fragrance.

F596.p: A person who is extraordinarily slow in movement or action.

F597.p: A woman who has no womb.

F598.p: An old woman produces a miraculous amount of milk.

F600.p: People who possess extraordinary powers beyond ordinary human abilities.

F601.r: *Types 301B, 513, 514, 571; *BP II 79, 95; *Benfey *Kleinere Schriften III 94; *Köhler-Bolte I 601 s.v. “Gefährten”; *Cosquin Contes indiens 431ff.; *Kittredge Arthur and Garlagon 226 n. 3; Jacobs’s list s.v. “Extraordinary Companions”; Alphabet No. 693; *Chauvin VII 125 No. 392.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5, Rotunda; Buriat: Holmberg Siberian 428; Koryak, Mongol-Turk: Jochelson JE VI 363; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: De Vries Nederlandsche Tijdschrift voor Volkskunde (1924) 97ff.; Korean: Zong in-Sob 163f.; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 27, 114, 128, 433; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 334ff., 345ff.
F601.p: A group of men with extraordinary powers who travel together as companions.

F601.0.1.p: Companions who are highly skilled at their crafts or tasks.

F601.1.r: *Types 513, 514; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 163ff.; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 345ff.
F601.1.p: Extraordinary companions carry out the hero's difficult tasks for him.

F601.2.r: *Types 513, 514; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 345ff.; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 74ff. No. 16.
F601.2.p: A hero is aided in completing suitor tests by companions who have extraordinary powers.

F601.3.r: *Type 301; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 334ff.
F601.3.p: Extraordinary companions turn against and betray the hero.

F601.4.p: A hero is rescued by a group of companions who have extraordinary powers.

F601.4.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 143.
F601.4.1.p: One of the extraordinary companions hides behind the hero so as to trick an enemy.

F601.4.2.p: An extraordinary companion saves the hero from being killed.

F601.5.p: The extraordinary companions are brothers, such as twins or triplets.

F601.6.p: The extraordinary companions are animals that have been transformed from human form.

F601.7.p: Animals serve as the hero's extraordinary companions.

F610.r: (Strong John). (Cf. X940, X959.1.) *Panzer Beowulf; *Types 301, 650*, 650**, 650, 1003—1013; *BP II 285ff., 300ff.; *Fb “styrke”, “stærk”, “Svend Felding”.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 86, 153 (Heimdall), *Boberg; French: Cosquin Lorraine Nos. 14, 46, 52, 69 and notes; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 8; Greek: Fox 75 (Herakles), Frazer Apollodorus I 259 n. 3; Jewish: Frazer Old Testament II 480ff. (Samson), *Neuman; Armenian: Ananikian 86; Hindu: Keith 172; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: *De Vries Nederlandsch Tijdschrift v. Volkskunde XXX 97ff.; Chinese: Graham; Buriat: Holmberg Siberian 428; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 334ff. incident A 2; West Indies: Flowers 435.
F610.p: A man of unusually great strength.

F610.0.1.r: Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 551, 902; Africa (Upoto): Einstein 128.
F610.0.1.p: A woman of unusually great strength.

F610.0.1.1.p: A remarkably strong woman defeats a man in a contest of archery and spear-throwing.

F610.1.p: A wild man who has superhuman strength.

F610.2.r: Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 24; Missouri-French: Carrière.
F610.2.p: A dwarf who is a hero of superhuman strength.

F610.3.r: (Cf. F1041.8.6.) Hdwb. d. March. I “Bärenhäuter”; Icelandic: *Boberg.
F610.3.p: A warrior of special strength who fights in a frenzy, called a berserk.

F610.3.1.p: A berserk who cannot be wounded or killed.

F610.3.4.1.p: A hero fights against a group of twelve berserks.

F610.3.4.2.p: A hero fights one berserk in a one-on-one duel.

F610.3.4.2.1.p: A berserk is killed in a single combat over a maiden.

F610.3.5.p: A berserk warrior of special strength competes with other berserks in their own feats, such as walking through fire.

F610.4.p: A man who has the strength of many men put together.

F610.4.1.p: A man who has the strength of four men.

F610.4.2.p: A man who has the strength of twelve men.

F610.4.3.p: A man who has the strength of seventy men.

F610.5.p: A man who has the strength of animals, not just humans.

F610.5.1.p: A man who has the strength of a lion.

F610.5.2.p: A man who has the strength of ten elephants.

F610.6.p: A man so strong that he breaks most things he touches.

F610.6.1.p: A man so strong that he has to be chained up except when he is going into battle.

F610.7.p: A strong man so heavy that no horse can carry him for a whole day.

F610.8.p: A strong man so heavy that only his own horse can carry him.

F610.9.p: A strong man performs superhuman tasks when God's spirit comes upon him.

F611.p: The birth and upbringing of a man of great strength.

F611.1.p: The birth of a man of great strength.

F611.1.1.r: *Types 301, 650; *Panzer Beowulf 16ff.; *Dickson 117 n. 48; *BP II 293, 300; Hdwb. d. Märch. s.v. “Bärensohn”; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 334ff.
F611.1.1.p: A very strong man is born to a bear that has stolen a human mother, so he has animal parentage and great strength.

F611.1.2.p: A strong man is born to a woman and a dwarf.

F611.1.2.1.p: A strong man is born to a woman and a forest spirit.

F611.1.3.p: A wild man is born to a woman whom a satyr overpowers and forces; he is the son of the satyr.

F611.1.4.p: A wild man is born to a woman who was overpowered by a robber in the forest.

F611.1.5.p: A strong man is born to a man and a she-bear.

F611.1.6.p: A strong man is born as the child of a human and a mare (a female horse), so his great strength comes from this unusual parentage.

F611.1.6.1.p: A strong man is accused of being the son of a man and a mare, usually as an insult or suspicion about his origins.

F611.1.7.p: A strong man is born to a human parent and a giant, so his immense strength is inherited from the giant side.

F611.1.8.p: A strong hero is conceived or born because his mother eats a particular fruit, which gives him great strength.

F611.1.9.p: A strong hero is born after being conceived by the wind, so his strength has an airborne, supernatural origin.

F611.1.10.p: A strong hero comes into being from a burning brand (a piece of burning wood), so fire is his origin.

F611.1.11.p: A strong hero hatches or is born from an egg, so his strength comes from this unusual birth.

F611.1.11.1.p: A strong hero is born from a noodle, a variant of the egg-birth in which a noodle serves as the origin.

F611.1.12.p: A strong hero is struck or formed by a smith out of iron, so his strength is made by a metalworker rather than born.

F611.1.13.p: A strong hero is the son of a man and a troll-woman, and the relations between them take place in a dream.

F611.1.14.p: A strong hero is the son of a woman of the sea, so his strength comes from a sea-dwelling mother.

F611.1.15.p: A strong hero is the son of a wood-spirit, so his strength comes from a forest supernatural being.

F611.2.p: The nursing or suckling of a strong hero as a baby, which gives him his unusual strength.

F611.2.0.1.p: A hero gains unusual strength by drinking his own mother's milk.

F611.2.1.p: A strong hero is suckled by an animal, which gives him great strength.

F611.2.2.p: A strong hero is suckled by a mermaid, which gives him the strength of twelve men.

F611.2.3.p: A strong hero is nursed for an unusually long time, which makes him strong.

F611.2.4.p: A strong hero is suckled by seven women, which gives him his strength.

F611.2.5.p: A strong hero is suckled by a giant, so he gains strength from the giant's milk.

F611.3.p: A strong hero acquires his strength in some way after birth, rather than having it from the start.

F611.3.0.1.p: A future strong hero gains his great strength by fasting for twelve years and eating nothing but earth.

F611.3.1.r: (Cf. F621.) Type 650; BP Il 287; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 92; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 435.
F611.3.1.p: The strong hero trains his strength by practicing uprooting trees.

F611.3.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 69, Snorra Edda Prol. III, *Boberg; Norwegian: Christiansen 92, India: *Thompson-Balys; Lau Islands: Beckwith Myth 483; Marquesas: Handy 105.
F611.3.2.p: The hero is unusually strong from a very young age, having full strength while still a small child.

F611.3.2.1.p: As a young child the strong hero drives a huge log into frozen ground with ease.

F611.3.2.2.p: As a baby the hero is tied to a millstone by a strap so he will not wander off, and he drags the heavy stone along after him.

F611.3.2.3.p: The precocious hero, while still a child, smashes an iron wall using only his fists.

F611.3.2.4.p: The precocious hero, while still a child, leaps across a river.

F611.3.2.5.p: A small child defeats a giant who challenges him.

F611.3.2.6.p: A twelve-year-old hero captures the town of his father's enemy.

F611.3.3.r: *Von Sydow Fâvne 22ff.; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo III 305, *Boberg.
F611.3.3.p: The strong hero tests weapons he is given, and he breaks the first swords he tries because they are too weak for him.

F611.3.3.0.1.p: The precocious strong hero, while still young, demands a bow and arrows for himself.

F611.3.3.1.p: The hero tests a sword by using it to cut a steer in two.

F611.3.3.2.p: The strong hero tests scythes, and every one of them breaks in his hands.

F611.4.p: A precocious, strong son saves his kingdom from danger.

F612.p: The strong hero is sent away from home, usually because his strength makes him a burden or a danger.

F612.1.r: *Type 650; BP II 293; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 92; *Fb “spise” III 495b, “æde” III 1140a; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “appétit”; Indonesian: De Vries Nederlandsche Tijdschrift voor Volkskunde XXX (1926) 97ff.; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 24.
F612.1.p: The strong hero is sent away from home because his appetite is enormous and his family cannot feed him.

F612.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; French: Cosquin Lorraine No. 52; N. A. Indian: *Thompson CColl II 334ff.
F612.2.p: The strong hero kills or overcomes his playmates, and for this he is sent away from home.

F612.3.p: The hero leaves home carrying enormous equipment suited to his great size and strength.

F612.3.1.r: *Type 650; *Cosquin Contes indiens 482ff.; *Fb “jærn” IV 249a; French: Cosquin Lorraine No. 52; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bâton”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXX 86; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 436.
F612.3.1.p: The strong man carries a giant walking cane that is large enough to hold fifty cattle.

F612.3.2.p: The strong man sets out carrying a giant hammer and a giant shield.

F613.p: A man of extraordinary strength hires himself out as a laborer, usually on a contract that the strength makes unusual.

F613.1.p: The strong man's labor contract ends with a single blow he is allowed to deal at year's end, and that blow sends his employer flying into the sky.

F613.2.p: The strong man's contract pays him all the grain he can carry, so he takes as much as his strength allows.

F613.2.1.p: A laborer's contract pays him as much money as his strong companion can carry, so the strong companion is the one who collects the wages.

F613.3.p: A strong man's contract is a contest of temper: whoever first becomes angry must receive the blow.

F613.4.p: A strong man is made to serve an ogre as punishment for stealing food from him.

F614.p: A remarkably strong man performs a range of heavy or destructive feats while doing ordinary work.

F614.1.p: The strong man drives an anvil into the ground with blows, as if it were a stake.

F614.2.p: The strong man pulls up a whole tree by the roots and uses it as a club or weapon.

F614.2.1.p: The strong man uses a pillar-stone, a heavy upright stone, as a weapon.

F614.2.2.p: The strong man uses a rafter, a roof beam, as a weapon.

F614.2.3.p: The strong man sinks an axe deep into a tree stump and pulls it out again with only his little finger.

F614.3.r: *Type 650; Finnish: Kalevala rune 31 (woods); Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 77 No. 650.
F614.3.p: Working as a gardener, the strong man destroys the plants by handling them too roughly.

F614.4.p: A man of great strength works as a rower and breaks the boat with his power.

F614.4.1.p: Working as a rower, the strong man pulls one oar so hard against the many oars on the other side that he breaks the boat.

F614.5.p: Working as a fisherman, the strong man destroys the fish and his nets.

F614.6.p: The strong man throws trees onto a roof so hard that he breaks it.

F614.6.1.p: The strong man throws a man back so hard that he breaks the man's bones, especially his legs.

F614.7.r: Type 1031; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21.
F614.7.p: The strong man uses the roof of a stable as a flail to thresh grain, breaking it apart in the process.

F614.8.p: The strong man fells a tree with a single blow of his axe.

F614.9.p: The strong man clears an entire plain of its obstacles or growth single-handedly.

F614.10.p: A very strong hero fights an entire army single-handed and defeats it.

F614.11.p: A strong man leaps across rivers in a single bound.

F614.12.p: A young man crushes coins into powder between his fingers.

F615.r: *Type 590, 650.—Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 143, *Cross; Hindu: Keith 173 (Krishna); Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 24; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 391.
F615.p: A strong man survives repeated attempts to kill him.

F615.0.1.p: The strong man is finally killed.

F615.1.p: A strong man is sent to the devil's mill and drives the devils out, herding them to his master's house.

F615.2.p: A strong hero is sent to catch or fetch wild animals.

F615.2.1.p: A strong man is sent to milk lions and brings the lions back with him.

F615.2.2.p: A strong man is sent to kill lions; he does so and frightens the king.

F615.2.3.p: A strong man is sent for wild horses and brings them back.

F615.2.4.p: A strong man is sent for bears and brings them back home.

F615.2.5.p: A strong man is sent for wolves and brings them back home.

F615.3.p: A strong hero overawes or intimidates his master.

F615.3.1.r: Sent to dig a well. Master throws the millstone on him. *Type 650; Fb “kilde” II 119a, “møllesten” II 650b; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; India: Thompson-Balys; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 112 No. 39.
F615.3.1.p: When the master tries to hurt the strong hero by putting a millstone on him, the hero simply wears it around his neck like a collar.

F615.3.1.1.r: *Type 650; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 435f.
F615.3.1.1.p: As his master drops a millstone on him, the hero complains only that chickens are scratching dirt on him, asking that they stop.

F615.3.1.2.p: Camels fall from the sky into a girl's eyes, and she tells her mother only that some grains of sand have fallen from the sky.

F615.4.p: A spear bends when it strikes the hero's chest, and he survives the ordeal unharmed.

F616.p: A strong man who is a champion boxer, able to win fights with his fists.

F617.p: A strong man who is a champion wrestler.

F617.1.p: A wrestler of extraordinary strength who can even wrestle an elephant.

F618.p: A man of great physical strength tames wild or dangerous animals.

F618.1.p: A strong hero breaks and controls a horse that no one else can handle.

F621.r: (Cf. F611.3.1, F614.2.) *Type 513; BP II 79ff.; *Fb “træ” III 867b.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “arbres”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 295 No. 13; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Dixon 90, Beckwith Myth 421; Samoa: Ibid. 254; Tonga: Gifford 127; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G 3/1323).
F621.p: A man of great strength who can pull up trees by the roots and carry them away.

F621.1.p: Animals that pull up trees by the roots.

F621.2.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “arbres”; Westphalian: Zaunert Westfälische 7, 8, 11; India: Thompson-Balys.
F621.2.p: A giant who pulls up trees by the roots.

F621.2.1.p: The giant Antichrist pulls up trees and plants them upside down in the ground.

F621.2.2.p: A giant cleans his teeth using a tree he has uprooted, as if it were a toothpick.

F621.3.p: A strong man uses an uprooted tree as an umbrella to shade himself.

F622.r: (Cf. X935.) *Type 513; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 432a n. 55.—Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 8, Rotunda; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “souffle”, “moulin.”
F622.p: A man with such powerful breath that he can turn a mill just by blowing.

F622.1.p: A mighty blower slows a princess in a race by blowing his breath at her, so that she loses.

F622.2.p: A mighty blower blows on a burning stick so sparks fly far, and blows sea waves back and forth.

F623.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “montagne”, “appuiemontagne”; Jewish: Neuman.
F623.p: A strong man holds up a mountain on his shoulders or with his hands.

F624.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Flateyjarbok I 523—24, MacCulloch Eddic 82, 93, Snorra Edda Prol. III, *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
F624.p: A man of great strength who lifts and throws heavy objects or animals.

F624.0.1.p: A saint who has the power to lift very heavy things.

F624.1.r: Fb “stærk”; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 250; Gaster Exempla 203 No. 92; Greek: Fox 100 (Theseus); Jewish: Neuman.
F624.1.p: A strong man lifts a horse, ox, or donkey.

F624.1.1.p: A strong man throws an elephant across the sea.

F624.1.2.p: A strong man throws a walrus.

F624.1.3.p: A strong man throws a leopard.

F624.2.r: Irish myth: Cross (F624.7); Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
F624.2.p: A strong man lifts a large stone.

F624.2.0.1.r: Greek: Odyssey XIII 184, IX 482, X 120, Iliad XII 381.
F624.2.0.1.p: A strong man throws an enormous stone.

F624.2.0.1.1.p: A strong man hurls a huge boulder or mountain-sized stone through the air.

F624.2.0.2.p: A strong man picks up and moves a very large rock.

F624.2.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “arracheur.”
F624.2.1.p: A strong man lifts a millstone, the heavy round stone used for grinding grain.

F624.2.2.p: A strong man lifts a large stone using only one hand.

F624.3.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “charrette.”
F624.3.p: A strong hero lifts a whole cart.

F624.3.1.p: A strong man throws a carriage, with its horses and driver still on it, onto a haystack, and the driver's ribs are broken in the fall.

F624.4.p: A strong man lifts a plow.

F624.5.p: A strong man lifts a ton of rye grain.

F624.6.p: A strong hero lifts an entire house.

F624.7.p: A strong man carries a boat or ship on his back or in his arms.

F624.8.p: A strong man throws his opponent high into the air.

F624.9.p: A little girl lifts and moves an enormous bow that no one had ever been able to carry before.

F624.10.p: A strong man carries a set of bellows, the device used to blow air into a forge fire.

F625.r: (Cf. X946.) *Fb “stærk” (bends horseshoe); Icelandic: Flateyjarbók I 524, Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “Brise-Fer”; India: Thompson-Balys.
F625.p: A strong man who can break iron objects with his bare strength.

F625.1.p: A hero drives a spear through seven iron plates stacked together.

F626.p: A strong man who can pull mountains down or flatten them.

F626.1.p: A strong man flattens a hill by knocking off or cutting away its top.

F626.2.p: A strong man kicks a mountain down.

F627.p: A strong man who can pull a building down.

F628.p: A strong man who is a mighty slayer, killing many enemies or monsters with his strength.

F628.0.1.p: A child who is strong beyond his years grows up to be a mighty slayer of monsters and beasts.

F628.1.p: A strong man kills wild animals using only his bare hands, without weapons.

F628.1.0.1.p: A strong man kills a monster by tearing its heart out.

F628.1.1.r: English: Child V 487 s.v. “lion”, Wells 151 (Richard Coer de Lyon); Hebrew: Judges 14: 6 (Samson); India: Thompson-Balys.
F628.1.1.p: A strong man kills a lion with his bare hands.

F628.1.1.1.p: A strong man kills a tiger alone, with his bare hands.

F628.1.1.2.p: A strong man kills a leopard, usually with his bare hands.

F628.1.1.3.r: S. A. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 687.
F628.1.1.3.p: A strong man kills a jaguar with his bare hands.

F628.1.1.4.p: A strong man kills a bear with his bare hands.

F628.1.1.5.p: A strong man kills a pack of wolves that are in the sea.

F628.1.2.p: A man kills an ox by striking it with the flat of his hand.

F628.1.2.1.p: A man kills a cow by striking it with the flat of his hand.

F628.1.2.2.p: A man grabs a wild steer by the horns, swings it round and round until it is dizzy, then throws it to the ground.

F628.1.3.p: A strong man kills a great serpent.

F628.1.3.1.p: A man kills serpents, toads, and dragons with his own hands.

F628.1.3.2.p: A child tears a live snake apart with his bare hands.

F628.1.4.p: A strong hero kills a water-dwelling animal with his bare hands.

F628.1.4.1.p: A strong hero kills many crocodiles with his bare hands.

F628.1.4.2.p: A strong hero kills sharks with his bare hands.

F628.1.4.3.p: A strong hero kills a walrus with his bare hands.

F628.1.5.p: A strong man kills a giant dog.

F628.1.6.p: A strong hero kills two elephants that have gone mad, using only his bare hands.

F628.2.r: Dickson 180; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
F628.2.p: A man of extraordinary strength kills other men.

F628.2.1.r: *Boje 103; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Judges 14: 19 (Samson), *Neuman; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 417, Rarotonga: ibid. 253; Africa (Upoto): Einstein 126.
F628.2.1.p: A very strong man kills many men at the same time in one blow or action.

F628.2.2.p: A strong man hurls one man off a wall so that he dies.

F628.2.3.r: Type 650* (Cf. F639.4.) Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Eskimo (Greenland): Holm 38; S. A. Indian (Cashinawa): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 686.
F628.2.3.p: A strong man kills a giant.

F628.2.4.p: A strong man commands or fights as part of an army made up of other strong men.

F628.2.5.p: A strong man kills men using only his bare hands, without weapons.

F628.2.6.p: A strong man kills many men with a hammer.

F628.2.7.p: A strong man swings a living man around and uses him as a club or weapon against others.

F628.2.8.p: A strong man kills a robber just by snapping his finger.

F628.2.10.p: A strong man cuts a horse and its rider in half with one sword blow.

F628.3.p: A strong man destroys or slays a spectre, which is a ghostly apparition.

F628.4.p: A strong man throws a spear or strikes a blow with a sword with tremendous force.

F628.4.1.p: A strong man drives his sword deep into a stone with a single thrust.

F628.5.p: A strong hero fights using several weapons at the same time.

F631.r: (Cf. F531.3.10, F624.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
F631.p: A strong man carries an enormous load that would be impossible for ordinary people.

F631.1.p: A strong man drags a whole mill away, carrying off the heavy grinding machine.

F631.2.p: A strong man carries off the gates of a city.

F631.2.1.p: A strong man carries off a door-frame together with the frame of a smoke-hole in the roof.

F631.3.p: A strong man swims across water while carrying fifty or many companions on his back.

F631.4.p: A very strong man carries an ox on his back.

F631.5.p: A very strong man carries a heavy oxhide in his hand.

F631.6.p: A very strong man carries a huge beam.

F631.6.1.p: Strong men knock on a door using a beam twenty elbow-lengths long.

F631.6.2.p: A man carries an eighteen-foot beam and at the same time clears a path through the jungle.

F632.r: (Cf. X931.) *Cosquin Contes indiens 427ff.; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 250.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 88, 93, Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 419; Tonga: ibid. 271, Gifford 172f.; Marquesas: Handy 42; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/620); S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 142; Africa (Fang): Tessman 117, (Wute): Sieber 117.
F632.p: A very strong man who eats enormous amounts, for example a whole ox at one time.

F633.r: (Cf. X932.) *Type 513; BP II 79ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Tonga: Gifford 159; Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 259; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 345ff.; Africa (Ba Ronga): Einstein 246.
F633.p: A very strong man who drinks enormous amounts, for example whole pools of water at once.

F634.p: A very strong man who fishes using a palm tree as his rod and an elephant as bait.

F634.1.p: A strong man bathing and diving in a river catches thousands of fish in his beard.

F635.r: (Cf. F934). Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5.
F635.p: A man who spits with remarkable force, for example spitting out a lake of soap.

F636.r: (Cf. F531.3.2., F624.0.1, F624.3.1, F624.8, F628.2.2, F628.4, X943.) Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1172; Hawaii: Beckwith 421; Samoa: ibid. 254.
F636.p: A man who throws things with remarkable force or skill.

F636.1.p: A man who throws iron with remarkable force, for example so that the field fills with scissors.

F636.2.r: Makes forest. Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5.
F636.2.p: A man who throws chips or wood fragments with remarkable force.

F636.3.r: Makes a river. Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5.
F636.3.p: A man who pours water with remarkable force or skill.

F636.4.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5; Jewish: *Neuman.
F636.4.p: A man who throws stones with remarkable force.

F636.4.1.p: A hero throws a stone into the air and, before it lands, drinks a full jar dry.

F636.4.2.p: A strong man catches stones that enemies hurl from catapults and throws them back at the besiegers.

F636.4.3.p: A strong man's thrown stone knocks away roof timbers.

F636.5.p: A hero catches a giant jug and tosses it about.

F637.p: A very strong man who holds a ship back.

F638.p: A man with extraordinary skill and strength as an archer, able to shoot far beyond ordinary limits.

F638.1.p: An archer shoots an arrow so powerfully that it flies about thirty miles up into the air.

F638.2.p: An arrow is shot and does not land until many years later, when it finally falls down.

F638.3.p: A man waits for a bird he shot eight days earlier to fall to the ground, because the arrow took that long to bring it down.

F638.4.p: A strong archer shoots an arrow so far that it reaches the otherworld, the realm of the supernatural beyond ordinary life.

F639.p: A miscellaneous group of stories about men with extraordinary strength or abilities that do not fit the other categories.

F639.1.p: A man with extraordinary digging ability, able to dig far more than ordinary people can.

F639.1.1.p: A strong man who digs tunnels with astonishing speed or power.

F639.1.2.p: A strong man pushes his finger into the ground so hard that water bursts out of the hole.

F639.2.r: Africa (Ziba): Rehse Zs. f. Kolonialspr. III 366f. No. 30, (Madagascar): Renel I 102ff. No. 15, (Malinke): Frobenius Atlantis VIII 145ff. No. 81.
F639.2.p: A strong man who can stay under water for an extraordinarily long time.

F639.3.p: A strong man throws his shield at a fleeing enemy and chariot, destroying both completely.

F639.4.p: A strong man defeats a giant in combat.

F639.5.p: A strong man kicks open a heavy door with his foot.

F639.6.p: A strong man tears a boat apart with his bare hands.

F639.7.p: A man squeezes twelve measures of oil out of olives or seeds by himself, without oxen to turn the press.

F639.8.p: A palace shakes when a strong man climbs onto its roof.

F639.9.p: A strong man crushes the ribs of a person he hugs.

F639.10.p: In anger, a strong man bites brass rods and spits them out as powder.

F639.11.p: A strong man grinds huge rocks into powder.

F639.12.p: Nine hundred horses pull the chariot in which a strong man rides.

F640.p: A person has extraordinary powers of perception, noticing or sensing things far beyond normal human ability.

F641.r: (Cf. X936.) *Type 513; BP II 79ff. *95; Fb “jord” II 45a; Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “ouie”; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5, III No. 8; Buriat: Holmberg Siberian 428.
F641.p: A person has remarkable hearing, able to catch sounds that ordinary people could never detect.

F641.1.r: *Type 513; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 432a n. 55; *BP II 95ff.; *Fb “høre” I 755b, IV 238b;—Icelandic: Boberg; Irish: Hyde Beside the Fire (London 1890) 23; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “avoine”.
F641.1.p: A man is so sharp of hearing that he can hear grass or wool growing.

F641.2.p: A man can hear an ant leaving its nest fifty miles away.

F641.3.p: A man can tell that someone is asleep by putting his ear to the ground and listening.

F642.r: (Cf. X938.) *Type 653; BP II 95, III 45ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 439; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 432b. n. 54; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 190.
F642.p: A person has remarkable eyesight, seeing things far beyond normal human vision.

F642.1.r: *Type 653; BP III 45, *57; Köhler-Bolte I 298f; India: Thompson-Balys.
F642.1.p: A person is an exceptional stargazer who can see birds sitting in a nest in a distant tree.

F642.2.p: A person with remarkable sight finds tracks of pigs that were stolen seven years before he was born.

F642.3.p: A person can see through solid, non-transparent objects.

F642.3.1.p: A person with remarkable sight can see through the hearts of trees.

F642.3.2.p: A wise man's keen sight lets him see a worm inside a loaf of bread.

F642.3.3.p: A blind man is able to see two unborn rats inside their mother rat.

F642.4.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 154, Boberg; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 886.
F642.4.p: A person can see just as well at night as in the daytime.

F642.5.p: A man can see heavenly nymphs dancing in the divine world.

F642.6.p: A one-eyed barber can see a thread of silk stretching all the way to the sea.

F642.7.p: A person with remarkable sight is able to see the soul.

F642.8.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 154, Boberg; Greek: Grote I 158; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 493.
F642.8.p: A person can see an enormous distance.

F645.p: A person is marvelously wise, far beyond ordinary human wisdom.

F645.1.p: A wise man is able to answer every question put to him.

F645.2.p: A man knows exactly how many grains are in a measure of grain.

F647.r: *Penzer VI 219, 288, VII 204ff.; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 265ff., *Boberg.
F647.p: A person with unusually sharp senses who can perceive things ordinary people cannot.

F647.1.r: Italian novella: Rotunda (J1661.1.8.); India: *Thompson-Balys, Penzer VI 288; Jewish: Neuman; Korean: Zong in-Sob 102 No. 55.
F647.1.p: Someone with extraordinary taste detects a corpse-like flavor in meat or wine, because the food came from something that had been near a grave.

F647.1.1.p: A woman with an extraordinary sense of taste notices garlic in a sauce made in a mortar from which the garlic had been removed.

F647.2.p: A person is physically pained just by watching someone else do work.

F647.3.p: A person is injured when a rose leaf falls on them.

F647.4.p: Women blush at the sight of a statue of a man.

F647.4.1.p: A woman refuses to look at a male fish out of modesty.

F647.5.p: A woman has a goat-like smell because she was raised on goat's milk.

F647.5.1.p: Someone detects from the smell or taste that meat is dog flesh, because the animal was suckled by a dog.

F647.5.2.p: Someone detects that food was grown in a particular kind of manure.

F647.5.3.p: A man recognizes the milk of his own stolen cows by its taste or smell.

F647.6.p: Wine can be seen passing down a woman's white throat when she swallows it.

F647.7.p: A person develops an ulcer or sore from the rays of the moon.

F647.8.p: A person faints from the noise of a wooden pestle and mortar.

F647.8.1.p: A person breaks a bone just from hearing a man chopping wood.

F647.8.1.1.p: A person gets a stitch in the side merely from being told about hearing a man chopping wood.

F647.9.p: A person gets a blister on the back from lying on rose leaves.

F647.9.1.p: A prince complains that he has slept on a beam, and a hair is found under the bedding.

F647.9.2.p: A man feels the tiny point of a simple thorn hidden in the middle of his clothes.

F647.10.p: A man refuses to eat the meat of a cow's fifth descendant, because he recognizes it as coming from his stolen cow.

F647.11.p: A person has such a fine sense of taste that they can tell that clarified butter was made from someone else's leftovers. It is a marvel of extreme sensitivity.

F647.12.p: A princess is so delicate that she can survive only on the scent of flowers and eats nothing else.

F648.p: A person can sense or communicate with wild animals at a distance, understanding their feelings or thoughts as if by mind-reading.

F651.p: A person has an uncanny ability to go straight to the nearest water source, even when it is hidden.

F652.r: (Cf. F647.5.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
F652.p: A person has an extraordinary sense of smell, far beyond what is normal.

F652.1.p: A man can tell who has picked berries just by smelling the berries.

F652.2.p: A man can smell pots boiling in a place about 400 miles away.

F654.r: (Cf. F692.) India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 908.
F654.p: A person has an extraordinary memory for faces, remembering every person he has ever met.

F655.p: Blind people are credited with an unusually keen ability to perceive things through their other senses.

F655.1.p: A blind man tests valuables and people by senses other than sight: he knows real pearls by smell, diamonds by touch, a good horse by feeling its ears, and a true noble raja by his generosity.

F655.2.p: A blind tiger identifies a man as a hypocrite just by hearing his voice.

F660.p: A person has exceptional skill at some task, often beyond what seems natural.

F660.1.r: *Types 653, 654, 1525; *BP III 10, 45ff., 379ff., 390 n. 1; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 7; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
F660.1.p: Brothers acquire extraordinary skill, which is then tested when they return home.

F660.2.p: A man who has no skill is made skillful by a holy man's blessing.

F660.2.1.p: A follower of a saint is miraculously turned into a famous preacher.

F661.r: *Types 304, 653; *BP II 503ff., III 45ff.; Fb “skytte” III 350a; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “chasseur”; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5, III No. 8, V No. 7; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1071.
F661.p: A person is an expert archer or marksman who never misses.

F661.1.p: A skilled marksman shoots meat out of a giant's hands without harming the giant.

F661.2.p: A skilled marksman shoots a pipe out of a man's mouth.

F661.3.r: Tell. *Hdwb. d. Abergl. s.v. “Meisterschuss Tell”; Fb “æble” III 1136a; English: Child III 17f., 28; Icelandic: Boberg.
F661.3.p: A skilled marksman shoots an apple off a man's head.

F661.3.1.p: A skilled marksman shoots a spear through a nose-ring, in the same type of feat as shooting an apple from a man's head.

F661.4.p: A marksman is so accurate that he shoots eggs scattered over a table without breaking them.

F661.4.1.p: An archer shoots an egg straight through its middle.

F661.4.2.p: An archer shoots and marks an egg lying in a nest without breaking it or disturbing the other eggs.

F661.4.3.p: A skilled marksman can hit an egg from a great distance.

F661.5.p: A skilled marksman shoots an animal, or a man, through the eye.

F661.5.1.p: A skilled marksman shoots a serpent through its left eye.

F661.5.2.p: A skilled marksman shoots a bird through the eye.

F661.5.3.p: A skilled marksman shoots the left eye of a fly from two miles away.

F661.5.4.p: A skilled marksman shoots both eyes of an ogre.

F661.5.5.p: A marvelous marksman can shoot the eye off a needle from a quarter-mile away.

F661.6.p: A skilled bowman shoots open the crater of Vesuvius.

F661.7.p: A skilled marksman throws needles so that one enters the eye of another, forming a straight line.

F661.7.1.p: A skilled marksman throws rushes into a curtain so that each one lodges in the one before it and stays attached.

F661.7.2.p: A skilled marksman throws swords and scabbards so that the swords are sheathed in the air.

F661.7.3.p: One arrow is shot into the end of the last arrow, making a rope of arrows.

F661.8.r: French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 18, Carrière.
F661.8.p: A skilled marksman casts a lance through a ring.

F661.8.1.p: A skilled marksman casts a lance through a hole in a leaf.

F661.9.p: A skilled marksman grazes the ear of a sleeping person, waking him.

F661.9.1.p: A husband shoots arrows that barely miss his wife's ears.

F661.10.p: A man shoots pearls from his wife's nose-ring.

F661.11.p: A skilled archer shoots an arrow that curves back around like a boomerang to return to him or hit its target from an unexpected direction.

F661.12.p: A hero shoots an arrow so precisely that it cuts a thread.

F662.p: A person who is an extraordinarily skilled tailor or sewer.

F662.0.1.p: A woman who is exceptionally skilled at sewing.

F662.0.1.1.p: A woman sews nine garments at once using only one needle.

F662.1.p: A skilled tailor sews broken eggs back together so they can hatch.

F662.1.1.p: Birds hatched from eggs that a skilled tailor repaired have a red line around their necks, showing where the eggs were broken.

F662.2.p: A skilled tailor sews scattered planks of a capsizing boat back together, saving it.

F662.3.p: A skilled tailor sews a bean back together after it has split apart from laughing.

F663.r: (Cf. F271.3.) *Fb “smed” III 402ab; Krappe Archiv für das Studium der neueren Sprachen CLX (1931) 166ff., CLXI (1932) 1—9; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
F663.p: A person who is an extraordinarily skilled blacksmith or metalworker.

F663.0.1.p: A skilled smith boasts that he is the master of all masters.

F663.1.p: A very skilled blacksmith is able to shoe a running horse without the horse slowing or stopping.

F663.2.p: A clever smith makes a needle sharp enough to pierce an anvil.

F664.p: A person who is an extraordinarily skilled at skinning animals.

F664.1.p: A skilled flayer skins a rabbit while it is still running.

F664.1.1.p: A woman skins a running deer.

F665.p: A person who is an extraordinarily skilled barber.

F665.1.p: A skilled barber shaves a hare while it is running.

F666.p: A person who is an extraordinarily skilled axe-man, able for example to fell a tree with one stroke.

F666.1.p: A skilled axe-man shapes spear shafts with only three cuts of his axe, and at the same time fits them into the spear-rings.

F667.p: A person who is an extraordinarily skilled swordsman or fencer.

F667.1.p: A master swordsman is so skilled that rain falling on him does not wet his sword.

F667.2.p: A swordsman is so skilled that he can strike every arrow shot at him with his sword and reduce each one to splinters.

F667.3.p: An expert swordsman slices a bag of clothes in two without damaging the clothes inside.

F668.r: Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
F668.p: A surgeon of extraordinary skill who performs operations no ordinary doctor could manage.

F668.0.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Africa (Konde): Gemuseus und Berger ZsES XXIII 151f. No. 13.
F668.0.1.p: A physician of extraordinary skill who cures illnesses beyond the reach of ordinary doctors.

F668.1.p: A skillful surgeon takes out vital organs from a person and puts them back, or replaces them.

F668.2.p: A surgeon removes a speck from a midge's eye in a single stroke, without hurting the tiny insect.

F668.3.p: A man is able to move a feather from one bird to another, grafting it onto the second bird.

F668.4.p: A skillful surgeon can tell, from examining a wound, which person or weapon caused it.

F668.5.p: A new arm is made for a person using an arm bone taken from another man.

F671.r: Irish myth: Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 7.
F671.p: A shipbuilder of extraordinary skill who can build boats far beyond ordinary craftsmen.

F671.1.p: A boat-builder works so quickly that he can build a boat in the blink of an eye.

F673.p: A man is so skilled or powerful that he can keep feathers together and unscattered even in a great wind.

F674.p: A painter of extraordinary skill who can paint a picture from someone's description of a dream.

F675.r: Penzer III 282—4, 296—300; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
F675.p: A carpenter of extraordinary ingenuity who builds remarkable and marvelous things.

F675.1.p: A king has a wooden peacock machine built for his son by a carpenter.

F675.2.p: Skilled craftsmen make a new moon to replace the old one.

F675.3.p: A carpenter builds a house of sandalwood that moves wherever its owner orders it to go.

F675.4.p: A skillful carpenter builds a large palace in a single night.

F676.p: A thief of extraordinary skill who can steal things that seem impossible to take.

F676.1.p: A thief is so skilled that he can eat food from a man's plate during dinner without the man noticing.

F676.2.p: A thief is so skilled that he can cut the soles off a man's boots while the man walks along the road, without the man noticing.

F677.p: A person with an extraordinary ability to follow tracks or trails.

F677.1.p: A tracker who never fails to follow a trail, whether it crosses land or sea.

F678.p: A person with an extraordinary skill at milking cows.

F678.1.p: A skillful milker who milks cows endlessly without stopping.

F679.p: A general heading for other marvelous feats of skill that do not fit the more specific categories.

F679.1.p: A herdsman of remarkable skill who sits on a mountaintop and summons cows from far away by calling them, and they come.

F679.2.p: A man can make a sword longer by twirling it between his fingers.

F679.3.p: A man can stand or walk on the edge or point of a weapon without being hurt, and can catch sharp blades without being cut.

F679.4.p: A man can stand upright on a barrel as it rolls down a hill.

F679.5.p: A person who is an exceptionally skilled hunter.

F679.5.1.p: A skillful hunter who is able to control and handle a pack of hunting dogs.

F679.5.2.p: A skillful hunter who can tell, just from the baying of his hounds, the order in which they come and what animal they are chasing.

F679.5.3.r: S. A. Indian (Yurakare): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 144.
F679.5.3.p: A hunter kills many tigers with a single arrow.

F679.5.3.1.p: A hunter kills seven stags with a single shot.

F679.6.p: A man with great throwing skill hurls a stone that catches the roof beam of a burning house and carries it away, thereby putting out the fire.

F679.7.p: A gambler who always wins, but who spends everything he earns the same day, so he never keeps any winnings.

F679.8.p: A person who is exceptionally skilled at playing chess.

F679.9.p: A skillful musician who plays nine mouth harps at the same time.

F680.p: A catch-all category for people who have extraordinary powers not covered by the more specific entries in this section.

F681.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 8; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: *Beckwith Myth 151, 337f.; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/928).
F681.p: A person with an extraordinary ability to run, far faster than any ordinary runner or horse.

F681.1.r: *Type 513; *BP II 79ff.; *Fb “ben” IV 32b; Buriat: Holmberg Siberian 428; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 345ff.
F681.1.p: A fast runner has one leg tied up so that he cannot run away.

F681.2.p: A marvelous runner is faster than the strong March wind.

F681.3.r: Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 190; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 81, 93, Boberg; N. A. Indian (Ojibwa): Michelson JAFL XXIV 249.
F681.3.p: A marvelous runner is as swift as a thought.

F681.3.1.r: Former wins. N. A. Indian (Ojibwa): Michelson JAFL XXIV 249.
F681.3.1.p: A runner as swift as thought competes with one who is as swift as sight, to see who is faster.

F681.4.r: N. A. Indian (Ojibwa): Michelson JAFL XXIV 249.
F681.4.p: A marvelous runner is as swift as sight, so fast that he is seen wherever the eye looks.

F681.5.p: A marvelous runner can run around the whole earth in five minutes.

F681.6.p: A marvelous runner can catch wild animals while running after them.

F681.6.1.p: A man is so fast that he can overtake a wild mare, seize her, and put a bridle on her.

F681.7.p: A marvelous runner can run backwards at great speed.

F681.8.p: A marvelous runner catches two of every kind of wild animal.

F681.9.p: A man who is too heavy for any horse to carry walks faster than people riding horses.

F681.10.p: A marvelous swift plower plows fields with astonishing speed.

F681.11.p: A marvelous swift mower cuts grass or hay with astonishing speed.

F681.12.r: Latin: Virgil Aeneid VII 807 ff.; Jewish: Neuman.
F681.12.p: A runner is so swift that he runs without bending the ears of wheat or the grass beneath his feet.

F681.13.p: A boy runs so fast that the snow he kicks up forms a rainbow behind him.

F682.r: Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 190.
F682.p: A man has the ability to stand on one foot all day long without tiring.

F682.0.1.p: A warrior manages to fight and act using only one leg, one hand, and one eye.

F683.p: A man's feet give off sparks, as if they were striking fire.

F683.1.p: A person's hands give off sparks or fire. This is one of the marvelous powers listed under people whose bodies produce sparks.

F683.1.1.p: A warrior can make fire drop from his fingers whenever he chooses to do so.

F684.p: A person with a marvelous ability to jump far or high beyond normal human power.

F684.1.p: A person with a marvelous ability to climb, able to scale surfaces that no ordinary person could.

F685.p: A person who can endure extreme cold without harm, far beyond what an ordinary person could bear.

F686.p: A person's body gives off a marvelous amount of heat. Its heat melts snow for thirty feet around and can be used as fuel for his companions.

F686.1.p: A cauldron is kept warm by the breath of nine maidens.

F686.2.p: A room is heated by the corpses of many people crowded together, which ghoulish ogres keep on hand for this purpose.

F687.p: A person has a remarkable or marvelous smell, whether pleasant or otherwise.

F688.p: A man whose voice has marvelous power, far beyond that of an ordinary speaker.

F688.1.p: A man's voice is so loud that it shakes the heavens.

F688.2.p: A man's shout lingers in the air for three days after he calls out.

F688.3.p: A person's voice can be heard across the whole land.

F688.4.p: Walls collapse because of a great shout from a man.

F691.r: *Ullrich Archiv für Literaturgeschichte XIV 69ff.; Irish myth: *Cross.
F691.p: A man can breathe under water for nine days.

F691.0.1.p: A hero fights a battle at the bottom of a lake that lasts a full day and night.

F692.p: A person who has an extraordinary memory, able to recall things far better than others.

F692.1.p: A whole epic poem is remembered after hearing it just once.

F693.p: Wounds inflicted by a certain man are always fatal, no matter how minor they seem.

F694.p: A saint can pass through closed doors without opening them.

F695.p: A person who can read in an extraordinary, supernatural way.

F930.p: Marvels involving seas or other bodies of water.

F930.1.p: A book dropped into water by a saint stays dry and is not soaked.

F930.1.0.1.p: A raging sea does not touch the cowl, or hood, of a saint.

F930.1.0.2.p: A robe sent to a saint who is standing in a stream stays dry.

F930.2.p: Waters rise up and drown a wrongdoer.

F930.3.p: The water sinks to the bottom while mud rises to the surface, so that a prophet is kept from drowning.

F930.4.p: Water turns to blood for one group of people but stays water for another group who are present at the same time.

F930.5.p: A stream or spring stops flowing once it is no longer needed.

F930.7.p: Water dissolves millstones, the heavy stones used for grinding grain.

F930.8.p: A chewed nut spread on water makes the water clear and clean.

F931.p: A general marvel in which something extraordinary happens involving the sea.

F931.1.p: The sea rises up and moves to a different place.

F931.1.1.p: The sea rises up and moves when a saint commands it.

F931.2.p: All the fish vanish from the sea as a punishment for a woman who washed a child with a fish.

F931.3.p: The sea does not spread over or erode the burial ground of a saint.

F931.6.p: People fish beneath the surface of the sea.

F931.9.3.p: The sea parts to form a separate dry path for each tribe, so each group can cross safely.

F931.10.p: The sea rises into a wall of water of enormous height, about sixteen hundred miles.

F931.11.p: The sea can speak, addressing people in words.

F931.12.p: The seas sing songs of praise.
