F960.1.1.2.p: A shower of gold and silver falls on the king's ship when his children are born.

F960.1.1.3.p: Storms reveal that a newborn child is of high or royal rank.

F960.1.2.p: Unusual natural events happen at the birth of a hero.

F960.1.2.1.r: (Cf. F962.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
F960.1.2.1.p: An unusual rain falls at the birth of a hero.

F960.1.2.1.1.p: A shower of lotus flowers falls at the birth of a hero.

F960.1.3.p: At the birth of a saint or holy person, a display of lights appears in the sky or around the place.

F960.1.4.p: At the birth of a saint, bells ring on their own, with no one touching them.

F960.1.5.p: At the rebirth of a hero, nature is shaken and the nine worlds tremble.

F960.1.6.p: When a girl princess is born, the whole earth fills with light.

F960.2.p: At the death of a holy person or hero, extraordinary things happen in nature.

F960.2.1.p: After a hero dies, the land produces no crops or fruit.

F960.2.2.p: At a saint's death, a rainbow reaches from the monastery up to heaven.

F960.2.3.p: When a hero dies, a rock suddenly bursts into flames.

F960.2.4.p: On the night a holy man dies, a great light appears in the sky.

F960.2.5.p: When an important person dies, the earth shakes in an earthquake.

F960.2.5.1.p: When a good man is murdered, an earthquake occurs.

F960.2.5.2.p: When a witch dies, an earthquake occurs.

F960.2.5.3.p: When a dragon dies, an earthquake occurs.

F960.2.6.p: At a saint's funeral, a winter day turns into a summer day.

F960.2.6.1.p: On the day of a hero's funeral, the sun shines for only two hours.

F960.3.r: (Cf. F1084.) Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
F960.3.p: During a furious battle, extraordinary things happen in nature.

F960.3.1.p: Nature mourns and laments when the Temple is destroyed.

F960.4.p: When a saint is angry, extraordinary things happen in nature.

F960.5.p: When a prisoner is miraculously released, extraordinary things happen in nature.

F960.6.p: On the night of a fratricide, which is the killing of a brother, extraordinary things happen in nature.

F960.7.p: Strange natural events, such as unusual weather or disturbances in nature, occur when an innocent person is cruelly treated.

F960.8.p: Unusual natural phenomena happen when a saint's remains are moved.

F960.9.p: An earthquake signals that a hero who has been away for a long time is returning in triumph.

F960.10.p: Extraordinary natural events occur when the Torah is given to Moses at Mount Sinai.

F961.p: Heavenly bodies such as the sun, moon, and stars behave in extraordinary ways.

F961.0.1.p: Several suns or moons appear in the sky at the same time.

F961.0.2.p: The sun and moon are eclipsed when they are near God.

F961.0.3.p: The heavenly bodies mourn or lament over something.

F961.0.3.1.p: The sun, moon, and stars stop shining for seven days in mourning for Adam's death.

F961.0.4.p: The heavenly bodies sing praise to God.

F961.0.5.p: The heavenly bodies testify for or against a person.

F961.1.p: The sun behaves in an extraordinary way.

F961.1.1.p: The sun refuses to shine when a murder is committed.

F961.1.2.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 164 n. 1; Jewish: Gaster Exempla 185 No. 2b, 201 No. 78, *Neuman.
F961.1.2.p: The sun travels from west to east.

F961.1.2.1.p: The sun goes back to sunrise to help a sick man.

F961.1.3.p: There are several suns in the sky.

F961.1.3.1.p: Two suns shine in the sky at once.

F961.1.3.2.p: Three suns shine in the sky at once.

F961.1.4.p: The sun warns a man that an assassin is approaching.

F961.1.5.p: The sun shines during the night, so that it is light when it should be dark.

F961.1.5.1.p: After a holy person dies, the sun keeps shining for twelve days and nights without setting.

F961.1.5.2.p: The sun goes down and then comes back up again after having set.

F961.1.5.3.1.p: The sun sets many hours later than it normally would.

F961.1.6.p: The sun does not shine at all on a particular island, which is home to druids.

F961.1.7.p: Through a holy man's prayer, the sun is made to move from one hour to another, such as going back or forward in time, as in the case of Moses.

F961.1.8.p: The sun appears blood red in color.

F961.1.9.p: The sun is eclipsed at the time of important historical events.

F961.1.10.p: The sun sets early so that a fugitive can hide from pursuers under cover of darkness.

F961.2.p: Stars behave in extraordinary or unnatural ways.

F961.2.1.r: *Toldo I 327; Matthew 2: 2; Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Babylonian: Spence 53.
F961.2.1.p: A bright star appears to announce the birth of a holy person.

F961.2.2.p: A star with a hairy, tufted appearance, like a comet, appears in the sky.

F961.2.3.p: A star is visible during the daytime.

F961.2.4.p: Stars and planets talk to people or to one another.

F961.2.5.p: A star that speaks aloud to people.

F961.2.5.1.p: The constellations mourn and lament when a man dies.

F961.2.6.p: Stars that fight each other have such heat that they melt iron chariots.

F961.2.7.p: One star swallows four other stars.

F961.2.8.p: A star travels across the sky from west to east, the opposite of the usual direction.

F961.2.9.p: When a magician performs a conjuration over a grave, stars fall down onto the grave.

F961.3.p: The moon behaves in some extraordinary, unnatural way.

F961.3.1.p: The moon turns red like blood.

F961.3.2.p: Several moons appear in the sky at the same time.

F961.3.3.p: The moon warns a sleeping man that an assassin is coming to kill him.

F962.p: Rain, snow, or other falling material from the sky happens in an extraordinary, unnatural way.

F962.0.1.p: Gifts fall from heaven or are received from it, such as flowers, roses, a golden crown, blossoms or thorns, bells, gems, books, or a sword.

F962.0.2.p: A storm knocks over an idol.

F962.1.p: An electrical storm splits an island into three parts.

F962.2.r: *Saintyves Essais de folklore biblique 1ff.; Irish: Plummer cxxxvii, cxxxviii, *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Moreno Esdras, *Neuman.

F962.2.1.p: A sacrifice is burned up by fire that comes down from heaven.

F962.2.2.p: A column of fire stretches from heaven down to earth.

F962.2.3.p: Fire from heaven cannot be put out with water.

F962.2.4.p: Fire from heaven both burns and freezes.

F962.2.5.p: Rain falls that is extraordinarily hot.

F962.3.p: A star falls from heaven and turns out to be money.

F962.4.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Marquesas: Handy 65.
F962.4.p: Blood falls from the sky like rain.

F962.4.1.p: A shower of blood lasts for three days and three nights.

F962.4.2.p: A repentant woman's fingers drip blood like dew.

F962.5.p: Hailstones of an unusual, extraordinary kind fall.

F962.5.1.p: A violent storm in which hailstones of enormous size fall.

F962.5.1.1.p: Hailstones fall that are each as big as a crabapple.

F962.5.2.p: Hail falls from the sky that is on fire, so the hailstones are burning.

F962.5.3.p: Hailstones that fall from the sky are shaped like triangles instead of round.

F962.6.p: Food of some kind rains down from the sky instead of water.

F962.6.1.p: Wheat falls from the sky like rain.

F962.6.2.p: Manna, a miraculous bread-like food, falls from heaven like rain.

F962.6.3.p: Honey falls from the sky like rain.

F962.6.4.p: Oil falls from the sky like rain.

F962.7.p: Dew that forms overnight is unusual in some extraordinary way.

F962.7.1.p: The dew that falls is sweet to taste.

F962.8.p: Other unusual kinds of showers that fall from the sky besides hail and food.

F962.8.1.p: Silver or money falls from the sky like rain.

F962.8.2.p: Precious jewels fall from the sky like rain.

F962.9.p: A saint gathers icicles to use as firewood, and they burn like wood.

F962.10.p: An unusually thick mist or darkness comes down over the land.

F962.10.1.p: A thick mist settles over a lake after a fight with a serpent.

F962.11.p: Snow that falls is unusual in some extraordinary way.

F962.12.p: A sacred or holy object comes down from heaven.

F962.12.1.p: A holy crozier (a bishop's staff) drops from the sky as a sign of a saint's sanctity.

F962.12.2.p: Altar cloths drop down from heaven.

F962.12.3.p: A wonderful painting falls from the sky during a storm.

F962.12.4.p: A written scroll or letter comes down from heaven.

F962.12.5.p: A mysterious leaf falls onto a church altar.

F962.13.p: Raindrops are as big as a man's hand.

F963.p: Wind behaves in extraordinary, unnatural ways.

F963.1.p: The wind serves King Solomon as a horse, carrying him wherever he needs to go.

F963.2.p: A strong wind turns arrows shot by Christians back against their enemy.

F963.3.p: A powerful wind bursts open the locked doors of a church, showing that a dead pope deserves burial there.

F963.4.p: A wind carries an ogre back to his castle.

F964.p: Fire behaves in extraordinary, unnatural ways.

F964.0.1.p: A column of fire appears in the sky.

F964.1.p: Fire bends a tree branch into the shape of a crozier (bishop's staff).

F964.2.p: Fire does not harm a saint's tunic, though the person wearing it is burned.

F964.3.p: Fire is kindled from an unusual or surprising material.

F964.3.1.p: Lamps that are magically lit burn with urine as their fuel.

F964.3.3.p: A dead body burns by itself, without any outside fire.

F964.4.p: A burning stick or torch keeps blazing even when it is dropped into water.

F964.5.p: A sacred or magical tank (pool of water) shines and glows with the color and brilliance of gold, as if it were on fire.

F965.p: Night falls early or the daylight suddenly goes dark, as an extraordinary marvel.

F965.1.p: Darkness falls in the daytime so that a maiden who is about to be executed is saved from death.

F965.1.1.p: Darkness falls early in the day when innocent people are about to be executed, sparing their lives.

F965.2.r: Usener Kleine Schriften IV 307; Jewish: Neuman; Icelandic: *Boberg.
F965.2.p: The sun goes dark when a holy person dies.

F965.2.1.p: The sun fails to rise on the day a hero dies.

F965.3.p: Darkness so thick that nothing can be seen through it.

F965.4.p: A supernatural darkness that cannot be lightened or driven away by lamps, torches, or other man-made light.

F966.r: *Penzer X 220 s.v. “Heaven”; Alphabet No. 800; *Loomis White Magic 53; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 314, 318, O’Suilleabhain 38, 49; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 I 367, *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
F966.p: A voice speaks from heaven or from the air, with no visible speaker.

F967.p: Clouds behave in unusual, marvelous ways.

F967.1.p: Clouds shelter and hide people who are fleeing from pursuers.

F967.2.p: Clouds that give off a sweet fragrance drifting down from paradise.

F967.4.p: A thin cloud shaped like a rainbow appears in the sky.

F968.p: Unusually violent or marvelous thunder and lightning.

F968.1.p: A violent electrical storm, with lightning, kills a thousand people.

F969.p: Miscellaneous marvelous natural phenomena that do not fit other categories.

F969.1.p: The sky splits open, revealing a company of heavenly beings.

F969.2.p: The earth rises up, as a marvel.

F969.3.p: A supernatural light appears, marking something extraordinary happening.

F969.3.1.p: A miraculous light shines and exposes a man who is hiding from a saint.

F969.3.2.p: A bright light glows around the head of a hero who has been driven to extraordinary acts of courage.

F969.4.1.p: The earth rumbles when a giant serpent is slain.

F969.4.2.p: A fight with a monstrous child makes the ground heave like ocean waves.

F969.5.p: Fields and farmland that were cultivated suddenly turn into barren desert.

F969.6.p: A sand dune grows up around a lover who is keeping watch until only his head is visible.

F969.7.p: A widespread lack of food and crops occurs as a marvel.

F970.p: Trees and plants behave in extraordinary, supernatural ways.

F971.p: Plants suddenly flower and bear fruit in a miraculous way.

F971.1.r: *Type 756 ABC, 757; BP III 463, 465, 471 n. 1; *Dh II 265ff.; Fb “nåde” II 726b, “stav” III 541b; RTP IX 504, XIII 505, XV 61, XIX 66, 336, 532, XXI 123, XXV 141; **Andrejev FFC LIV 34, LXIX 126, 129ff., 241ff.; Saintyves Essais de folklore biblique 61ff.; Zs. f. Vksk. X 196f., XIII 72, XV 393; Alphabet No. 568; *Loomis White Magic 94, 114; Goebel Jüdische Motive im märchenhafte Erzählungsgut (Gleiwitz, 1932) 34ff.; Irish: Plummer cliv, *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 108, Beal XXI 318, 334; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 186; Jewish: *Neuman; West Indies: Flowers 438.
F971.1.p: A dead, dry stick or rod suddenly sprouts blossoms.

F971.1.1.p: A dry rod blossoms on the night a saint is born.

F971.1.2.p: A switch cut from a tree, used as a witch's horse, sprouts blossoms.

F971.1.3.p: Moss grows overnight on a staff.

F971.2.r: Type 755; Fb “sten” III 554a, “rose” III 80a; P. Saintyves Le Thème du bâton qui reverdit (Revue d’Histoire et de Littérature religieuses, III [1912] 330—49, 421—54).
F971.2.p: A rose grows up from a table or stone.

F971.3.p: A thorn growing in a wound turns into a tree.

F971.4.r: Done at saint’s request. *Dh II 9; Alphabet No. 290; Irish: Plummer cliv, *Cross.
F971.4.p: A tree that normally bears no fruit suddenly produces fruit.

F971.4.1.p: An ash, alder, willow or similar barren tree bears apples, described as "fair fruit."

F971.5.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 686; Alphabet No. 475; *Pease Cicero De Divinatione 217 (U. of Illinois Studies in Language and Literature); Stier in Pauly-Wissowa XV (1932) 2026; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 102, MacCulloch Eddic 320; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
F971.5.p: Flowers bloom in the middle of winter.

F971.5.1.p: A saint asks for fruit, and it appears on the tree even though it is not the season for it.

F971.5.2.p: A tree bears apples only at Christmas: it blossoms at midnight and is loaded with apples by morning.

F971.5.2.1.p: On Twelfth Night, at midnight, the tree suddenly comes into blossom.

F971.6.p: When a saint strikes the ground, flowers spring up from the spot.

F971.7.p: Crops are sown and harvested on the same day.

F971.8.p: When God enters paradise, the trees there put forth leaves.

F971.9.p: A climbing plant blossoms only once every thousand years.

F973.p: Plants and trees are miraculously prevented from bending when someone passes over or among them.

F973.1.p: Trees stay straight and do not bend under a person's weight or passage.

F973.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 189.
F973.2.p: A person walks on blades of grass without bending them.

F974.r: Fb “græs” I 499b, IV 188a; Taylor Attila and Modern Riddles, JAFL LVI (1943) 136—37; Icelandic: Boberg.
F974.p: Grass refuses to grow in a certain spot, because an extraordinary event has happened there.

F974.1.p: Grass will not grow on ground where a murdered person's blood was spilled.

F975.p: A garden turns into a wilderness.

F975.1.p: A garden becomes a wilderness because its owner is wicked.

F975.2.p: After a persecuted queen is driven from the palace, the trees bear no fruit, the flowers stop blooming, and the birds stop singing.

F979.p: Miscellaneous extraordinary behavior of trees and plants that does not fit the other headings.

F979.1.r: *Loomis White Magic 80; Irish: Plummer cliv, *Cross; Japanese: Ikeda.
F979.1.p: A saint makes sour fruit sweet.

F979.2.p: A tree's leaves open and close to let a saint pass through.

F979.3.p: A tree's leaves make music for saints.

F979.4.r: Africa (Nago): Trautmann La Littérature populaire à la Côte des Esclaves (Paris, 1927) 6ff.
F979.4.p: A tree seizes a person and lifts him up into the air.

F979.5.p: A branch or bough, usually of a sacred or holy tree or bush, catches fire yet is not burned or consumed by the flames.

F979.5.1.p: A bush that burns with fire but is not consumed by it, so the flames never destroy it.

F979.6.p: A tree grows through the handle of a saint's bell, so that the handle becomes enclosed in the wood.

F979.7.p: A hollow in a tree closes over by growth, so that relics kept inside are sheltered and protected.

F979.8.p: A whole forest grows up from a single twig or from a few twigs.

F979.9.p: Flowers that have been pressed are miraculously turned into wine.

F979.10.p: A flower from the otherworld or Land of Promise miraculously appears to holy persons, such as saints.

F979.11.p: Trees spring up to mark the birth of a primitive hero, demigod, or deity.

F979.12.p: Trees grow up from blood that has been spilled on the ground.

F979.13.p: Trees hold a meeting or assembly, as a convention of trees.

F979.14.p: The urine of a grub or larva waters a tree and makes it grow.

F979.15.p: A tree drops all its leaves out of sympathy for a person or event.

F979.16.p: A magic tree lets a person take only two of its fruits, no more.

F979.17.p: Plants grow up without anyone having sown or planted seed.

F979.18.p: Grass grows back fresh again every night.

F979.19.p: An extraordinary tree holds up a devout man and his family, supporting them.

F979.20.p: A tree's branches lift upward when idolaters, worshippers of false gods, rest beneath it.

F979.21.p: A tree has two blossoms that sing.

F979.22.p: A tree acts as master of ceremonies, directing the proceedings while gods drink.

F979.23.p: Trees wither and dry up when tragic or sad events happen.

F980.p: A general heading for wonders involving animals, where animals behave in strange or extraordinary ways.

F981.p: A general heading for tales in which an animal dies in an extraordinary or unusual way.

F981.1.p: A serpent splits apart and dies in a sudden, violent way.

F981.1.1.p: An animal bursts apart because of its own anger.

F981.2.p: A bull melts away into nothing after an evil spirit has come out of its body.

F981.3.p: Animals are killed when a trickster breaks wind (passes gas), which is so powerful that it kills them.

F981.4.p: A bolt of fire falling from heaven kills a destructive animal.

F981.5.p: Animals are dissolved when ashes are thrown into a stream.

F981.6.p: An animal dies because its heart is broken by grief or sorrow.

F981.6.1.p: The heart of an animal that died of a broken heart is vomited or thrown up from its body.

F981.7.p: The king of the cats is killed by a glowing mass of iron thrown by a saint.

F981.8.p: A giant magic boar is slain by having its entrails torn out through its back end.

F982.p: A general heading for tales in which animals carry some extraordinary load or burden.

F982.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 388; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 12.
F982.1.p: Eagles lift a castle and carry it through the air.

F982.1.1.p: A great flock of birds lifts a greyhound and clothing up into the air.

F982.3.p: A hawk carries a man's hand to a saint who is displeased by the handclasp.

F982.4.p: A bird brings a flower from a faraway foreign land.

F982.5.p: A crocodile carries some extraordinary load or burden.

F982.6.p: A toad carries seven stone mortars balanced on its head.

F982.7.p: A toad is said to carry a whole tree on its back, a marvel showing how strong an animal can be.

F982.8.p: A crab is said to carry a cat, a tiger, bamboo plants and a river inside its ear, an absurdly exaggerated load.

F983.p: An animal grows to an extraordinary, unnatural size.

F983.0.1.p: An animal grows unnaturally fast, reaching its full size in a very short time.

F983.1.r: N. A. Indian (Tahltan): Teit JAFL XXXIV 229 No. 36, (Tlingit): Swanton BBAE XXXIX 151.
F983.1.p: A snail grows so large that it fills an entire house.

F983.2.r: *Type 621; BP III 483; *Köhler-Bolte I 134, *601a; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XVI 242 No. 23, XVII 229; Polívka Archiv. f. slav. Philol. VII 317 No. 65, XXVI 464; Sébillot France III 334 n. 4; Leskien Balkanmärchen No. 20; *Cosquin Contes indiens 529ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5; Algerian: Desparmet Contes Pop. rec. à Blida 407; India: Thompson-Balys.
F983.2.p: A louse becomes fat and swollen to an extraordinary degree.

F983.3.p: A cat grows as large as a cow within a minute.

F983.4.p: An ox's horns grow to an extraordinary, unnatural size.

F984.p: An animal is given unusual, magical protection or armor.

F984.1.p: A hero's horse is sewn into nine buffalo hides to protect it against a larger, stronger horse.

F985.p: Animals change their color in a magical or extraordinary way.

F985.1.r: (Cf. H1023.6.) Types 425, 428, 756C*; Andrejev FFC LIV passim; Boberg Classica et Medievalia I 1938.

F986.p: Marvelous events happen in connection with catching fish.

F986.1.p: Clerics (religious holy men) catch fish reliably, whenever they wish.

F986.2.p: Salmon are caught out of season to serve a saint.

F986.3.p: Salmon come to a certain place only once every seven years.

F986.4.p: Fish stranded on the shore do not rot for a whole year.

F986.5.p: Shores are flooded with sea fish, so that fish cover the coast.

F987.p: An animal determines the sex of its offspring by magic or extraordinary means.

F987.1.r: three under each wing and one under breast. The right wing hatches three red males, the left three green females. The egg under the breast shares the characteristics of both sex and color—but dies. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
F987.1.p: A bird controls the sex and appearance of its young, and hatches seven eggs.

F988.p: A general heading for marvels in which the limbs of animals behave in strange, unnatural ways.

F988.1.p: An ox's leg acts on its own as if it were a person, doing things a human would do.

F988.2.p: A horse's hooves fall off its feet when it becomes overheated.

F988.3.p: The openings in an animal's body are sealed shut when it is in a certain land.

F989.p: A miscellaneous category of marvels involving strange or wonderful events concerning animals that do not fit other groups.

F989.1.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “cheval”. Cf. Type 530.
F989.1.p: A horse leaps over a very high wall.

F989.1.1.p: A horse makes an amazing, tremendous leap.

F989.2.r: N. A. Indian (Maidu): Dixon BAM XVII 65.
F989.2.p: A bird's red eye is so intense that by staring at meat it heats the meat and cooks it.

F989.3.p: A bird that calls out the hours, like a cuckoo clock.

F989.4.r: (Cf. B557.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
F989.4.p: A man rides on the back of a wild boar while it is running away.

F989.5.p: Sheep are never attacked or harmed by wild beasts.

F989.5.1.p: Sheep turn on and kill wolves.

F989.6.p: Only one bull and one cow survive a plague that kills all other animals.

F989.7.p: Pigs kick trees so that their fruit falls down.

F989.8.p: An animal is made to feel mother-love, caring for young that are not its own.

F989.9.p: Milk from a saint's cows flows out and forms a lake.

F989.10.p: Animals divide up parts of a man's body as a prophecy foretells.

F989.11.p: A general heading for an animal that drinks an enormous amount.

F989.11.1.p: A cow drinks so much water that it lowers the level of the ocean.

F989.12.p: A sea animal is found far inland, away from any ocean.

F989.13.p: An animal dives into a lake and vanishes without a trace.

F989.14.p: Birds gather and hover over a battlefield.

F989.15.p: A marvelous animal of magical nature is hunted by someone, typically a hero or prince, who pursues it through the story.

F989.16.p: Extraordinarily huge flocks of birds appear, far beyond anything normal.

F989.16.1.p: A vast flock of quails appears and provides food for the Israelites.

F989.16.2.p: Swarms of birds are so dense that they block out the light of the sun and moon.

F989.17.p: A horse of unbelievable speed, far faster than any ordinary horse.

F989.18.p: A wild boar is caught and hung up in a spider's web, which is absurdly strong.

F989.19.p: A rooster has enormous ears made of silver.

F989.20.p: An egg transforms into a crowing rooster.

F989.21.p: A spider spins a web that stretches across the whole sky.

F989.22.p: Animals eat unusual or extraordinary foods that ordinary animals would never eat.

F989.22.1.p: Fowls eat gold and silver as their food.

F989.22.2.p: A tiger lives on food that cooks itself.

F989.23.p: A frog is able to pierce the hardest metals and even marbles.

F989.24.p: Frogs throw themselves into oven fires and then eat bread.

F990.p: Inanimate objects behave as though they were alive, moving, acting, or reacting like living beings.

F991.p: An inanimate object bleeds as if it were a living body.

F991.1.r: (Cf. D1086.) *Brown PMLA XXV (1910) 1; *Gaster FL II 57; Irish myth: *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 202.
F991.1.p: A lance bleeds, and a stream of blood flows from it into a silver cup.

F991.1.1.p: A knife bleeds, like the bleeding lance.

F991.2.p: A man cuts into a dry bone and it bleeds, as if it were living flesh.

F991.2.1.p: A dry bone gives off a smell that signals the dead person has forgiven someone.

F991.3.p: A cake bleeds when it is cut, as if it were living flesh.

F991.3.1.p: A loaf of bread bleeds when it is cut.

F991.4.p: A shrine or holy place bleeds, showing blood as a sign of something wrong or sacred.

F991.4.1.p: An altar that has been defiled or desecrated bleeds.

F991.5.p: A rock bleeds, as if it were a living body.

F992.p: A plant shrieks or cries out when it is pulled from the ground.

F992.1.r: Stark Der Alraun; Taylor JAFL XXXI 561.
F992.1.p: A mandrake plant shrieks when it is pulled up from the ground.

F993.r: *Sartori Zs. f. Vksk. VII 113, 270, VIII 29; England: Baughman; Finnish-Swedish: Wessman 72 No. 610; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3610.
F993.p: A bell that has sunk under water makes sound.

F993.1.p: A sunken bell rings only at certain times.

F994.p: An inanimate object shows sorrow or grief, as a person would.

F994.1.p: Books fall from their shelf to show sorrow when their owner dies.

F994.2.p: At the death of a hero, chariots, stones and weapons join in mourning and keening.

F995.p: A shield shrieks or cries out during a battle.

F996.p: Waters respond to the words of a poet.

F997.p: A sword pierces a rock when its owner intends to break it.

F997.1.p: A sword is addressed and spoken to as if it were a human being.

F998.p: A combat takes place involving a horse's sex organ.

F1001.p: Severed heads behave like living objects, acting on their own.

F1002.p: A silver hand that has been put in place of a real hand is treated as though it were flesh and blood, so it behaves like a living hand.

F1005.p: Cooked food that is planted in the ground sprouts and grows, as if it were a living seed or plant.

F1005.1.p: A cake is planted in a field, grows over time, and then bears more cakes as its fruit.

F1006.p: Mountains behave in extraordinary ways, as if they were alive and able to act on their own.

F1006.1.p: A mountain moves so that its rocks slide into the caves of another mountain.

F1006.2.p: A mountain moves over to a particular person, going to where they are.

F1009.p: A non-living object behaves as though it were alive, acting on its own or responding like a creature.

F1009.1.p: A doorpost of a room rises up to make way for a holy person, as if the object were alive.

F1009.2.p: A gate swallows axes that people try to use to force it open.

F1009.3.p: An altar shakes when a man who is not worthy is chosen for office or elected.

F1009.4.p: Twelve separate stones join together and become a single stone.

F1010.p: A general heading for other extraordinary events that do not fit the earlier categories of marvels.

F1011.p: A sunbeam serves as something to hold objects up, so that things hang or rest on a ray of sunlight.

F1011.1.r: Fb “solstråle”; De Vries Germanischromanische Monatsschrift 1922, 40 n. 2; *Loomis White Magic 29; Irish: Plummer cxxxix, *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 101, 106, Beal XXI 332f.; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 301 No. 19, 306 No. 19, 309 No. 10, 328 No. 6; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 146 No. 1805A, 1805B.
F1011.1.p: Clothes are hung on a sunbeam as if it were a line or hook.

F1011.1.1.p: A gospel-book hangs from a saint's shoulders with no strap or other support holding it.

F1011.2.p: A person sits or hangs on a sunbeam as though it were a seat or support.

F1014.p: A dice game goes on for nine years without ending.

F1015.1.p: A pair of shoes is worn out by supernatural means, without ordinary wear.

F1015.1.1.r: *Type 306; BP III 78; *Fb “sko” III 288b; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 39 No. 8**.
F1015.1.1.p: A girl's shoes are danced to pieces every morning, having been worn out by dancing through the night.

F1015.1.2.p: A woman walks so much that she wears out a whole carriage-load of shoes.

F1015.2.p: A person wears shoes only while crossing a river, and goes barefoot otherwise.

F1015.3.p: A bill of sale is written on a man's sandal.

F1016.p: A man carries an impossibly large amount of baggage or an absurdly oversized load.

F1016.1.p: A man hides his horse up his sleeve when he has no use for it, carrying it there until he needs it.

F1017.p: A man does the laundry while blindfolded.

F1021.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 91, 92; Jewish: *Neuman.
F1021.p: People fly through the air by extraordinary means.

F1021.1.r: *Type 575; *BP II 131; Penzer IX 149; Köhler-Bolte I 120; *Chauvin V 231 No. 130; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 139 n. 2 (Daedalus); India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Ferguson 35.
F1021.1.p: A person flies using artificial wings.

F1021.2.p: Some surprising effect happens to people or things because they fly very high.

F1021.2.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 139 n. 2 (Icarus).
F1021.2.1.p: A flier goes so high that the sun melts the glue holding his artificial wings together.

F1021.2.2.p: A flier goes so high that the cold makes his eyelids drop shut.

F1021.3.p: A man learns how to fly.

F1021.4.p: A man is kicked so hard that he sails through the air and is never seen again.

F1022.p: Someone descends into the ocean by an extraordinary means.

F1022.1.r: Jewish: Gaster Exempla 186 No. 5; bin Gorion Born Judas@2 III 136, 306, *Neuman.
F1022.1.p: A person goes down into the ocean inside a glass box.

F1023.p: A person is created through the combined skill of several craftsmen working together.

F1025.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 161.
F1025.p: Inanimate objects or creatures travel together on a journey.

F1025.1.p: A bean, a piece of straw, and a coal set off together. The coal sets the straw on fire and falls into the water. The bean laughs so hard that it bursts open.

F1025.2.r: N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 302 n. 108. Cf. Japanese: Mitford 185ff., Ikeda.
F1025.2.p: A turtle gathers a war party of strange objects such as a knife, a brush, and an awl, along with animals. Because of their natures, the companions get into trouble.

F1025.2.1.p: An eggplant, a needle, and cowdung set out on the warpath together.

F1031.p: A ship is wrapped in feather beds and canvas and thrown overboard or pitched into the sea so that it is saved from damage or sinking.

F1032.p: A person walks without stopping for a year.

F1032.1.p: A person wanders without ceasing for a hundred and fifty years.

F1033.r: Type 706; Irish myth: *Cross; German: Grimm No. 31.
F1033.p: A person lives for a year or longer without eating or drinking.

F1033.1.p: A person survives a year drinking only water from a holy well.

F1034.p: A person is hidden inside another person's body.

F1034.1.p: A husband hides inside his wife's ear.

F1034.2.r: Wesselski Märchen 186 No. 1; *Cosquin Études 276ff.; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 378 No. 109.
F1034.2.p: A magician carries his mistress inside his body with him; she in turn has a lover hidden inside her body.

F1034.2.1.p: An ascetic carries a woman hidden in his hair, but she has two lovers hidden in her cloak and outwits him.

F1034.3.p: A person hides something or someone in his or her thigh.

F1034.3.1.p: A man hides his sister in a wound in his thigh to protect her.

F1034.3.2.p: A bottle is hidden inside a person's thigh.

F1034.3.3.p: A garment is hidden in a hole cut into a person's thigh.

F1034.3.4.p: A jewel is hidden in a wound cut into a person's thigh.

F1034.4.p: A person hides something in his or her armpit.

F1034.5.p: Some other part of a person's body is used to hide something.

F1034.5.1.p: The key to a house is hidden inside a man's heart.

F1035.p: A man eats himself up or cuts himself into pieces until he disappears or is destroyed.

F1036.p: A hand comes down from heaven and writes a message on the wall.

F1037.p: An object is thrown down from heaven.

F1037.1.r: *Type 800; *BP I 342; *Hdwb. d. Märch. s.v. “Schneider im Himmel”.
F1037.1.p: A footstool is flung down from heaven to earth, an example of an object hurled from the sky by supernatural means.

F1038.r: *Type 755; H. C. Andersen “Skyggen”; Fb “skygge” III 347; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 133ff.; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 47 No. 325A*.
F1038.p: A person who has no shadow, a supernatural marvel in which someone casts no shadow.

F1038.1.p: A man goes to the devil's school to learn witchcraft and afterward has no shadow.

F1038.2.p: A man gets a witch's help in a reaping contest on the condition that the devil gets whoever finishes last. The devil tries to take the man but ends up with his shadow instead.

F1041.p: Unusual bodily reactions of people, where someone's body responds in a strange or extraordinary way.

F1041.0.1.p: A novice feels no pain when a saint's staff pierces his foot.

F1041.1.p: A death that is extraordinary or unusual in its cause or manner.

F1041.1.1.r: Penzer II 132, VII 24f., 103; Heptameron No. 9; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Grote I 134; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 439.
F1041.1.1.p: Someone dies of a broken heart.

F1041.1.1.1.p: A person's heart breaks and they die at the third drink from a silver canister.

F1041.1.1.2.p: A girl's heart breaks and she dies when she hears her lover kiss another woman.

F1041.1.1.3.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 439a n. 267; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 883.
F1041.1.1.3.p: Someone's heart breaks from sorrow and they die.

F1041.1.1.4.p: Two lovers' hearts break and they die when they are told their beloved is dead.

F1041.1.2.p: Someone dies from grief over the death of a lover or close relative.

F1041.1.2.1.p: A lover dies beside a sweetheart who is dying.

F1041.1.2.2.p: A woman dies on hearing of her husband's death.

F1041.1.2.2.1.p: A woman swoons and nearly dies on hearing of her husband's or lover's death.

F1041.1.2.2.2.p: The first woman in Ireland to die of grief for her husband.

F1041.1.2.2.3.p: A man dies on hearing that his wife has died.

F1041.1.2.2.4.p: A woman dies on hearing that her son or sons have died.

F1041.1.3.p: Someone dies from sorrow or chagrin, meaning deep disappointment or humiliation.

F1041.1.3.1.p: A maiden who has been wrongly accused seems to die of grief. She revives when she is being prepared for burial.

F1041.1.3.2.p: A servant dies of grief over his master's death, and in his sorrow he kills his wife and then himself.

F1041.1.3.3.p: A woman dies of shame when her secret love affair is made public.

F1041.1.3.4.p: A priest dies of sorrow after being tricked into a deceptive bargain.

F1041.1.3.5.p: A man dies of shock and grief when he learns that his wife has been unfaithful to him.

F1041.1.3.6.p: A girl's heart breaks when she learns that men have been killed in battle because of her.

F1041.1.3.7.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 69; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
F1041.1.3.7.p: A woman dies of a broken heart on learning that her former husband, whom she had remarried believing him dead, is still alive.

F1041.1.3.8.r: Cent Nouvelles Nouvelles No. 77; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
F1041.1.3.8.p: A man dies of grief over the death of his mother.

F1041.1.3.9.p: A person dies from excitement or shock on hearing news of Christ's crucifixion.

F1041.1.3.10.p: A man dies of chagrin because he cannot answer a question.

F1041.1.3.10.1.p: Guilty people who are confronted with their crimes become numb and motionless, like trees.

F1041.1.4.p: A person dies from longing for someone or something they cannot have.

F1041.1.5.r: Heptameron No. 9; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer VII 103.
F1041.1.5.p: A person dies from excessive joy.

F1041.1.5.2.p: A stranger dies of joy after being rewarded by a ruler.

F1041.1.5.3.p: A mother dies of joy on greeting her long-absent son.

F1041.1.5.4.p: A person dies from the joy of a kiss.

F1041.1.6.p: A person dies at the sight of a beautiful woman.

F1041.1.6.1.p: A person faints away at the sight of a goddess.

F1041.1.7.p: A man dies when he learns that a storm was caused by magic.

F1041.1.8.p: A person dies at the moment they see hell or its torments.

F1041.1.9.p: A person dies because of jealousy.

F1041.1.10.p: A person dies of illness caused by envy.

F1041.1.11.1.p: A person kills themselves out of fear of starving.

F1041.1.11.2.p: A person dies of fear of demons.

F1041.1.11.3.p: A person kills themselves out of terror at a prophecy of evil.

F1041.1.11.4.p: A man dies after a frog bites him, because he believes it is a snake's bite.

F1041.1.13.1.p: A girl dies of shame after being seen naked.

F1041.1.13.2.p: A woman dies of shame after seeing her naked husband.

F1041.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Hindu: Penzer I 120, VII 60, 139 n. 2, 179, VIII 46 n. 1, 94 n. 1; Korean: Zong in-Sob 83; Missouri French: Carrière.
F1041.2.p: A person's hair stands on end in an extraordinary way from joy, anger, or love.

F1041.3.p: A person becomes blind from weeping too much.

F1041.4.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Africa (Efik-Ibibo): Dayrell Folk Stories from Southern Nigeria (London, 1910) 84; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 263 No. 68.
F1041.4.p: A person melts away from heat.

F1041.5.p: The poison of the hydra eats away at the skin.

F1041.6.p: Buttons burst off clothing because of a violent emotion.

F1041.6.1.p: A necklace bursts apart because of a violent emotion.

F1041.7.r: *Chauvin VII 112 No. 379 bis n. 1; Korean: Zong in-Sob 81.
F1041.7.p: A person's hair turns gray from terror.

F1041.8.1.p: A person goes mad simply from seeing a woman of great beauty.

F1041.8.1.1.p: A person goes mad simply from seeing a man of magical, extraordinary beauty.

F1041.8.2.p: A person goes mad from grief.

F1041.8.3.p: A person goes mad from seeing a hideous ogre.

F1041.8.4.p: A person goes mad from thirst.

F1041.8.5.p: A person goes mad from eating too much.

F1041.8.6.p: Warriors become wildly frenzied and lose their senses in battle.

F1041.8.7.p: Warriors gone mad with battle frenzy rise up and fly into the clouds.

F1041.8.8.p: A person goes mad after hearing a prophetic voice speaking from the air.

F1041.8.9.p: A knight goes mad from regret at having abandoned his wife.

F1041.8.10.p: A person goes into a mad rage on hearing that his brother has died.

F1041.8.11.p: A person goes mad after losing his fortune.

F1041.9.p: A general category of unusual sickness brought on by a strange physical or emotional cause.

F1041.9.1.p: A person takes to bed and stays there because of sorrow.

F1041.9.1.1.p: A man stays in bed, grieving over his drowned son.

F1041.9.1.2.p: A king stays in bed, grieving over a bride who vanished.

F1041.9.1.3.p: A woman takes to her bed when she learns that her lover has died.

F1041.9.2.p: A person becomes ill because he is keeping a secret.

F1041.9.2.1.p: A young man keeping a secret gets a huge boil on his forehead.

F1041.9.3.p: A person falls ill from shame at being scorned by enemies.

F1041.10.p: A man's body reacts to great physical exertion in a marvelous way: he sweats blood, and hair sinks into his head.

F1041.11.r: *De Vries FFC LXXIII 213; Gaster Exempla 130 No. 352; India: *Thompson-Balys, *Bloomfield JAOS XXXVI 54—89, *Penzer VII 261; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 160 No. 43, 286 No. 78.
F1041.11.p: A person laughs and cries at the same time, for various stated reasons.

F1041.11.1.p: A person laughs out of chagrin, that is, laughs from embarrassment or vexation at a disappointment.

F1041.11.2.p: A man's complexion changes color (turning pale, red, or blue) because of strong emotion or physical strain.

F1041.12.p: A man sweats heavily in winter while telling of a frightening vision he has seen.

F1041.13.p: A person bites his own fingers to find out whether he is dreaming or awake.

F1041.14.r: (Cf. E783.) North Carolina: Brown Collection I 686.
F1041.14.p: A man who has been beheaded goes on to swim.

F1041.15.p: A person feels an intense, almost supernatural longing for something.

F1041.16.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 88.
F1041.16.p: A person's body undergoes some extraordinary physical change when angry.

F1041.16.1.p: An enraged man spits fire from his mouth.

F1041.16.2.p: When angry, a person's one eye sinks back into the head while the other sticks out.

F1041.16.3.p: A man, on hearing of the Crucifixion, is so enraged that he fells a tree with his sword, and dies.

F1041.16.3.1.p: Anger gives a man such strength that he breaks a binding chain.

F1041.16.3.2.p: Anger gives a man such strength that he breaks a stone.

F1041.16.3.3.p: Anger gives a man such strength that he tears his opponent apart.

F1041.16.4.p: A saint's anger is so intense that its heat sets his monk's hood on fire.

F1041.16.5.p: A warrior's anger twists his body into an extraordinary, unnatural contortion.

F1041.16.6.r: (Cf. F1041.8.7.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
F1041.16.6.p: Warriors in battle undergo extraordinary physical changes because of their fury.

F1041.16.6.1.p: In battle fury, a stream of blood rises up from a warrior's head.

F1041.16.6.2.p: In battle fury, a warrior grows larger in size.

F1041.16.6.3.p: When a warrior is furious in battle, pillars of fire shoot up in front of him.

F1041.16.6.4.p: When a warrior is angry in battle, his face bursts into flame.

F1041.16.6.5.p: When a warrior is angry in battle, his skin turns red and purple.

F1041.16.6.6.p: When an angry warrior is dipped into water, the water boils.

F1041.16.6.7.r: Die at end of battle. Irish myth: Cross.
F1041.16.6.7.p: A soldier who is badly wounded keeps fighting because of his fury.

F1041.16.6.8.p: The breath of an angry warrior heats his enemy's armour so much that the enemy has to surrender.

F1041.16.6.9.p: A bowstring, arrow or oar snaps when an angry warrior grips it.

F1041.16.7.p: A king is about to kill his foster son because the son gave an evil interpretation of a dream; the two jump into the sea and drown.

F1041.16.8.p: A person's face and body turn black from anger.

F1041.16.9.p: A chief beheads a sentinel who fails to recognize him.

F1041.16.10.p: A man in a rage throws his cereal and spoon on the floor because he has to eat together with his brother.

F1041.16.11.p: An earl in a rage throws a jar of water after a messenger he does not want.

F1041.17.p: Fear causes some extraordinary physical result in a person.

F1041.17.1.p: A woman or man becomes unable to have children because of a fright.

F1041.18.p: When a man presses his forehead, foul-smelling decay flows from his head.

F1041.19.p: A person becomes mute because of disgust.

F1041.21.p: Various extraordinary bodily reactions result from excessive grief.

F1041.21.1.p: A person falls ill because of excessive grief.

F1041.21.1.1.p: A person weeps tears of blood because of excessive grief.

F1041.21.2.r: Icelandic: Egils saga in ASB 3 (1894) ch. LXXVIII 14ff., Völsunga saga ch. 31 (29), Boberg.
F1041.21.2.p: A man swells up physically because of overwhelming grief.

F1041.21.3.p: A person becomes so grief-stricken that they refuse to eat.

F1041.21.3.1.p: A person becomes so grief-stricken that they refuse to speak, in the same way they refuse to eat.

F1041.21.4.p: A man bursts into tears on hearing that a friend has died.

F1041.21.5.p: A man is so stunned with grief on hearing of his father's death that he loses consciousness; while senseless, he cuts himself with a knife without feeling it, and another man presses dice into his skin until he bleeds.

F1041.21.6.p: A grieving person tears out their hair and rips their clothes in mourning.

F1041.21.6.1.p: A person wounds themselves out of excessive grief.

F1041.21.6.2.p: A grieving bird pulls out its own feathers.

F1041.22.p: People who are deaf and mute suddenly are able to speak.

F1041.23.p: A saint's head sends up smoke and his brow sweats profusely because of shame.

F1041.24.p: A slap spins a man's face completely around so it faces backward.

F1044.p: A man on the scaffold at his execution suddenly grows a long gray beard.

F1045.r: *Type 327A, 613; Icelandic: *Boberg; German: Grimm No. 163; India: Thompson-Balys.
F1045.p: A hero climbs into a tree and spends the night there.

F1047.p: An anchor floats on water instead of sinking.

F1047.1.p: Empty flasks or bottles that should not float rise to the surface of the water.

F1051.r: Usually by saint. Toldo II 96; India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 633; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 87, 260f.; Africa (Upoto): Einstein 127.
F1051.p: Someone weeps so prodigiously that the weeping is itself a marvel.

F1051.1.r: Ward II 664; Herbert III *341, 475; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
F1051.1.p: A barrel is miraculously filled with the tears of a penitent person.

F1051.2.p: A miraculously loud sound of mourning is heard for a dead hero.

F1054.p: Tree climbers take their bones out of their bodies temporarily so the bones will not break during the climb.

F1055.p: Books in a church are read aloud by themselves, without anyone's tongue or voice doing the reading.

F1057.p: A giant wades across the sea, with the water only reaching partway up his body.

F1061.p: A flame appears as a supernatural sign that reveals something hidden or important.

F1061.1.r: (Cf. F1041.8.1. and cross references.) Malay, Indonesian: Dixon 222 n. 26.
F1061.1.p: A flame shows that a beautiful woman is nearby.

F1061.2.p: The color of a flame tells what is burning: blue for furniture, white for money, red for a person.

F1061.3.p: A burning pit will not go out or close until an armed rider plunges into it.

F1061.4.p: A flame shows the place where an innocent person was murdered.

F1063.r: N. A. Indian: Kroeber JAFL XXI 224.
F1063.p: A hero leaves a place and takes his entire house along with him when he departs.

F1065.p: A man pulls two blind women up out of a well with his fishing line.

F1066.r: Hdwb. d. Märch. I 102a; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
F1066.p: An arrow shot up into the sky comes back down covered in blood.

F1066.1.p: A knife plunged into the earth comes back out bloody.

F1068.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 107, Beal XXI 334; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
F1068.p: A dream is so realistic that it has real effects on the dreamer's waking life.

F1068.1.p: A man brings back real objects that he was given during a dream.

F1068.2.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 222f., 534 nn. 90—97; Alphabet No. 299; Icelandic: Boberg; England: Baughman.
F1068.2.p: A person is wounded in a dream and the wound is still there when they wake up.

F1068.2.1.p: A man is beaten or mistreated in a dream and feels the pain the next day.

F1068.2.2.p: A man fights in a dream and the fight has real results when he wakes.

F1071.r: Type 530; Cosquin Contes indiens 333ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Philippine (Tinguian): Cole 103; Marquesas: Handy 114; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/499).
F1071.p: A person makes an extraordinarily long jump, for example up to the fourth story of a building.

F1071.1.p: A person crosses a river by using a fig tree whose branches reach to the opposite bank.

F1071.2.p: A person jumps over what looks like a small ditch but is really a vast ocean.

F1071.2.1.p: A man clears a river of enormous width in a single leap.

F1072.p: Two unrelated children of opposite sexes look so alike that even their own parents cannot tell them apart.

F1073.p: A woman who has been widowed twenty-two times marries a man who has been widowed twenty times, a marriage of two very experienced widows and widowers.

F1075.p: The blood of a brother and sister refuses to mix, and even the smoke from their funeral pyres stays apart.

F1076.p: A person tightens a belt to stop feeling hungry, and when the belt is loosened they fall dead.

F1078.p: Striking a spark to light a fire sets off a huge explosion that hurls ships far out to sea.

F1081.p: A tub of water is dropped, yet it neither breaks nor spills.

F1082.p: A person's skin or complexion changes color through a marvelous cause.

F1082.1.p: A person's face is red and black after being burned.

F1083.p: An object rises up into the air without visible support.

F1083.0.1.p: An object hangs or floats in the air rather than resting on the ground.

F1083.0.1.1.p: An altar floats in the air.

F1083.0.1.2.p: An ark hangs suspended in the air.

F1083.0.1.3.p: The city of Jerusalem hangs suspended in the air.

F1083.1.p: A stone cross rises up into the air.

F1083.2.p: A man and his camels rise up into the air.

F1084.p: A fierce, violent battle takes place, marked by extraordinary events.

F1084.0.1.p: A decoration set into a sword melts out from the heat produced when the blade strikes something.

F1084.0.2.p: In a furious battle, weapons are caught and held by nets made of flying hair.

F1084.0.3.p: The fighting goes on continuously, with the combatants getting no rest or food.

F1084.0.4.p: Marks left behind by a furious battle are still visible in solid rock.

F1084.1.p: During a fierce battle, blood flows in deep streams across the ground.

F1084.2.p: Warriors who have run out of weapons keep fighting by biting their enemies with their teeth.

F1084.3.p: Soldiers fight so closely packed together that the force of their struggle pushes a river out of its bed.

F1085.p: A person strains their voice so hard that one of their eyes bursts out of its socket.

F1086.p: A saint preaches continuously for three days and three nights without stopping.

F1087.p: A hero's magical sword falls on an enemy and cuts off the enemy's hand.

F1088.p: A general heading for extraordinary escapes, where a character survives a danger that should have killed them.

F1088.1.p: A hero or heroine is spared from death because of their great beauty.

F1088.2.p: A hero is unharmed when a serpent coils around his waist.

F1088.3.r: Icelandic: Snorra Edda Gylf. XLI, Boberg; Danish: Schmidt DF XXXIX 44ff.; Maori: Clark 29.
F1088.3.p: A character escapes from drowning in an extraordinary way.

F1088.3.1.p: Clerics and their property are miraculously carried safely to shore when enemies try to drown them.

F1088.3.2.p: A fisherman is dragged through the sea by a seal but escapes.

F1088.4.p: An animal escapes danger by slipping out of its skin.

F1091.p: Food placed on a saint's clothing does not spoil.

F1092.p: A vessel of poisoned ale is turned upside down, and only the poison pours out, leaving the ale inside.

F1093.p: A stake is miraculously bent during the night.

F1094.p: Milk tastes like wine and honey.

F1095.p: A person's arm grows longer as a reward for giving alms to the poor.

F1096.p: A person keeps living after being cut completely through by a sword.

F1096.1.p: A person keeps living after their heart has been cut out, and the heart moves around inside their chest.

F1096.2.p: A person continues to live even though their intestines hang out of their body after being cut open by a sword.

F1096.3.p: A person's head, cut off from the body, still bites the ground.

F1097.p: Miraculous supernatural force keeps two armies from fighting or coming together for battle.

F1097.1.p: An angel orders two armies not to come near each other, so they cannot fight.

F1098.p: A broken object is restored to wholeness by a miracle.

F1098.0.1.p: An object is broken by a miracle rather than by ordinary means.

F1099.p: A general heading for other miraculous events that do not fit elsewhere in this group of marvels.

F1099.1.p: Every member of a household dies on the same night.

F1099.2.p: Roads miraculously appear on Hallowe'en night.

F1099.2.1.p: Roads miraculously appear on the day a hero is born.

F1099.3.p: People hear words that were only thought silently, never spoken aloud.

F1099.4.p: Corn sprouts and takes root in a man's hair.

F1099.4.1.p: Stalks of corn grow through the hair of a saint as a reward for guarding a corn kiln.

F1099.6.p: A field is plowed by extraordinary, supernatural means.

F1099.6.1.p: A field is plowed using teeth instead of an ordinary plow or oxen.

F1099.7.p: Pious people die on their birthday.

F1099.8.p: A man meets his future descendants, who give him instruction.
